2026-10-02.title: PROMO: Preference-conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Robots
2026-10-02.authors: Amr Mousa , Rifny Rachman , Neil Karavis , Michele Caprio , Richard Allmendinger
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-02.comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Project website, code, and videos: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
Quadrupedal locomotion requires balancing conflicting objectives such as command tracking, stability, and energy efficiency, yet conventional reinforcement learning (RL) hard-codes these priorities into a fixed scalar reward at training time.
We present PROMO (Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning), a semantic multi-objective framework that makes this trade-off an explicit runtime input to a single locomotion policy. PROMO conditions the policy on deployment-facing preferences while keeping embodiment-specific locomotion priors fixed, thereby separating operator intent from reward-shaping terms required for viable gait generation.
Compared with fixed-objective controllers, multi-objective baselines, and independently trained specialists, PROMO achieves objective specialization and robustness from a single deployable policy.
Across 100 100 sampled preferences in simulation, 67 67 behaviors are non-dominated under exact Pareto dominance, with a mean preference–objective correlation of 0.843 0.843 , demonstrating broad Pareto coverage and predictable preference response.
The same policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree Go2, where preference changes alone reduce specific energy by up to 30.4 % 30.4\% , position error by 38.7 % 38.7\% , and peak body-attitude deviation by 59.0 % 59.0\% relative to the balanced preference.
These results establish preference-conditioned multi-objective RL as a practical runtime interface for adaptive legged locomotion, extending its role beyond offline Pareto-set construction.
Open-source code and videos are available at https://amrmousa.com/promo/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robotic locomotion via rl ( rl ) has moved quadrupeds from controlled demonstrations toward agile and deployable systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Most learned controllers, however, optimize a scalar reward that fixes the trade-off among command tracking, stability, energy efficiency, and locomotion regularization. This is restrictive in long-horizon autonomy, where terrain, payload, mission urgency, operator intent, or hardware state can change which objective should dominate.

After training, a robot can receive new motion commands, but the objective trade-off governing how those commands are executed remains locked. Changing that trade-off usually requires a reward redesign, policy retraining, or controller switching. The deployment challenge is therefore to learn robust locomotion while making the underlying objective priorities selectable after training.

morl ( morl ) provides a principled basis for adapting trade-offs by representing distinct objectives through vector-valued rewards and optimizing their utility under a preference [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, directly treating locomotion reward terms as independent objectives creates a fundamental mismatch with learned locomotion. Robotic rewards typically combine many shaping terms for posture, contact timing, smoothness, joint limits, and other requirements for viable motion [ 2 , 3 , 7 ] . Making each term an objective yields a high-dimensional Pareto space that becomes harder to optimize as dimensionality grows [ 8 ] , while exposing low-level coefficients that do not express behavioral intent.

This objective-definition problem is central to deployable robotic morl : the optimized dimensions need not coincide with the components used to shape a robust controller. We therefore separate a compact semantic objective vector—tracking, stability, and efficiency—from fixed locomotion priors. This keeps embodiment-specific requirements internal to the controller and makes the preference vector a meaningful runtime interface rather than a reformulation of the full reward function.

Behavior-conditioned locomotion addresses flexibility through a different interface. Methods such as Walk These Ways [ 9 ] expose gait descriptors that specify how the robot should move through morphology, timing, or stance parameters. Preference-conditioned control instead specifies what the robot should prioritize, leaving the physical gait realization to the policy. This distinction matters for deployment: semantic preferences should retain their meaning across commands, disturbances, and operating conditions rather than become handcrafted gait-tuning variables.

These observations motivate promo ( promo ), a preference-conditioned morl framework that turns a fixed reward trade-off into a runtime semantic behavior interface . A single policy is conditioned on preferences over three deployment-facing objectives—tracking, stability, and efficiency—while embodiment-specific locomotion priors remain fixed.

The resulting preference vector is both a deployment-time control input and an interpretable representation of behavioral intent. Rather than manipulating latent gait codes or implementation-level reward weights, the operator specifies why behavior should change—for example, by prioritizing stability over tracking—and the policy learns how to realize that trade-off.

We evaluate whether this interface is controllable in simulation and remains preference-responsive after zero-shot transfer to hardware. In simulation, promo remains competitive at the balanced operating point while providing tracking, stability, and efficiency specialization from a single policy, with lower failure rates than the evaluated preference-conditioned and specialist baselines. A dense 100-preference study shows that these anchor behaviors lie within a broader controllable interface. On a Unitree Go2, changing only the preference produces large, directionally consistent changes in tracking, stability, and energy efficiency across five trials per condition. To our knowledge, this is the first real demonstration of semantic preference-conditioned morl on a robotic platform, moving morl from offline Pareto optimization toward an operator-facing mechanism for adaptive robot behavior.

Our core contributions are:

A semantic locomotion interface. We formulate runtime-adjustable quadruped control as preference-conditioned morl over tracking, stability, and efficiency, making the objective trade-off an explicit deployment-time input that represents operator intent.

Objective/prior factorization for controllable locomotion. We address the mismatch between vector-valued morl objectives and dense robotic reward design by separating operator-facing semantic objectives from fixed embodiment-level locomotion priors. Ablations show that this factorization is critical for controllability and reliability: the fixed-prior formulation attains a 6 % 6\% fall rate under challenging evaluation conditions, whereas alternative designs increase it to as much as 21.8 % 21.8\% and degrade preference controllability.

Zero-shot semantic morl on a real quadruped. We provide, to our knowledge, the first real-robot demonstration of semantic preference-conditioned morl for locomotion. A single policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree Go2 and modulates tracking, stability, and efficiency through preference alone. Relative to a balanced configuration, preference modulation reduces specific energy by up to 30.4 % 30.4\% , position error by up to 38.7 % 38.7\% , and peak body-attitude deviation by up to 59.0 % 59.0\% .

Open-source implementation and complete experimental suite. We release the implementation of promo together with all evaluated baselines, experimental tasks, evaluation protocols, and ablation studies, enabling reproduction of the complete experimental pipeline and facilitating future benchmarking and extensions.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III formulates promo and describes its training and deployment. Sections IV and V evaluate the framework in simulation and on the Unitree Go2 robot, respectively. Section VI discusses the implications and limitations, and Section VII concludes the paper.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learned Quadruped Locomotion

rl -based locomotion has made quadruped control increasingly robust to sim-to-real transfer, partial observability, and environmental uncertainty. Actuator modeling [ 10 ] , domain randomization [ 11 ] , privileged adaptation [ 1 ] , massively parallel training [ 2 ] , perception-aware control [ 3 , 12 ] , implicit adaptation [ 13 , 14 ] , and teacher-aligned representations [ 7 ] have enabled reliable deployment under challenging conditions. Most controllers nevertheless remain sorl ( sorl ) policies: commands and observations may change at runtime, but the reward-level priority among tracking, stability, efficiency, and regularization is fixed.

This raises a question: which parts of the locomotion objective should remain fixed, and which should be exposed for runtime adaptation?

## II-B Reward Design and Runtime Behavioral Interfaces

Modern locomotion rewards mix task objectives with posture regulation, contact shaping, actuator smoothness, joint-limit penalties, and other embodiment-specific terms [ 2 , 3 , 7 ] . These dense components suppress different failure modes and collectively shape viable motion, but they do not all represent objectives over which an operator should express a preference. Treating contact regularity, posture, or action smoothness as independent objectives would expose reward-engineering decisions as deployment controls and enlarge the preference space whenever another shaping term is introduced. Reward shaping [ 15 ] , constrained rl [ 16 ] , constrained morl [ 17 ] , and inverse reward design [ 18 ] similarly distinguish task objectives from auxiliary signals or constraints. promo operationalizes this distinction through semantic objective/prior factorization: task-level trade-offs define the preference vector, whereas embodiment-level requirements remain fixed locomotion priors.

Runtime flexibility can also be achieved through behavior conditioning [ 9 , 19 , 20 ] . These methods show that one policy can span diverse behaviors through operator-controlled gait variables, but the interface primarily specifies how the robot should move through morphology or timing. Semantic preference conditioning instead specifies what the robot should prioritize.

This shifts the problem from commanding behaviors to trading off objectives: how can a single policy realize a continuum of semantic preferences?

## II-C MORL Preference Conditioning

morl formalizes control with multiple conflicting objectives through vector-valued returns [ 4 ] , scalarization and utility theory [ 6 ] , and Pareto optimality [ 5 ] . The algorithmic literature includes Pareto-front approximation [ 21 ] , decomposition [ 22 ] , constrained optimization [ 23 ] , diversity-driven coverage [ 24 ] , and preference-conditioned policy learning [ 25 , 26 ] . Standardized frameworks such as MO-Gymnasium and MORL-Baselines support systematic comparison [ 27 , 28 ] .

Preferences may be introduced a priori, a posteriori, or interactively, and expressed through weights, reference points, or solution comparisons [ 29 ] . A fixed a priori weight vector yields one scalarized solution; promo instead learns a weight-conditioned approximation of the supported Pareto front, enabling a posteriori behavior selection at deployment.

Preference-conditioned single-policy methods are attractive for deployment because one policy can represent a continuum of trade-offs. They are based on universal value function approximation [ 30 ] and reward-conditioned rl [ 31 , 32 ] . In our evaluation, moppo ( moppo ) provides a single-policy preference-conditioned ppo ( ppo ) baseline [ 33 ] , whereas dpmorl ( dpmorl ) represents a multi-policy route to Pareto-front approximation [ 34 ] .

Robotics applications remain comparatively limited, including prediction-guided multi-objective continuous control [ 21 ] , constrained robot control [ 35 ] , and gradient-conflict resolution [ 36 ] . These works establish the relevance of morl to robotics, but do not address how preference-conditioned optimization should be formulated and deployed for contact-rich legged robots.

This leaves an interface-level question: does learning a broad Pareto set make preferences useful as deployment-time controls?

## II-D From Pareto Coverage to Behavioral Control

Standard morl benchmarks ignore failures, dense reward structure, embodiment-specific priors, sim-to-real transfer, and hardware deployment. Strong Pareto performance therefore does not necessarily imply that preferences provide a reliable control interface on a physical robot.

Hypervolume is the principal Pareto-front approximation metric used in our study. It is Pareto compliant and measures the objective-space volume dominated by an approximation set and bounded by a reference point, summarizing convergence and diversity [ 37 ] . However, it does not establish whether changing a preference predictably changes behavior. Recent work therefore considers preference sensitivity, monotonicity, objective alignment, and behavioral consistency [ 38 , 39 , 40 ] . A policy may approximate a broad Pareto front while still providing an unreliable interface if preferences map inconsistently to realized behaviors.

For physical deployment, Pareto quality must be evaluated together with preference controllability, robustness, and semantic interpretability. promo combines semantic objective specification, preference-conditioned control, locomotion-specific priors, interface-oriented evaluation, and physical deployment in a single framework.

2026-10-02.title: ColoACT: Multi-Cue Action Chunking for Smooth Autonomous Colon Navigation on a Self-Propelled Endoscopic Robot
2026-10-02.authors: Jian Hu , Shujing He , Leixin Chang , Zongze Li , Ding Huang , Chaoyang Shi , Chengzhi Hu
2026-10-02.abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different ex-vivo porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4% and 72.5% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70% success in 90-degree turns and 60% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Endoscopic examination remains the gold standard for the prevention and early diagnosis of colorectal diseases [ 1 ] . While traditional colonoscopy is widely adopted, it still suffers from a steep learning curve, limited automation, and risks of loop formation or tissue trauma during navigation [ 2 ] . Robotic endoscopic systems are therefore being explored to improve navigational safety and consistency [ 3 ] , and to reduce the cognitive and physical burden on physicians.

Autonomous colonoscopic navigation is challenging due to large anatomical variability with frequent bends and collapses [ 4 ] , weak texture and specular highlights, and strongly nonlinear, time-varying interactions [ 5 ] between the endoscope and viscoelastic tissue [ 6 ] . These factors demand a closed-loop policy that is robust under imperfect perception and contact disturbances while producing smooth, stable motion. Existing robotic navigation solutions fall into geometry-driven pipelines [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] and learning-based approaches [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Geometry-driven methods are often efficient and interpretable, but their reliance on manually engineered features and switching logic can make the behavior brittle under challenging visual conditions and contact-rich interactions.
Learning-based strategies derive policies directly from data and can handle nonlinear dynamics. However, they remain limited by unreliable geometric cues under weak-texture/specular observations [ 13 ] , where learned depth/geometry can be temporally inconsistent or overly smooth and obscure fine topographic structures [ 14 ] , and by sim-to-real gaps in simulation-trained variants (e.g., reinforcement learning) due to difficulty of faithfully modeling viscoelastic, contact-rich colon interactions [ 15 , 16 ] .

To address the challenges of robustness under weak-texture conditions, smooth control consistency, and the sim-to-real gap, we propose ColoACT, a holistic navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E input that combines appearance (RGB) and geometry (RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map) based Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) policy for smooth, continuous closed-loop control and a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER) designed to provide the mechanical and visual stability required by learning-based navigation. To the best of our knowledge, we present the first imitation-learning-based navigation policy for a self-propelled colonoscopic robot in ex-vivo tests. We validate the full system in ex-vivo porcine colons, achieving success rates of 85.4% in straight and 72.5% in curved segments ( ∼ \sim 60 cm). The system further succeeds in highly tortuous anatomies, successfully negotiating sharp 90-degree turns (70%) and double-bend paths (60%), and remains feasible even in extreme triple-bend scenarios. The contributions of this work are as follows:

We proposed an RGB-D-E ACT navigation policy (ColoACT Policy) that leverages multi-cue geometric representations to improve robustness in challenging colonic environments, while generating smooth and stable actions.

We proposed an RGB-D-E ACT navigation policy (ColoACT Policy) that leverages multi-cue geometric representations to improve robustness in challenging colonic environments, while generating smooth and stable actions.

We design a compact self-propelled BGER mechanism that ensures transmission stability and supports reliable visual feedback for autonomous control.

We demonstrate system-level validation of ColoACT on ex-vivo porcine colons, showing strong performance across straight, curved, and complex tortuous segments.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Geometry-Driven Navigation for Robotic Endoscopy

Geometry-driven pipelines have been widely investigated for autonomous navigation in the colon. A common paradigm is to extract explicit geometric features from endoscopic observations and then derive motion commands through deterministic logic. Typical approaches estimate the lumen direction/center by fitting geometric primitives (e.g., circles [ 7 ] , ellipses and triangles [ 8 ] ) or by detecting haustral folds [ 17 ] to guide the robot. These methods are attractive for interpretability and computational efficiency, but often require manually engineered thresholds and rule-based mode switching, leading to discrete behaviors and sensitivity to perception noise and contact-induced disturbances, especially under weak texture and specular highlights. Moreover, these studies are validated primarily on idealized silicone phantoms [ 18 ] , whereas real colons are deformable and time-varying, so the lumen geometry may deviate substantially from assumed analytic shape, thereby limiting generalization. Consequently, geometry-driven pipelines often fail to sustain stable and consistent closed-loop navigation when visual cues are unreliable or when the colon undergoes deformation and intermittent collapse.

## II-B Learning-Based Navigation for Robotic Endoscopy

Learning-based approaches for intraluminal navigation span geometry inference and policy learning. On perception, deep models estimate depth [ 11 , 12 ] and mapping [ 19 , 20 ] to recover lumen geometry, but colon deformation, weak texture, and specularities often impair accuracy and temporal consistency [ 13 ] ; moreover, monocular depth can over-smooth texture-poor regions, attenuating fine cues such as haustral-fold ridges that help infer lumen direction. On control, Reinforcement learning (RL) offers model-free nonlinear navigation with demonstrations in bronchoscopy [ 21 ] and colonoscopy [ 22 , 23 ] settings, yet safety constraints push training to simulation, where viscoelastic, contact-rich interactions are hard to model, yielding a pronounced sim-to-real gap. IL learns policies from expert demonstrations [ 24 ] , reducing dependence on accurate physics [ 25 ] , but naive behavior cloning (BC) suffers a covariate shift and step-wise prediction can break long-horizon consistency [ 26 ] , producing jittery maneuvers. These gaps motivate using explicit, stable geometric cues and temporally coherent closed-loop actions under visual degradation and contact disturbances.

2026-10-02.title: EIDA: Execution-Interface Dynamics Adaptation for Real-to-Sim-to-Real Robot Navigation
2026-10-02.authors: Yiwei Qian , Shanze Wang , Qingyuan Hu , Xinming Zhang , Wei Zhang
2026-10-02.abstract: Simulation-to-robot transfer can fail when velocity commands produce motion and feedback that differ from those modeled during policy training. We present execution-interface dynamics adaptation (EIDA), which fits these responses from target-platform execution data without reconstructing actuator dynamics. A model of body-frame pose increments updates simulator geometry, while a separate model predicts the velocity feedback observed by the policy; a short history of velocity feedback is included in the policy input. The fitted models are used within a lightweight GPU-parallel simulator. On the full Jackal and Go2 validation sets, the fitted models reduced position and yaw prediction errors relative to the simulator’s predefined motion model. Across 100 benchmark navigation environments evaluated in a separate physics-based simulator, EIDA achieved the highest success rate and navigation score among the compared learned policies, both with and without global guidance. Feedback ablations further supported the need to match policy-facing velocity estimates. On a physical Unitree Go2, EIDA reached the goal without collision in all 20 static-scene trials, compared with 4 of 20 for the baseline. These results show that execution-interface adaptation can improve navigation transfer without detailed actuator simulation.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Efficient and reliable autonomous navigation is fundamental to the safe
operation of mobile robots in complex environments. Deep reinforcement
learning (DRL) can acquire behaviors for collision avoidance and goal reaching
through large-scale interaction [ 1 , 2 ] , while
GPU-parallel simulation substantially reduces navigation policy training
time [ 3 ] . However, strong performance in simulation does
not ensure effective transfer to a physical robot.

This transfer gap involves both perception and execution. Prior studies improve
robustness to visual appearance and sensing errors [ 4 , 5 ] , but action modeling and collision handling also affect how
well simulation predicts physical navigation performance [ 6 ] .
Velocity commands pass through a platform-specific low-level controller, with
the resulting motion and feedback affected by actuator response, control
latency, and recent commands. Identical commands can therefore produce
different trajectories in simulation and physical execution, potentially
causing drift, turning overshoot, or collisions. At higher speeds, less time is
available for closed-loop correction, making small response errors more
consequential.

Robustness to dynamics mismatch can be improved by training across varied
simulation parameters and adapting their distribution with real
experience [ 7 , 8 ] . Reproducing
detailed actuator and contact dynamics is another option, but increases
computational cost without ensuring better transfer. Truong et
al. [ 9 ] showed that simplified motion models fitted from
real execution can outperform slower, more detailed simulation in navigation
transfer. In local navigation, collision avoidance and goal progress depend on
pose evolution relative to the environment. This motivates modeling that
evolution together with the velocity feedback available to the policy.
Can navigation policies trained in a lightweight simulator transfer to a
physical robot without reconstructing detailed low-level actuator dynamics?

This paper addresses this question through execution-interface dynamics
adaptation (EIDA), as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Using target-system execution data, EIDA fits body-frame pose
increments to update simulator geometry and a separate causal model to predict
the velocity feedback available to the policy. Recent velocity observations
help the policy account for history-dependent execution responses. At
deployment, physical motion and sensor feedback replace the learned simulation
interface, while the existing low-level controller is retained.
EIDA shows that this is possible when pose evolution and policy-facing velocity
feedback are fitted to target-system execution data and incorporated into a
lightweight simulator. Physical Unitree Go2 trials provide direct evidence of
transfer, while evaluation on 100 BARN environments [ 10 ] assesses navigation transfer across simulators. The main contributions of this work are
summarized as follows:

An execution-interface dynamics adaptation framework that learns
body-frame pose increments from execution data collected on the target system
and uses them to update simulator geometry during navigation policy training.

A separated representation of motion evolution and velocity feedback
observable to the policy, together with recent observations that capture
temporally dependent execution responses.

Validation across wheeled and legged platforms, demonstrating that
adapting execution responses relevant to navigation improves navigation
transfer while preserving efficient parallel policy training.

1. An execution-interface dynamics adaptation framework that learns
body-frame pose increments from execution data collected on the target system
and uses them to update simulator geometry during navigation policy training.

2. A separated representation of motion evolution and velocity feedback
observable to the policy, together with recent observations that capture
temporally dependent execution responses.

3. Validation across wheeled and legged platforms, demonstrating that
adapting execution responses relevant to navigation improves navigation
transfer while preserving efficient parallel policy training.

# II Related Work

One class of methods addresses dynamics mismatch by training policies over a
distribution of simulated systems. Dynamics randomization samples physical
parameters during training [ 7 ] , whereas SimOpt
uses experience from the target system to update the distribution of simulation
parameters [ 8 ] . Both approaches improve robustness to
variations in dynamics without explicitly replacing the simulator transition
function with a response model fitted to a specific target platform.

Other methods use real execution data to modify simulated transitions or the
mapping from actions to motion. Grounded Action Transformation combines a
target-domain forward model with a simulator inverse model to transform
actions [ 11 ] . Neural-Augmented Simulation learns a recurrent
model of the discrepancy between simulated and physical trajectories and
applies the predicted correction to the simulator [ 12 ] . For
robot navigation, Truong et al. [ 9 ] showed that simple
motion models fitted from real data can yield better transfer than slower
simulations based on more detailed physics. Bono et
al. [ 13 ] fitted a second-order model that represents the
response of the robot and its low-level controller, and incorporated this model
into Habitat for navigation policy training. In a broader setting, NeRD
replaces low-level dynamics and contact solvers with robot-centric neural
dynamics; the resulting simulator supports policy learning and can be refined
with physical data [ 14 ] .

Learned dynamics models can also be used during online planning rather than to
define the dynamics of the policy training environment. Forward models have
been combined with sampling-based model predictive control to predict robot
trajectories and collision risk during navigation [ 15 , 16 ] .
By contrast, the Robotic World Model learns autoregressive transitions from
observation–action histories and optimizes policies using imagined
rollouts [ 17 ] . RWM-U extends this model with ensemble-based
uncertainty estimates and uncertainty penalties to support policy optimization
from offline data [ 18 ] .

EIDA focuses on the execution interface used during navigation policy training.
It uses body-frame pose increments fitted from target-system execution data to
update the geometric state of the simulator, while a separate causal model
predicts the velocity feedback available to the policy. EIDA therefore differs
from prior methods that transform actions, replace low-level physical
simulation, use learned dynamics for online planning, or model the full
observation transition through a recurrent world model.

2026-10-02.title: AFD-CAMLs: Agile Force-Distribution-Aware Planning and Control for Cable-Suspended Aerial Multi-Lifting Systems
2026-10-02.authors: Antreas Kourris , Sihao Sun
2026-10-02.abstract:
Multiple UAVs can cooperatively transport heavy payloads while controlling
their position and orientation. Trajectory-based methods offer high agility
while satisfying system constraints, but can produce uneven force distributions
when the tension-to-wrench allocation is redundant or ill-conditioned,
particularly under geometric mismatch and low-level tracking errors. We propose
a hybrid planning-and-control framework to address this problem. A global
planner generates payload trajectories and cable-force references by exploring
the allocation null space under a prescribed internal-force setting. These
references augment the cost of a centralized local planner, promoting feasible
force distributions while generating trajectories for all UAVs. An admittance
filter then compares the planned forces with onboard cable-tension estimates
and adjusts the kinematic references to improve force tracking in degenerate or
near-degenerate configurations. Simulations and experiments involving four to
ten UAVs demonstrate more balanced tension distributions during both hovering
and demanding agile maneuvers, without compromising agility or payload-tracking
performance.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Teams of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can cooperatively transport payloads
beyond the capacity of a single vehicle [ 1 , 2 ] .
Adding UAVs increases lifting capacity but can make the cable-force distribution
non-unique. Accurate payload-pose tracking therefore does not ensure that the
load is shared safely and evenly among the vehicles. This distinction is
especially important for cable-suspended systems: the net force and moment on
the payload determine its motion, whereas internal-force components can change
the individual cable tensions without changing that net wrench. Excessive
tension can saturate or destabilize a vehicle, while insufficient tension can
cause cable slackness and invalidate the assumed system dynamics.

Existing methods can broadly be divided into position- and force-based
approaches. Quasi-static position-based methods determine UAV configurations
from payload poses, cable geometry, and static equilibrium [ 1 , 3 ] . These
methods are effective for slow motion but neglect dynamic coupling and do not
guarantee feasible cable tensions. Force-based methods compute the required
payload wrench from a dynamic model and allocate it among the cables [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , allowing
secondary objectives such as tension or internal-force regulation [ 7 ] . Most retain a cascaded wrench-allocation and
inner-loop structure whose time-scale separation limits agile operation. Their
force commands also depend on nominal payload and cable parameters. The
resulting distribution is therefore sensitive to uncertainty in payload mass
and inertia, attachment locations, and cable lengths [ 5 , 8 ] .

Recent work introduced a trajectory-based approach that replaces the
conventional cascaded force controller with a centralized whole-body nonlinear
model predictive control (NMPC) planner and onboard trajectory-tracking
controllers [ 9 , 8 ] . The planner predicts the coupled
load-cable dynamics and generates dynamically feasible trajectories for all
UAVs while enforcing thrust, cable-tautness, collision-avoidance, and
obstacle-avoidance constraints. Agility is improved because the onboard
controllers track complete kinematic references rather than realizing
instantaneous force commands through separate control layers. This formulation
also allows the planner to anticipate coupled payload and cable motion over a
finite horizon instead of allocating a wrench independently at each instant.

For four or more UAVs, however, multiple cable-force distributions can produce
the same payload wrench. The planner generates kinematic trajectories from a
nominal geometric model, and the low-level controllers do not directly enforce
the corresponding tensions. Attachment-point and cable-length errors, combined
with trajectory-tracking errors, can therefore shift the physical system toward
a different force equilibrium. The payload may still track accurately while
some UAVs become overloaded and other cables approach slackness. Improving
payload-pose tracking alone cannot correct this internal-force component because
it does not affect the resultant payload wrench. The problem becomes most
pronounced when the tension-to-wrench allocation matrix is degenerate or nearly
degenerate, because small geometric or tracking errors can then produce large
changes in the individual tensions. A practical solution must therefore select
a feasible distribution during planning and regulate its realization without
sacrificing the agility of the trajectory-based architecture.

This work extends the trajectory-based framework [ 8 ] with
explicit planning and feedback regulation of the cable-force distribution. An
internal-force-aware global planner explores the null space of the payload
wrench-allocation matrix to generate feasible cable-force and direction
references. These references are incorporated into the centralized NMPC cost so
that the locally planned trajectories account for the desired force
distribution. Because the cable forces are still realized indirectly through
vehicle motion, an admittance filter compares each planned tension with an
onboard estimate and converts the error into position, velocity, and
acceleration corrections. The resulting hybrid motion–force architecture
combines predictive whole-body planning with local force feedback.

The three main contributions are:

an internal-force-aware global planner that preserves the required
payload wrench while generating tension-feasible cable-force and direction
references through null-space optimization;

a force-reference-aware NMPC formulation and an admittance filter that
uses onboard tension estimates to regulate the realized force distribution
through local kinematic corrections; and

simulation studies with four to ten UAVs and real-world experiments with four UAVs (Figure 1 ) that
demonstrate improved force distribution under geometric and inertial-model
mismatch while preserving agile payload tracking.

2026-10-02.title: Recova: Agent-Guided Failure Recovery for Autonomous Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Isabella Liu , An-Chieh Cheng , Johan Bjorck , Zhiding Yu , Hongxu Yin , Jan Kautz , Linxi Fan , Yuke Zhu , Sifei Liu
2026-10-02.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
Manipulation failures can leave scenes in states from which a task policy
cannot recover. Learning corrective behaviors requires scalable failure
exploration and physical grounding. We present Recova, an agent-guided
framework that jointly develops task execution and recovery in a reconstructed
digital twin, then verifies and refines both through real-world experience.
In the twin, the agent diagnoses failures, tests corrective programs, and
collects successful task and recovery rollouts for separate policies. During
deployment, it monitors progress, invokes a learned or programmatic recovery,
verifies scene restoration, and resumes execution. When no suitable recovery
is available, a human demonstration resolves the failure and enters the
learning loop, allowing the system to expand its recovery capabilities.
Physical rollouts and human demonstrations are routed to the corresponding
policy for DAgger training. Across six LIBERO-Pro settings and four
MolmoSpaces categories, Recova achieves 78.8% and 64.9% mean success,
compared with 71.7% and 38.0% for the strongest baselines. With parallel
collection across four real-robot workstations, DAgger fine-tuning raises mean
success from 23.8% to 77.5%, and recovery skills further raise it to
87.5%. Over four collection rounds on one task, observed human intervention falls
from 87.5% to 0%. Together, these results show how agent-guided recovery
turns failures into reusable capabilities, improving robustness while
progressively reducing human intervention.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse
manipulation tasks from language instructions ( 6 ; 26 ; 48 ) , from folding laundry
and assembling boxes to cleaning unfamiliar homes ( 4 ; 3 ) . However, even a small mistake can halt an
otherwise capable policy. A tipped cup must be set upright before pouring can
continue; a pencil caught across a box rim must be moved before the lid can
close. In both cases, the robot must restore a workable scene before resuming
the task.

Most VLA training data, however, contain successful trajectories from
standard initial states and provide little guidance for restoring a failed
scene. Failures create a long tail of unusual configurations, and correcting
them may require undoing a previous action, repositioning an object, or
temporarily moving away from the nominal task goal. Consequently, policies
may struggle when objects appear in unfamiliar arrangements ( 70 ) or when asked to continue after a failed attempt ( 39 ) . Simply retrying the task policy often leaves the
underlying obstruction unresolved. Robots therefore need a complementary
recovery capability that can expand as new failure modes arise.

Learning such recovery behaviors directly on hardware is costly, as exploring
failures requires frequent resets and risks damaging objects ( 58 ; 29 ) . Reconstructed digital twins provide a
safer and more scalable setting for reproducing failures and testing
corrections ( 58 ) , while physical experience remains
essential for verifying and refining them under real contacts and
observations. Effective recovery therefore requires a loop that discovers
behaviors in simulation, validates them on the robot, and feeds physical
experience back into learning.

Language-model agents are natural candidates to coordinate this loop. Recent
models combine multimodal understanding with the ability to use tools,
execute code, and revise solutions from feedback ( 2 ; 51 ) . Prior robotics systems show
that agents can interpret failures and develop reusable programs ( 40 ; 31 ; 41 ) . The central challenge is to
connect these abilities into a complete recovery process: diagnose a failure,
select or develop a correction, verify that it worked, retain successful
solutions, and use the resulting data to improve the appropriate policy. The
agent must also decide whether new experience should become a reusable
program, a task-policy demonstration, or a recovery-policy demonstration.
When no suitable recovery is available, human demonstrations enter the loop
to resolve the failure and expand future recovery capabilities ( 35 ) .

We present Recova ( Fig. 1 ), an agent-guided framework that
develops task execution and scene recovery in a reconstructed digital twin,
then continually improves both through real-world experience. In the twin,
the agent explores task execution, diagnoses failures, and develops corrective
behaviors. Successful task and recovery rollouts initialize separate task and
recovery policies, while programs that compose perception and motion
primitives capture reusable recovery strategies. Keeping these data pathways
separate allows the task and recovery policies to specialize in their
distinct roles.

During real-world deployment, the agent monitors task progress, invokes an
applicable learned or programmatic recovery, verifies that the scene is
workable again, and resumes execution. When no suitable recovery succeeds, it

# 2 Related Work

Expressive imitation-learning policies ( 10 ; 68 ) and large, diverse datasets, including cross-embodiment robot data and
egocentric human video ( 7 ; 50 ; 8 ) , have
produced generalist manipulation policies, including vision-language-action
(VLA) models that map images and language instructions to actions ( 6 ; 49 ; 26 ; 4 ; 52 ; 3 ; 48 ; 15 ) .
Language models ground plans in robot affordances ( 1 ) ,
replan from closed-loop feedback ( 23 ) , write
plans, policy code, value maps, and rewards ( 55 ; 31 ; 24 ; 43 ) ,
and accumulate reusable skills ( 60 ) . A task-management
vision-language model can also direct a VLA over long horizons by replanning
subtasks and visual traces ( 38 ) . For manipulation, CaP-X
benchmarks coding agents ( 16 ) , RATs learns skills through
self-directed play ( 67 ) , and ASPIRE refines robot programs,
accumulates validated skills, and transfers simulation experience to
real-robot programming ( 41 ) .
Recova coordinates learned and programmed recoveries around a task policy,
with human demonstrations for refinement.

Prior work explains manipulation failures from summarized experience ( 40 ) , detects and analyzes them with fine-tuned
vision-language models ( 14 ; 66 ) , monitors execution
against constraints written by a language or vision-language model ( 19 ; 69 ) , or predicts them from policy
features, uncertainty, or learned dynamics ( 18 ; 65 ; 36 ) . Runtime steering filters a
policy’s proposed actions with a vision-language model before they execute ( 63 ) , and neuro-symbolic methods combine failure detection
with recovery planning ( 11 ) .
Separate recovery controllers have substantial precedent. Recovery RL
separates task reward from constraint satisfaction ( 56 ) ; RecoveryChaining learns to return to states
from which nominal controllers can complete the task and demonstrates
sim-to-real transfer ( 59 ) . FARL keeps its offline
recovery policy fixed during online task-policy learning ( 29 ) . RACER guides task execution and recovery through a shared
visuomotor actor ( 13 ) , while FailSafe generates and verifies corrective-action
data for a VLM that assists VLAs ( 32 ) . ReSYNC expands
recovery skills and planning abstractions from failures ( 28 ) . Recova connects recovery development in a reconstructed
scene with visual restoration checks, learned and programmed executors,
and human demonstrations for separate policy updates during deployment.
Benchmarks evaluate perturbation robustness ( 30 ; 33 ; 70 ; 27 ) and
recovery from failed executions ( 39 ) ; our protocol
also tracks human intervention alongside task and recovery outcomes.

DAgger aggregates expert labels on the states a learner visits ( 53 ) . Human-gated variants let an operator take over ( 25 ; 45 ) , and robot-gated variants request
help based on uncertainty, novelty, risk, or predicted action discrepancy,
including across robot fleets ( 47 ; 21 ; 20 ; 22 ) .
Deployed robots also improve from human interventions ( 35 ; 37 ) , language corrections ( 54 ; 34 ) , human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning ( 42 ) , and autonomously collected experience ( 5 ; 71 ; 17 ) .

2026-10-02.title: Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation under Embodiment Mismatch
2026-10-02.authors: Yoshiki Takebayashi , Giovanni Perantoni , Hikaru Sasaki , Matteo Saveriano , Takamitsu Matsubara
2026-10-02.abstract:
With the increasing use of robot-free demonstration interfaces that provide state trajectories without action labels, imitation from observation has become a promising approach for learning robot behaviors from human demonstrations. However, due to differences in embodiment and dynamics between humans and robots, demonstrated human motions may not be feasible for the robot, potentially degrading policy performance. In this study, we propose Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO), which estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstrations from the robot’s own experience rather than relying on explicit dynamics models or large prior exploration datasets. A key feature of EF-GAIfO is that the notion of feasibility evolves with policy learning: as the policy improves and the robot experiences a broader range of state transitions, the feasible region is progressively expanded, allowing additional demonstrations to be incorporated into learning.
This enables feasibility-aware imitation that adapts to the current stage of policy learning, rather than relying on a pre-designed feasibility criterion.
We validate the effectiveness of EF-GAIfO on a locomotion task in simulation and on a real quadruped robot performing a object-reaching-and-grasping task.
2026-10-02.introduction:
In recent years, imitation learning approaches using human demonstrations collected through robot-free demonstration interfaces have attracted increasing attention.
Several approaches have been proposed, ranging from purely video-based ones [ 1 ] to those based on external infrastructures [ 2 , 3 ] , and those based on self-contained onboard tracking [ 4 , 5 ] .
Such interfaces allow users to provide demonstrations through their own hand movements without directly teleoperating a robot.
However, demonstrations collected through such interfaces typically consist of state trajectories without corresponding robot action labels.
Imitation from Observation (IfO) [ 6 , 7 ] , which learns policies from state-only demonstrations, is therefore a suitable framework for utilizing such data.

However, due to an embodiment mismatch between humans and robots, demonstrated state transitions collected via robot-free demonstration interfaces are not necessarily feasible for the robot.
Such demonstrations may contain state transitions that cannot be reproduced under the robot’s embodiment.
If these demonstrations are directly used for IfO, the learned policy may be influenced by robot-infeasible motions.
Consequently, the learned policy may be encouraged to reproduce robot-infeasible motions, potentially resulting in falls or degraded task performance.

To reduce the influence of infeasible demonstrations,
model-based approaches evaluate whether demonstrated motions are feasible for the robot using a robot dynamics model [ 8 , 9 ] .
These methods predict the feasibility of demonstrated motions using known or learned robot dynamics models.
However, whole-body dynamics are strongly coupled, and contact interactions and balance constraints must also be considered.
Therefore, constructing an accurate dynamics model is not straightforward.

These limitations motivate a different approach to feasibility estimation: rather than explicitly modeling, what the robot can do, we infer feasibility from what it has actually experienced (Fig. 1 ).
During policy learning, the robot continuously generates state transitions that are physically realizable under its embodiment, providing direct evidence of feasible motion.
We therefore use this experience distribution as an embodiment-specific reference: demonstration transitions well supported by the robot’s experience are likely to be feasible, without requiring an explicit dynamics model.

In this study, we propose Experience-based Feasibility-aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO).
EF-GAIfO estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstration transitions using experience data collected during GAIfO-based policy learning and reduces the influence of demonstrations with low estimated feasibility.
For feasibility estimation, we train a state-transition reconstruction model using the robot’s experience data and evaluate demonstration transitions based on their reconstruction error.
The estimated feasibility is incorporated into the discriminator objective as a weight, allowing the policy to preferentially imitate demonstration transitions that are supported by the robot’s experience.
We evaluate the proposed method through experiments in a point-mass environment and a quadruped robot environment.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Imitation Learning from Observation

Unlike behavior cloning, which uses state-action pairs, imitation from observation aims to learn from demonstrations consisting only of state sequences or visual observations.
A possible approach to learn, despite the absence of expert actions, consists of inferring the missing actions through a learned inverse dynamics model that maps state transitions to actions [ 6 ] .
Another approach to infer the missing action involves learning a latent action space directly from state observations that will be later aligned to the true action space using a small number of environment interactions [ 10 ] .
Liu et al. [ 11 ] , instead, translate a demonstrator’s raw video observations into the imitator’s own context, enabling imitation in scenarios where the demonstrator’s viewpoint or environment configuration is not the same as that of the imitator.
A separate line of work extends adversarial imitation learning to observation-only settings by matching distributions over state transitions instead of state-action pairs [ 12 ] , using a Wasserstein formulation to handle rough or partial demonstrations [ 13 ] , an inverse dynamics disagreement objective [ 14 ] , or off-policy reuse of past interactions to improve sample efficiency [ 15 ] .

Previous methods for learning from observation mainly focus on observation-only or partial demonstrations, but they do not fully address the feasibility problem caused by differences between the demonstrator and the robot. When the demonstrator and the robot have different physical capabilities, some observed transitions may be difficult or impossible for the robot to reproduce. In contrast, this work introduces an experience-based feasibility estimation mechanism to reduce the influence of robot-infeasible transitions during imitation learning.

## II-B Imitation Learning from Imperfect and Infeasible Demonstrations

In practical imitation learning, demonstration data are not always optimal, clean, or suitable for the robot. Demonstrations may contain suboptimal actions, mistakes, noisy trajectories, or motions that cannot be executed by the robot. To address imperfect demonstrations, several studies have investigated methods for estimating the quality or confidence of demonstration data.
A common approach is to downweight low-quality demonstrations by estimating a per-sample confidence or quality score, either by using a subset of explicit confidence labels [ 16 ] , or by adding a negative-risk term to counteract bias toward frequently occurring state-action pairs [ 17 ] .
In offline settings, one can distinguish expert from non-expert data without environment interaction, using cooperative discriminator training [ 18 ] or importance-sampling-weighted behavior cloning [ 19 ] .
Another popular approach consists of ranking the demonstrations by quality to extrapolate reward functions that can surpass the best available demonstration [ 20 ] , an idea later extended to incorporate the generator’s own experience into the ranking process [ 21 ] .
Wang et al. [ 22 ] , instead, learn per-demonstration weights directly within the adversarial imitation learning framework.

A paradigm more related to the proposed method, even though less explored, is feasibility-aware imitation learning, which considers whether demonstrated motions are executable by the imitator.
Existing work addresses mismatched dynamics between demonstrator and learner [ 23 ] , the question of whether to follow potentially non-reproducible behavior [ 24 ] , and the estimation of feasibility for demonstrations collected via hand-mounted interfaces, using either a robot dynamics model [ 8 ] or multimodal visual and haptic feedback [ 25 ] .

These methods focus on demonstration quality, require confidence labels, rely on explicit or learned robot dynamics models, or use prior robot execution data.
In contrast, the proposed method estimates demonstration feasibility from state transitions collected online during policy learning.
This enables the policy to reduce the influence of robot-infeasible demonstrations without requiring confidence labels, an explicit dynamics model, or a separate prior exploration dataset.
Therefore, this work focuses on experience-based feasibility estimation for IfO with demonstrations that may contain robot-infeasible motions.

2026-10-02.abstract:
Autonomous robots on one-shot missions run over horizons far longer than the
trajectories seen during training, under a fixed onboard compute budget. We
present FRANK, a 507K-parameter recurrent
architecture that combines tau-gated recurrent modules, content-addressable
memory, and a feedforward reflex pathway. We evaluate it against recurrent,
state-space, and reduced modular baselines at matched parameter count on four
algorithmic sequence tasks, trained at length 5–20 and evaluated out to two
million tokens. At 100,000 × 100{,}000\times the maximum training length, 6 of 10
FRANK seeds retain exactly 100.0% accuracy, while none of the 50 baseline
configurations does, five architectures at ten seeds each with none left
incomplete (Fisher exact, two-sided p = 4.2 × 10 − 6 p=4.2\times 10^{-6} ). Targeted
lesions across the four tasks yield four distinct component-reliance profiles,
consistent with task-dependent allocation across the recurrent, memory, and
reflex pathways. Separately, a FRANK policy trained in simulation
drives a physical ground vehicle to commanded waypoints through obstacles
without teleoperation.

Deep ocean and deep space exploration share a constraint terrestrial robotics

anyone rehearsed. A controller reliable for the length of a test campaign that
quietly degrades beyond it is the failure a one-shot mission cannot detect in
time.

This is a length generalization problem, and the standard tools fail it in
different ways. Transformers with learned absolute positional embeddings cannot
represent positions past their training range, and relative schemes built for
extrapolation do not rescue the task we study: an ALiBi [ 7 ] probe
collapses to chance by 100 × \times . Attention’s O ⁡ ( L 2 ) O(L^{2}) cost is a harder
limit: at two million tokens the score matrix alone would hold roughly 4 × 10 12 4\times 10^{12} entries. Recurrent models run at any length but drift:
gated recurrent unit (GRU) [ 9 ] baselines match our model at 10 × \times and land at 10–30% at 100,000 × \times ; Mamba [ 8 ] , a selective
state-space model, is at chance by 100 × \times on every seed.

Prior work reports early results for FRANK [ 1 ] and a
single-seed lesion analysis [ 2 ] ; the ten-seed re-run with
swept learning rates, the statistical testing, and the hardware deployment
(Fig. 1 ) are new.

2026-10-02.title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending
2026-10-02.authors: Yifan Hu , Luhang Hong , Mingkang Long , Danning Wang , Chengfeng Jia , Rong Su , Junjie Fu , Guanghui Wen
2026-10-02.abstract: Coordinated multi-humanoid loco-manipulation is promising yet challenging due to high-dimensional whole-body control, decentralized decision making, and scalability. While recent reinforcement learning methods have improved single-humanoid whole-body control, extending them to the multi-humanoid setting remains nontrivial and often requires substantial reward engineering or task-specific design. We propose MASkillBlender, a general multi-agent reinforcement learning framework to achieve decentralized multi-humanoid whole-body coordination. By learning a shared decentralized high-level policy over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills, MASkillBlender enables coordinated behaviors using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references. To improve learning efficiency, we further introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy for homogeneous multi-humanoid systems, and theoretically show that the permuted samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples under the homogeneous Markov game formulation. We evaluate MASkillBlender on multiple multi-humanoid coordination tasks across two humanoid embodiments. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently achieves strong task performance and enables coordinated behaviors across different tasks and humanoid embodiments.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humanoid robots have substantial potential to replace or assist humans in completing daily tasks across diverse environments due to their human-like morphology [ 15 ] . With advancements in reinforcement learning (RL) and robot hardware, the loco-manipulation capabilities of humanoids have been significantly enhanced [ 17 ] . Nevertheless, many real-world tasks require multiple humanoids to coordinate their actions [ 50 ] . Compared with single-humanoid control, multi-humanoid settings introduce additional challenges due to complex inter-agent dependencies. Developing general learning methods for coordinated multi-humanoid control therefore represents an important step toward scalable and capable humanoid teams.

Recent studies have demonstrated increasingly sophisticated multi-humanoid whole-body interactions, showing the potential of learning-based approaches for coordinated humanoid control [ 10 ] . However, existing methods typically rely on human motion references to guide policy learning through motion imitation or tracking objectives. While such motion priors provide effective guidance for acquiring natural whole-body behaviors, they also introduce additional data and supervision requirements, and the resulting motion-based objectives may compete with task rewards during optimization, potentially constraining the policy from discovering coordination strategies that are most effective for the task [ 34 ] . Beyond the reliance on motion supervision, incorporating observations of other humanoids into each agent’s policy has been widely adopted to facilitate coordination. While such inter-agent information can improve learning and coordination performance, it may hinder scalability to larger teams and complicate robust real-world deployment.

For single-humanoid loco-manipulation, skill-based learning has emerged as an effective paradigm that does not rely on task-specific motion references [ 38 , 25 ] . By blending pre-trained primitive skills into the control policy, humanoids can reuse existing motor capabilities and reduce the burden of low-level control learning during downstream task training. However, extending this paradigm to multi-humanoid control is not straightforward, since skills pre-trained for individual humanoids do not encode the inter-agent coordination required by downstream tasks. Learning how to compose these skills across agents under coupled task dynamics therefore remains challenging.

In this work, we propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based multi-agent RL (MARL) framework for decentralized coordination in homogeneous multi-humanoid systems. Under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), a shared decentralized high-level policy learns to coordinate the composition of reusable pre-trained primitive skills across humanoids using local observations. The primitive skills remain fixed during downstream training, allowing the policy to focus on high-level skill composition and inter-agent coordination using only task-level rewards. To improve learning efficiency, we introduce a permutation-based data augmentation strategy that exploits the permutation symmetry of homogeneous multi-humanoid systems. To evaluate the proposed framework, we build three representative multi-humanoid coordination tasks spanning cooperative object manipulation and coordinated locomotion across two distinct humanoid embodiments, using only task-level rewards and limited local observations. To summarize, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based MARL framework that learns decentralized multi-humanoid coordination over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references.

We propose MASkillBlender, a general skill-based MARL framework that learns decentralized multi-humanoid coordination over reusable pre-trained single-humanoid skills using only task-level rewards, without requiring task-specific motion references.

We incorporate a permutation-based data augmentation strategy into MASkillBlender and theoretically show that the augmented samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples.

We evaluate the proposed MARL framework on diverse multi-humanoid coordination tasks across different embodiments, and extensive simulation results show that the learned policies produce versatile coordinated behaviors and effectively handle all tasks in a fully decentralized manner.

2. We incorporate a permutation-based data augmentation strategy into MASkillBlender and theoretically show that the augmented samples preserve the policy-gradient direction of the original samples.

3. We evaluate the proposed MARL framework on diverse multi-humanoid coordination tasks across different embodiments, and extensive simulation results show that the learned policies produce versatile coordinated behaviors and effectively handle all tasks in a fully decentralized manner.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

RL has become a key paradigm for humanoid whole-body control, facilitating complex locomotion and manipulation [ 35 , 14 , 7 , 6 , 26 ] . Existing RL-based methods can be broadly categorized according to whether the control policy relies on task-specific motion references. Reference-conditioned methods learn versatile whole-body behaviors by tracking motions obtained from MoCap datasets [ 8 , 24 , 44 ] or human teleoperation [ 11 , 19 , 18 , 39 , 47 , 3 ] . While effective for single-humanoid loco-manipulation, extending this paradigm to multi-humanoid coordination requires coordinated motion references that are substantially more difficult to acquire. In contrast, task-driven methods learn loco-manipulation behaviors without conditioning on task-specific reference motions [ 38 , 25 , 9 , 48 ] . To address the difficulty of learning in high-dimensional state-action spaces, these methods typically employ task decomposition [ 9 , 48 ] or skill-based hierarchical control architectures [ 38 , 25 ] . For the latter, pre-trained low-level skills are reused and composed by a high-level policy to reduce the burden of learning whole-body control from scratch, which empirically improves learning efficiency and enables diverse loco-manipulation behaviors across downstream tasks.

Learning coordinated whole-body behaviors among multiple humanoids has recently received growing attention. SMPLOlympics [ 30 ] explores competitive interactions between physically simulated humanoids in diverse sports environments. For cooperative coordination, reference-based methods retarget multi-person motions to humanoids and learn interaction policies through motion tracking and interaction-specific objectives [ 29 , 5 ] , enabling complex whole-body interactions such as contact-rich social behaviors and synchronized motions. To alleviate the scarcity of multi-person motion data, CooHOI [ 12 ] and TeamHOI [ 28 ] instead leverage single-human motion priors to facilitate cooperative object manipulation. CooHOI transfers single-agent object-interaction skills to cooperative settings, while TeamHOI employs masked motion priors and a teammate-aware policy to support cooperative carrying with varying team sizes. Note that these methods are typically task-specific and require high-quality motion retargeting to obtain suitable humanoid references. CDA-PPO [ 2 ] follows a conventional MARL formulation and learns cooperative object transportation from scratch without motion supervision. However, it is specifically designed for a two-humanoid setting and relies on extensively engineered locomotion and cooperation rewards as well as explicit teammate observations. As a result, it remains a huge challenge to develop general reference-free RL methods for diverse multi-humanoid whole-body coordination with lightweight reward engineering.

2026-10-02.title: OrbitTAMP: Grounding Language Models for Task and Motion Planning in Spacecraft Rendezvous
2026-10-02.authors: Yuji Takubo , Daniele Gammelli , Marco Pavone , Simone D'Amico
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Spacecraft rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are currently planned through an expertise-intensive process in which engineers translate high-level operational intent into safe, dynamically feasible trajectories, creating a bottleneck to scalable operations.
Large language model (LLM)-based agents could offer an intuitive interface for this process, although their outputs are not inherently grounded in orbital dynamics, operational constraints, or the structure of admissible spacecraft maneuvers.
To exploit their semantic reasoning while ensuring the generated plan’s physical validity, this paper presents a hierarchical framework for spacecraft task-and-motion planning (TAMP) that grounds LLM reasoning in a graph of reusable behaviors and domain-specific planning modules.
Within this framework, a pretrained LLM maps a natural-language command to a partial mission specification. The associated planners then resolve unspecified decisions within the admissible operational space.
Finally, trajectory optimization converts the completed mission specification into a dynamically feasible trajectory.
Numerical experiments demonstrate that this architecture substantially improves intent recovery over direct LLM generation, achieving 98% exact recovery of partial mission specifications across all evaluated splits when backed by frontier LLMs.
Additional test-time-compute experiments show that, for a compact 9B model, verifier-guided revision increases exact recovery from 75% to 88%, while broader behavior-plan search independently improves selection among admissible trajectory realizations.
Overall, these results establish a scalable and auditable foundation for language-driven agentic planning of spacecraft RPO.
2026-10-02.introduction:
The proliferation of distributed space systems, such as swarms and constellations, is increasing the need for scalable spacecraft operations.
Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO), in particular, require complex maneuver sequences for inspection, repair, refueling, and other servicing tasks.
Traditionally, teams of operators and mission designers translate high-level mission intent or concepts of operations (CONOPS) into explicit trajectory specifications using their knowledge of astrodynamics, mission constraints, and available guidance modes.
This dependence on specialized expertise limits the scalability of future spacecraft operations.

Large language models (LLMs) have the potential to establish natural language as an intuitive and broadly accessible interface between high-level mission intent and executable spacecraft trajectories.
Specifically, recent advances in agentic LLM frameworks have demonstrated that foundation models (FMs) can interpret high-level instructions, decompose objectives into multistep plans, invoke external tools, and coordinate reasoning with action across interactive decision-making, autonomous scientific experimentation, and embodied operations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
For spacecraft RPO, however, semantic interpretation alone is insufficient. Language-model outputs must be grounded in spacecraft-specific behavior structures, operational constraints, and orbital dynamics before they can support safe execution. The central challenge is therefore not merely to translate language into a quantitative configuration, but to embed LLM reasoning within a planning architecture that converts incomplete intent into admissible and physically realizable spacecraft motion.

Consider the command:
“ approach the target slowly from the − V -V -bar, circumnavigate it for two orbits, and then depart to a 50 ​ m 50\,\mathrm{m} along-track separation. ”
To a human operator, this command conveys a clear maneuver intent through an ordered composition of familiar spacecraft behaviors: approach, circumnavigate, and depart.
Such reusable behaviors provide abstractions for organizing complex motion, similar in function to skills [ 3 ] or meta-actions [ 4 ] in broader robotic systems.
As a trajectory-planning specification, however, the command remains incomplete.
It dictates several explicit requirements, including the two-orbit circumnavigation and final separation, while leaving other decisions such as phase durations, intermediate waypoints, and trajectory constraints unspecified.
This distinction is central to spacecraft trajectory planning: conventional task and trajectory planners typically operate on formally defined actions, objectives, and constraints, whereas natural-language mission commands generally specify only a subset of this information, and the unstated remainder is where mission-design expertise must be applied.
Grounding such a command therefore requires identifying the stated intent, resolving unspecified decisions within the admissible spacecraft operational space, and constructing a dynamically feasible and safe trajectory.

To address this problem, this paper introduces a hierarchical framework for grounding LLM reasoning for spacecraft task-and-motion planning (TAMP), illustrated in Fig. 1 .
Extending the preliminary concepts of structural decomposition for spacecraft behavior planning [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , the framework organizes the planning process into three stages: semantic grounding, completion of unspecified mission decisions, and physical trajectory verification.
A pretrained LLM first maps the natural-language command to a partial mission specification that preserves the operator’s stated intent while explicitly representing unspecified information.
A graph of reusable spacecraft behaviors, together with domain-specific planning modules, then completes the behavior sequence, timing, and waypoint decisions within the admissible operational space.
Finally, trajectory optimization instantiates the resulting candidates as state-control trajectories and ensures their dynamical feasibility and safety.
This hierarchical architecture grounds LLM reasoning at each stage while enabling multistage planning, computational tool use, and intermediate verification.

The central contribution of this paper is a hierarchical planning formulation in which operator underspecification is preserved and systematically completed, realized as an agentic architecture that scaffolds pretrained, off-the-shelf LLMs with structured, spacecraft-specific planning and verification modules.
Because every stage completes the same partial specification, stated intent is preserved by construction rather than by prompt compliance and remains checkable throughout, while unstated decisions are resolved by the behavior graph and planning modules under orbital dynamics and safety constraints rather than left to the LLM.
This design is motivated by both the scarcity of domain-specific training data for space applications [ 8 ] and the need for transparent, verifiable, and explicitly constrained decision-making in safety-critical spacecraft operations.
The resulting architecture provides an auditable human–spacecraft interface and supports scalable language-driven planning for future distributed space systems.
Specifically, the contributions of this work are as follows:

A spacecraft RPO planning representation comprising a graph of reusable behaviors and a structured mission configuration that preserves partial operator specifications and supports hierarchical completion of behavior, timing, and waypoint decisions.

An LLM-backed TAMP formulation that uses these representations to decouple intent parsing from trajectory realization, grounding semantic decisions in the admissible behavior structure and resolving unstated decisions within operational constraints and spacecraft dynamics.

A stage-wise and end-to-end evaluation over 300 procedurally generated commands and multiple LLM backends and a deterministic parsing baseline that quantifies the effects of the grounding scaffold, model capability, and targeted test-time computation through verifier-guided revision and behavior-plan search.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Sec. II compares the proposed framework with spacecraft planning, language grounding, and robotic TAMP.
Sec. III defines the common mission representation, behavior graph, and systematic completion process.
Sec. IV describes the on-orbit inspection case study and its specific implementations.
Sec. V reports the module-level and end-to-end evaluation results.
Finally, Sec. VI concludes the paper and discusses future work.

1. A spacecraft RPO planning representation comprising a graph of reusable behaviors and a structured mission configuration that preserves partial operator specifications and supports hierarchical completion of behavior, timing, and waypoint decisions.

2. An LLM-backed TAMP formulation that uses these representations to decouple intent parsing from trajectory realization, grounding semantic decisions in the admissible behavior structure and resolving unstated decisions within operational constraints and spacecraft dynamics.

3. A stage-wise and end-to-end evaluation over 300 procedurally generated commands and multiple LLM backends and a deterministic parsing baseline that quantifies the effects of the grounding scaffold, model capability, and targeted test-time computation through verifier-guided revision and behavior-plan search.
