2026-10-02.title: eRLT: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Action-Relevant Token Routing
2026-10-02.authors: Dehao Huang , Jianbang Liu , Jianpan Gao , Chao Tang , Zilang Cen , Zedong Dan , Jiaheng Wang , Tingguang Li , Yue Wang , Hong Zhang
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide strong behavioral priors for robotic manipulation, yet efficiently adapting them to downstream tasks remains challenging. Recent work addresses this challenge by adapting frozen VLAs through online reinforcement learning (RL), whose sample efficiency depends on the quality of the state representation used by the actor and critic. Existing methods construct such representations either with VLA-independent visual encoders or through fixed compression of internal VLA representations. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, therefore limiting sample efficiency. To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across both tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. Specifically, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features at multiple depths, while a lightweight layer router combines these summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is initialized using expert demonstrations to capture features predictive of expert actions and then refined using critic feedback from online interactions for action-value estimation. Across seven LIBERO and RoboTwin tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by up to 23.7 % 23.7\% over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments on USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion further show AUC improvements of 108.9 % 108.9\% and 46.7 % 46.7\% , respectively, over the strongest baseline.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit broad visual and semantic knowledge from internet-scale pretraining and learn generalist control from diverse robot data, enabling generalization across tasks and environments ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2026 ) . However, achieving high reliability on a specific downstream task often requires further adaptation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is effective, but heavily relies on collecting additional high-quality task-specific demonstrations, whose coverage of states encountered during deployment is inherently limited. Online reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach by collecting experience from the policy’s own deployment distribution and learning from both successful and failed interactions ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In this work, we focus on lightweight online RL methods that keep the pretrained VLA frozen and adapt its behavior through a small actor-critic.

The success of lightweight online RL depends critically on the state representation supplied to the actor and critic. A VLA trained for generalist control encodes rich information about visual observations, language instructions, robot states, and actions. For task-specific adaptation, an effective state representation should retain the task-specific action-relevant information needed for action refinement and action-value estimation, including robot-object relations that determine appropriate corrections and task-progress cues that determine the expected return of those corrections. Such information is distributed across the VLA’s tokens and layers, and the most useful features vary across tasks. Existing methods construct the state representation either with visual encoders independent of the VLA ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) or by compressing representations from a predetermined layer and token set ( Kowshik et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . The former constructs the state representation outside the VLA and therefore cannot directly reuse its internal task-specific action-relevant features. The latter reuses VLA features, but restricts feature extraction to a predetermined layer and token set regardless of which features are most useful for the target task. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, limiting sample efficiency under constrained online interaction budgets.

To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across the tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. At each selected VLM layer, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features, while a lightweight layer router combines these layer-wise summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is firstly initialized by predicting expert action chunks from existing VLA SFT demonstrations, encouraging the RL token to retain information useful for action refinement. Then, during online RL stage, the critic’s Bellman objective further refines the routing module using online transitions, adapting the retained information for action-value estimation. The VLA remains frozen throughout both stages. By focusing the RL token on task-specific action-relevant VLA features, eRLT facilitates action refinement and action-value estimation, thereby supporting sample-efficient actor-critic learning from limited online interactions.

We evaluate eRLT on manipulation tasks from LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and RoboTwin ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , as well as two real-world high-precision manipulation tasks: USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion. Across the seven simulation tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by 23.7 % 23.7\% relative to baselines with fixed VLA feature compression and by 7.1 % 7.1\% relative to baselines with VLA-independent state encoders. On the two real-world tasks, eRLT improves learning-curve AUC by 108.9 % 108.9\% and 46.7 % 46.7\% , respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, and on USB connector insertion raises the final-window success rate from 50 % 50\% to 90 % 90\% under the same interaction budget. Ablations further validate the complementary roles of layer-wise routing, token-wise routing, task-specific action-relevant initialization, and online adaptation.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

We provide controlled evidence that the VLA layers and tokens most useful for online RL vary across downstream tasks.

We propose eRLT, which constructs an effective RL token by routing task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers. The routing mechanism is initialized via expert action prediction and subsequently refined online using critic feedback.

We evaluate eRLT across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and two real-world precision high-precision manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over existing state representations.

1. We provide controlled evidence that the VLA layers and tokens most useful for online RL vary across downstream tasks.

2. We propose eRLT, which constructs an effective RL token by routing task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers. The routing mechanism is initialized via expert action prediction and subsequently refined online using critic feedback.

3. We evaluate eRLT across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and two real-world precision high-precision manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over existing state representations.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Lightweight Online Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models

Lightweight online RL adapts a pretrained policy through small trainable modules while preserving its behavioral prior. Early residual RL learns corrections for conventional controllers ( Johannink et al., 2018 ; Silver et al., 2018 ) ; recent VLA methods instead keep the pretrained policy frozen and train a lightweight actor to correct its actions or steer its generative process ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Kowshik et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Some further incorporate human guidance or improved initialization ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . eRLT adopts this frozen-VLA actor-critic framework and studies how to construct the state representation supplied to the actor and critic from the VLA’s internal representations.

Within this framework, the actor and critic must infer which decisions lead to higher returns from an effective state representation, making the task-specific action-relevant information retained in this representation central to sample-efficient learning. Existing methods construct the state representation either with VLA-independent visual encoders or by compressing a predetermined layer and token set. DSRL and PLD use the former design ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) ; MiDAS mean-pools internal VLM tokens, while RLT compresses final-layer tokens using reconstruction ( Kowshik et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . The former constructs state representations separately from those already available in the VLA, while the latter uses only prescribed layers and tokens. Both designs therefore lack a mechanism for selecting the internal VLA information most relevant to task-specific action refinement and action-value estimation, limiting sample efficiency under constrained online interaction budgets. eRLT instead learns to aggregate task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers into an effective RL token.

## 2.2 Internal VLA Representations and Feature Aggregation

Frozen VLA representations encode object relations, robot and action states, task progress, failures, transitions, and future success ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Molinari et al., 2025 ) . Intervention studies further show that motion- and action-related features can influence robot behavior ( Häon et al., 2025 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ; Swann et al., 2026 ; Grant et al., 2026 ) . These signals are distributed: different layers provide complementary representations ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , while selective token aggregation can improve action generation ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) . These findings support eRLT’s use of frozen internal VLA representations as the source of the RL token supplied to the actor and critic.

Feature aggregation methods extract such distributed information either by compressing tokens within a layer or by combining representations across layers. Learned tokens and queries compress visual or multimodal features within a layer ( Ryoo et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025a ) , and recent VLA methods use related mechanisms for action generation ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . Other methods combine hidden representations across depths ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . These representations target visual-language understanding or VLA action generation; eRLT adapts both forms of aggregation to construct a fixed-dimensional RL token that retains task-specific action-relevant information for the actor and critic.

2026-10-02.title: Screw Attention: Rigid-Body Algebra Inside a Transformer
2026-10-02.authors: Aly Magassouba
2026-10-02.abstract: Learned manipulation policies rediscover from data the spatial relations that rigid-body mechanics supplies in closed form. This costs data, and it leaves the policies fragile to geometric changes in the scene. We present Screw Attention, a transformer layer in which the relation between two bodies is a spatial transform rather than a graph edge. Every token is a body with a pose. Each pair of tokens carries the relative pose and, for robot joints, the joint screw. Messages are transported along this relation into the receiver’s frame, while the attention scores see only frame-invariant quantities. By construction, the messages are equivariant to an independent change of frame at every token, and a single layer can express the velocity recursion of rigid-body mechanics. On simulated manipulation tasks, Screw Attention matches or outperforms controls of the same size, including graph, transformer and flat networks on LIBERO-Spatial. With 16,162 parameters it reaches 97.3% on LIBERO-Spatial from object poses (without images or language), above a flat network with 27 × 27\times more parameters. Under a change of per-link frame convention its success is unchanged, while every other learned network falls below 3%. Placed on an analytic controller as a gated residual, it raises insertion success by 17.3 points. It is unaffected by pose noise up to 10 mm and by joint offsets within the factory calibration of a Franka arm. These results suggest a criterion: geometry is decisive when the task requires relations between frames that no other part of the system supplies. Code and trained policies will be released.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Learned policies have become one of the main approaches to robot manipulation,
using scale as their principal lever. For instance, vision-language-action models with billions of
parameters, trained on large corpora of demonstrations, now perform multi-step tasks from
raw images and natural language. However, recent robustness analyses expose a sharp weakness:
displacing the manipulated objects, or altering the robot’s initial configuration, degrades the
accuracy of such policies drastically [ 1 , 2 ] . These failures are
not only of perception, but of representing spatial relationships.

Yet those relations are exactly what rigid-body mechanics supplies in closed form. The kinematic model specifies how motion at one joint propagates to distant links, how a force applied at the gripper is distributed across the actuators, and how the gripper pose relates to any commanded frame. These relations are available a priori, long before any data are collected. Classical controllers are built on this structure, which is why such controllers remain compact, predictable, and reliable within the regimes they are designed to cover. The limitations of this approach are equally well-defined: analytic methods cannot easily express contact, friction, deformation, uncertain payload properties, or any task whose objective is not a fixed set-point. In this respect, analytic methods and learned policies form two complementary paradigms. One is given the geometry but cannot represent what the model omits; the other can represent what the model omits but must rediscover the geometry.

Several lines of work have therefore reintroduced structure into learned policies, although each retains only part of it. Embodiment-aware policy
transformers [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] encode the robot’s
connectivity as an abstract graph, through per-limb descriptors or by biasing attention toward links that are neighbours in the
kinematic tree. Equivariant manipulation policies [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] preserve the geometry of the scene, so that behaviour is consistent when the scene is
transformed, but they represent the robot only through its end-effector pose.
Kinematics-structured policies [ 9 , 10 ] do carry the poses or transforms of
individual links, yet process them with learned matrices, discarding the very structure that made those poses worth carrying. In all cases, the relation between two bodies is either abstracted into a graph or reduced to coordinates that a learned map is free to reinterpret.

That relation is neither abstract nor arbitrary, and this observation underpins our approach. It is a physical relation with explicit content: the distance between two bodies, their relative orientation, and, when a joint is present, the axis of rotation or translation. Robotics provides a concise formalism for exactly these notions, the spatial or screw algebra of rigid-body
mechanics [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . In this formalism such a relation is a single
object and composing two of them determines directly how motion of one body induces motion of another. A policy given these relations is therefore not required to learn kinematics from scratch, since the kinematic structure is already encoded in the relations themselves.

The question then becomes how to build an architecture that can make direct use of this kinematic
structure, rather than relearning it implicitly. To this end, we adopt a transformer [ 14 ] whose
tokens exchange screws (the velocities and forces of rigid-body mechanics) rather than only
feature vectors. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , in our architecture, each input token is a body with a pose, which may be a robot link or an object in
the scene. Standard transformers relate tokens only through a learned compatibility between their features. In our approach, each pair of tokens also carries a given term that represents the physical relation between the two bodies, read from the kinematic model or, for objects, from perception. This addition enables two architectural shifts.

First, any message sent from one token to another is transformed into the receiving body’s own
frame. Indeed, quantities defined at different locations cannot be combined until they are expressed in
a common frame, so the message must be transformed before the receiving token can use it.
Second, the attention weights access the relation only through frame-invariant quantities (e.g.,
distances, joint types, adjacency), which enter as an attention bias. The distinction matters: a bias on the
scores is a reweighting a transformer can in principle learn unaided, whereas transporting a quantity
between coordinate frames is an operation it cannot express on its own. The physics therefore
enters where it adds genuine capability, on the messages.

Three properties follow from this construction. (i) The recursion that propagates velocities along the kinematic chain lies within what the layer can express, so the policy need not learn mechanics from data and can spend its capacity on the phenomena that mechanics omits. (ii) The geometry is
combined only through operations admitted by the spatial algebra, and these operations commute with changes of coordinate frame. As a result, the transported messages do not depend on how a frame is attached to a link, which is a modelling convention with no physical meaning. (iii) Because the readout emits the same command as an analytic controller, a joint torque or an end-effector twist, the layer can be used alone or on top of such a controller as a residual. Closing a gate recovers the controller exactly, so the balance between analytic and learned control is a choice made per task rather than fixed by the architecture.

In robotics, every link carries its own frame. The choice of where that frame is attached is a convention that varies across description formats [ 15 ] and sometimes even across descriptions of the same robot [ 16 ] . A policy whose behaviour depends on this convention can fail on a robot that is physically identical but described differently. Existing equivariant architectures [ 17 , 8 ] are equivariant only to a single, global change of frame applied to the entire scene. By contrast, our layer is equivariant to an independent change of frame on every link, which is the freedom a robot description actually has.

With this foundation, our contributions are as follows.

An embodiment-aware attention layer grounded in rigid-body mechanics. Tokens are related through the physical relation between bodies rather than an abstract graph, and messages are transported into the receiver’s coordinate frame. As a result, the computation of how motion propagates along the robot can be expressed by the layer rather than learned from data (Section III-D ). Moreover, the layer can be used on its own or as a residual on top of an analytic controller.

An embodiment-aware attention layer grounded in rigid-body mechanics. Tokens are related through the physical relation between bodies rather than an abstract graph, and messages are transported into the receiver’s coordinate frame. As a result, the computation of how motion propagates along the robot can be expressed by the layer rather than learned from data (Section III-D ). Moreover, the layer can be used on its own or as a residual on top of an analytic controller.

An extensive empirical study across diverse tasks and a standard benchmark. We evaluate our architecture on three simulated manipulation tasks and on LIBERO-Spatial, comparing it against mechanism-matched controls. The structured policy outperforms graph, transformer and flat networks of the same size on LIBERO-Spatial, and even surpasses a flat network with 27 × 27\times more parameters. Under changes to the per-link frame convention, it is the only model whose success is unchanged, whereas all controls collapse to 0.0–2.3%. Used on top of an analytic controller on a contact-rich insertion task, it raises the success rate by 17.3 points. These results show that the structure contributes capability (Sections IV , V and IV-G ).

A hypothesis for when the structure is decisive . Across the tasks studied, we identify a simple condition under which the geometry affects performance: the structure is decisive when the task requires reasoning over relations between coordinate frames that are not otherwise supplied by an analytic controller. When this condition is met, correct relations yield large gains over incorrect ones. When it is not, the correctness of the relations makes no measurable difference. This hypothesis is consistent with all results reported here (Section V , Appendix H ).

# II Related Work

Four strands of prior work are directly relevant to this study: policy transformers that encode the robot’s structure, equivariant policies that preserve scene geometry, architectures that represent the robot’s kinematics explicitly, and methods that introduce physics through the training objective rather than the network. Each preserves a different aspect of the physical structure available to a manipulation policy.

Embodiment-aware policy transformers. This strand aims to exploit the robot’s structure in a policy. MetaMorph [ 3 ] assigns a token to each limb and conditions it on per-limb morphology descriptors. Body
Transformer [ 4 ] restricts attention using a mask derived from the body
graph, and morphology-embedded transformers [ 5 ] add a topology-aware
bias to the attention scores, with per-joint descriptors as ordinary features. In all cases, the kinematic tree enters only as connectivity: which parts exist and which are connected. The physical content of the relation between two links, how far apart they are and about which
axis one moves relative to the other, is however left for the network to infer. The scene is likewise represented as flat features rather than as additional bodies with poses.

Equivariant manipulation policies. Whereas the first strand structures the robot, this strand structures the scene. Motivated by data efficiency and by generalisation to new object placements, Diffusion-EDFs [ 6 ] , RiEMann [ 18 ] ,
EquiBot [ 19 ] , EquAct [ 7 ] and SAVLA [ 8 ] build policies whose output transforms consistently when the scene is rotated or translated, and general-purpose architectures such as the geometric-algebra transformer (GATr) [ 17 ] provide the underlying machinery. These methods obtain a strong geometric representation of the objects, but they represent the robot only through its end-effector pose. SAVLA is the closest to our layer in construction, carrying typed scalar and vector channels through its action head, yet it has no per-link tokens, no relative transforms between them and no joint motion subspaces.

Our layer differs from these architectures in its aim and in its symmetry. Their defining property is equivariance to one transformation of the whole scene, with every feature expressed in one common frame. In Screw Attention, invariance is a consequence of building the layer on the screw algebra of rigid-body mechanics rather than its aim, and the same construction reproduces classical computations of robot mechanics. Its symmetry group is also larger: the global frame change handled by existing equivariant architectures is the special case in which every token’s frame is transformed in the same way (Appendix C ). Finally, the first two strands have been geometric about different halves of the problem, the robot’s structure and the scene’s geometry. Our layer applies the same typing to the robot’s own bodies and to the objects of the scene, within a single token space.

Kinematics-structured policies. A third strand brings the robot’s kinematics inside the network rather than encoding only its connectivity. XMoP [ 9 ] tokenises the
links as poses and predicts link-wise pose transformations to transfer across manipulators. The Rodrigues Network [ 10 ] makes forward kinematics a learnable operator as
a prior for action learning, and ABD-NET [ 20 ] mirrors the articulated-body algorithm in a graph network with learnable inertia parameters. These methods carry the same
quantities that our layer uses, but XMoP and the Rodrigues Network process them with learned matrices applied directly to geometric coordinates, and ABD-NET replaces the edges and the inertias by learned ones. These operations do not in general commute with a change of frame. The output can then depend on how the reference frames are attached to the links, a modelling convention rather than a physical property. XMoP compensates for this with frame-randomising data augmentation and reports losing 68.1 % 68.1\% of its success rate on unseen embodiments without it. Our screw attention layer, instead, keeps the transforms, screws and inertias as the model’s own quantities and the geometry inside operations that commute with a change of frame. Messages are transported by the relative pose between bodies rather than mapped from their coordinates. This is also what makes the velocity recursion an exact special case of the layer (Section III-D ) rather than a function it may approximate.

Physics outside the architecture. A final strand introduces physical knowledge without constraining the network itself. The policy of [ 21 ] achieves
equivariance to changes in the definitions of the end-effector and camera frames through an analytic decoder. This is possible because its inputs, images and language, do not change
when these frames are redefined. In our setting, however, altering the per-link frames changes every quantity the policy reads, so the invariance must be a property of the network rather than the decoder.

Other approaches keep physics in the objective or in a separate model. PIPER [ 22 ] regularises the policy objective with analytic dynamics, and KING [ 23 ] represents the robot as a kinematic graph but estimates its motion instead of predicting commands. By contrast, residual policy learning [ 24 , 25 ] keeps an analytic controller at run time and learns a correction added to its output with an unstructured network. These approaches constrain the objective, the
prediction target or the command, and are actually compatible with the constraint on the function class proposed in this paper.

2026-10-02.title: TOAST: Stochastic Robot Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-02.authors: Keisuke Shirai , Tomohiro Motoda , Hanbit Oh , Ryoichi Nakajo , Roman Mykhailyshyn , Ryo Hanai , Shotaro Miwa , Yukiyasu Domae
2026-10-02.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models often represent continuous robot actions as discrete token sequences, enabling action prediction with standard next-token objectives. FAST has substantially improved this representation by compactly encoding action containing diverse temporal frequencies into relatively few tokens. However, while such compression reduces the number of action tokens required for autoregressive prediction, it does not necessarily improve the efficiency of policy learning from limited demonstrations. In particular, FAST typically assigns a single deterministic tokenization to each quantized action sequence, although multiple token sequences can represent and decode to the same robot motion. We investigate whether exploiting this representational redundancy can improve policy learning. In this paper, we propose TO kenization of A ction Sequences with ST ochastic Sampling (TOAST), a stochastic action tokenization method that samples alternative tokenizations of the same quantized action sequence during policy training. This diversifies the discrete supervision while preserving the underlying robot action and requires no additional demonstrations. Experiments on LIBERO show that TOAST consistently improves over its deterministic counterpart, with the improvement increasing as training data decreases, achieving a 6.8 point gain in success rate when only 1 / 16 1/16 of training data is available. Across four real-robot manipulation tasks, TOAST further improves mean success rate by 15.8 15.8 points over the deterministic counterpart. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of stochastic action tokenization for autoregressive robot policy learning, particularly when training data are limited.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs), backed by the success of imitation learning [ 1 ] , have been drawing attention as an approach for realizing general-purpose robot policies [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Autoregressive VLAs [ 2 , 5 , 10 , 9 ] are policies that use a backbone multimodal large language model (MLLM) to predict action sequences as tokens via next-token prediction. Autoregressive VLAs offer advantages over flow matching-based ones [ 6 , 7 ] of having a simpler architecture [ 11 ] , leveraging MLLM’s pre-trained knowledge effectively [ 12 ] , and realizing faster convergence [ 10 ] . In building autoregressive VLAs, the tokenizer determines what the policy has to predict, and recent work has explored efficient compression of action chunks in two ways: learned vector quantization, as in VQ-VLA [ 13 ] , or training-free frequency-based compression, as in FAST [ 10 ] , which applies byte pair encoding (BPE) [ 14 ] to the quantized coefficients of a discrete cosine transform. Both make prediction easier by shortening the token sequence.

However, the tokenization boundaries produced by frequency-based compression such as BPE are not necessarily physically meaningful for robot actions. Once the vocabulary contains tokens spanning multiple quantized action values, the same quantized action sequence can be represented by different token sequences, all of which decode to exactly the same motion. Deterministic tokenizers nevertheless select a single tokenization according to corpus-level frequency statistics, and the policy is trained under cross-entropy to reproduce only that sequence. A similar ambiguity has long been recognized in natural language processing, where stochastic tokenization [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] mitigates over-reliance on a single segmentation and has shown particular benefits when training data are limited. This issue can be especially important in robot learning, where demonstrations are costly to collect. When only limited training data are available, repeatedly supervising each action sequence with the same deterministic tokenization may encourage the policy to overfit to specific token patterns or segmentation boundaries that are not uniquely tied to the underlying motion.

To address this issue, we propose TO kenization of A ction Sequences with ST ochastic Sampling (TOAST), the first stochastic action tokenization framework for autoregressive robot policy learning. As shown in Figure 1 , TOAST samples multiple tokenizations of the same action sequence during training, exposing the policy to different discrete representations while preserving the underlying motion. Moreover, because multiple valid token sequences can be obtained from each demonstration without collecting additional robot trajectories, TOAST increases the diversity of supervision available from limited data. We therefore hypothesize that stochastic action tokenization becomes increasingly beneficial when fewer demonstrations are available. We instantiate this framework with a unigram tokenizer that enables probabilistic segmentation, together with dimension-major flattening for frequency-based action sequence compression.

We evaluate this hypothesis through both controlled simulation and real-world manipulation task experiments. The results show that stochastic tokenization consistently improves policy performance over its deterministic counterpart across training-set sizes, flattening orders, and vocabulary corpora. Notably, the relative benefit of stochastic tokenization is greater when fewer demonstrations are available, indicating improved data efficiency in policy learning. We further observe substantial gains on real-robot manipulation tasks, where collecting demonstrations is particularly expensive. These results show that stochastic action tokenization provides a simple and effective means of extracting more useful supervision from limited robot demonstrations.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify deterministic action tokenization as a source of over-reliance on a single discrete representation and formulate stochastic tokenization as a representation-level regularization effect for autoregressive VLAs.

We introduce TOAST, which samples equivalent tokenizations of the same motion during training, yielding more diverse supervision from each demonstration without additional robot data.

1. We identify deterministic action tokenization as a source of over-reliance on a single discrete representation and formulate stochastic tokenization as a representation-level regularization effect for autoregressive VLAs.

2. We introduce TOAST, which samples equivalent tokenizations of the same motion during training, yielding more diverse supervision from each demonstration without additional robot data.

# II Related work

Vision-language-action models and action tokenization. Inspired by advances in foundation models for natural language processing and computer vision [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to generalist robot policy learning [ 3 , 23 , 2 , 4 , 5 , 24 , 7 , 25 ] . Autoregressive VLAs formulate action prediction as next-token prediction [ 2 , 5 , 10 , 9 ] , making the representation of continuous robot actions as discrete tokens an important design choice. Early approaches use uniform binning to discretize each action dimension and timestep independently [ 2 , 5 ] . More recent methods exploit temporal or cross-dimensional structure to obtain more compact action representations. BEAST [ 26 ] represents action sequences using B-spline control points, while vector-quantization-based methods [ 27 , 28 ] , such as VQ-VLA [ 13 ] , learn discrete latent representations of continuous actions. FAST [ 10 ] instead provides a training-free tokenizer by applying the discrete cosine transform (DCT) followed by byte pair encoding (BPE) [ 14 ] . Our work builds on this frequency-based approach, but focuses on stochastic tokenization of action sequences rather than introducing another compression scheme.

Stochastic tokenization with frequency-based tokenizers. In natural language processing, subword tokenizers such as BPE [ 14 ] and unigram language model [ 15 ] tokenization construct vocabularies from corpus statistics. Given a fixed vocabulary, the same underlying sequence can generally admit multiple valid segmentations, although standard tokenization selects a single one deterministically. Subword regularization [ 15 ] instead samples alternative tokenizations during training, and subsequent work has explored related stochastic tokenization strategies [ 16 , 17 , 29 , 30 ] . These methods have been shown to enable efficient learning in low-resource settings. Frequency-based action tokenizers such as FAST [ 10 ] admit the same segmentation ambiguity, but whether sampling equivalent tokenizations improves robot policy learning has remained unexplored. This work investigates this question.

2026-10-02.title: Real-Time Human-Adaptive Task Allocation for Multi-Human Multi-Robot Supervision
2026-10-02.authors: Seabin Lee , Sujeong Park , Nayoung Kim , Sungjin Park , Haechan Jung , Changjoo Nam
2026-10-02.comment: . This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-02.abstract: We propose a human-factor-aware method of allocating robot supervision tasks to multiple human operators. In scenarios where multiple operators occasionally teleoperate multiple robots to help the robots overcome difficulties, the allocation of the supervisory control tasks to humans needs to consider the real-time cognitive states of individual operators. However, most existing methods assume fixed supervisory capacity per operator and overlook fluctuations in the human factors such as workload and fatigue. As a result, workload distribution can be unbalanced where some operators become overloaded while the others remain underused. Our method dynamically regulates supervisory capacity and allocates tasks in a way that maintains balanced mental workload, prevents overload, and improves overall team performance. The allocation method uses a greedy strategy that minimizes estimated operator workloads with task prioritization. Robots are assigned to operators by reflecting their current supervisory capacity where the required effort depends on the types of tasks. In the user study, the analysis across predefined time intervals shows that the proposed method consistently achieves higher performance and lower behavioral signs of fatigue compared to a baseline method that does not consider human factors. These results highlight adaptive capacity adjustment as an effective preventive mechanism for sustaining operator performance in long-duration, high-demand settings.
2026-10-02.introduction:
The deployment of multi-robot systems in real-world environments continues to expand, aiming toward full autonomy. Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) increases throughput and coordination by determining which robot performs which task [ 1 ] . Although MRTA followed by task and motion planning advances autonomy, current systems still require human supervisors to intervene when robots fail to deal with unexpected events and dynamic changes [ 2 ] . Human supervision remains essential because it pairs robotic precision with human judgment and can enhance safety and accuracy. This means that another task allocation is required between human operators and the dynamically emerging supervision tasks.

However, there are only a few studies on multi-human task allocation in the context of supervising multi-robot systems, and the existing ones typically assume fixed throughput of the human operators, overlooking variations in workload, fatigue, and task performance [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . This assumption would no longer be valid if a small number of operators supervise many robots, as human cognitive resources are fundamentally limited [ 2 ] . During prolonged supervision, workloads tend to increase and performance can decline, requiring the human interface to adapt to the cognitive and physiological states of operators in human-in-the-loop settings [ 6 ] . In addition, operators may differ in skill and performance even for the same type of tasks. Therefore, an effective human-task allocation must not only satisfy mission requirements but also account for real-time human factors and technical capacity.

We propose H uman-factor- A ware M ulti-robot A llocation (HAMA), an adaptive method for multi-human multi-robot (MHMR) supervision that maintains robot task performance while considering human states. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , HAMA estimates human factors such as workload and fatigue and updates the supervisory capacity of each operator (i.e., the maximum number of tasks that can be supervised) at predefined time intervals. We focus on two task types that require supervisory intervention: multi-robot deadlock resolution and docking at charging stations, where failures frequently occur in real-world scenarios. For missions with changing task priorities, HAMA supports reallocation to prioritize more urgent robots over earlier assignments. HAMA also accounts for differences in human factors between task types and across operators by using Area-Of-Interest (AOI) dwell time to estimate visual demand. Then robots requiring teleoperation are assigned to operators based on task priority, visual demand, and current capacity.

HAMA introduces dynamic supervisory capacity that adapts to human factors and mission performance, replacing fixed capacity limits used in prior systems. By integrating subjective reports, behavioral indicators, and physiological signals into a unified update rule, HAMA provides individualized operator capacities and enables real-time robot–operator reallocation as middleware. In user studies, HAMA improved team performance by about 10% and reduced blink counts by 16% compared to a fixed-capacity baseline, demonstrating that adaptive capacity can increase multi-robot throughput while mitigating fatigue in long-duration, high-demand settings.

# II Related Work

## II-A Task Allocation Strategies

The task allocation problem has been widely studied to improve efficiency and mission throughput in multi-robot systems, with more recent work incorporating safety considerations such as collision avoidance to enable scalable and reliable coordination [ 1 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . While most MRTA formulations focus on allocating tasks among robots, human-in-the-loop systems additionally require allocating robots to human operators [ 10 , 11 ] . Prior studies have shown that the number of robots an operator can manage is closely tied to workload and decision time, exhibiting strong sensitivity to human state [ 12 ] . Building on this insight, collaborative human–robot scheduling approaches explicitly model human assignments, availability, and performance constraints within the optimization process [ 13 , 14 ] . Together, these works indicate that operator capacity should be treated as a variable influenced by human factors, rather than as a fixed constant in the allocation problem.

## II-B Human-in-the-Loop Control

Supervisory control often requires continuous monitoring, managing multiple robots simultaneously, and making rapid decisions in time-sensitive situations. These demands place heavy strain on attention and working memory, which can be depleted during prolonged supervision [ 2 , 15 ] . As a result, operator workload and fatigue have a direct impact on task performance [ 16 ] . To mitigate these effects, prior studies have explored interface-level support strategies such as guiding visual attention and adjusting interface transparency [ 7 , 17 ] . However, such approaches typically intervene only after performance degradation becomes apparent and do not adjust task allocation in response to ongoing changes in operator state. Moreover, even under identical task conditions, operators differ substantially in how quickly they become fatigued or overwhelmed, and these individual differences can affect overall team performance.

Motivated by these limitations, recent work has begun to integrate human factors directly into task allocation frameworks [ 18 , 19 ] . For example, [ 18 ] proposed a model that incorporates cognitive workload and affective state when distributing tasks across multiple operators. However, such methods rely on pre-recorded data and trained models, making it difficult to reflect real-time changes or adapt to individual differences during live operation. Despite these advances, empirical research on task allocation frameworks that dynamically update operator capacity and adapt task distribution in real time remains limited. Accordingly, the present study examines how real-time estimation of operator state can enable adaptive and balanced task distribution in multi-human–multi-robot environments.

## II-C Human Factors in Measuring Cognitive States

In practical teleoperation settings, operator state cannot be fully explained by a single factor [ 20 , 21 ] , as cognitive workload and fatigue interactively influence overall performance.
For example, even under low workload conditions, accumulated cognitive fatigue can lead to performance degradation. In contrast, operators with lower fatigue can maintain performance despite high workload demands. Consequently, relying on a single measure introduces limitations in sensitivity and interpretability.

To address this limitation, recent studies [ 22 , 18 ] have integrated physiological, behavioral, and self-reported questionnaire data to achieve more comprehensive estimation of operator state. Each measure captures a distinct aspect of the human cognitive state [ 23 ] , and their integration provides a more comprehensive and complementary representation of human performance dynamics [ 18 ] .
Reliable task allocation in MHMR systems requires accurate estimation of the cognitive state for each human operator. While many previous studies [ 24 , 25 ] have focused on real-time cognitive workload as a predictor of immediate task demands, prolonged operation also induces cognitive fatigue, which gradually depletes mental resources over time. To maintain consistent supervision performance and prevent overload, it is important to consider both mental workload and fatigue together [ 26 ] .

Mental workload represents the cognitive effort required during task execution and can fluctuate based on task complexity, frequency of attention shifts, and decision-making demands [ 27 , 28 ] . As noted by Wickens [ 29 ] , excessive load on shared cognitive channels can lead to interference and reduce task efficiency. Although NASA-TLX [ 30 ] is widely used to measure workload subjectively, it lacks the temporal resolution to track changes continuously during operations.

To overcome this limitation, several studies [ 31 , 32 ] have employed objective indicators such as AOI dwell time obtained through eye-tracking. AOI dwell time reflects how long an operator focuses on specific elements of the interface, making it a sensitive real-time indicator of cognitive workload [ 26 ] . These patterns vary by individual and task types, offering insight into the perceived difficulty of tasks. Accordingly, combining subjective workload rating with objective eye-tracking measures can provide a more accurate and robust estimate of mental workload than either modality alone [ 33 ] .

Cognitive fatigue refers to the gradual decline in cognitive efficiency that occurs during prolonged task engagement [ 34 , 35 ] . It results from the depletion of attentional and mental resources over time, leading to reduced alertness, attention span, and slower decision-making. According to the vigilance decrement model [ 36 ] , sustained cognitive effort without sufficient recovery can diminish performance and reduce operational reliability. In remote environments such as teleoperation [ 37 ] , supervisory control of autonomous systems [ 38 ] , or prolonged VR-based monitoring [ 39 ] , fatigue can gradually accumulate over time. This can undermine human-system coordination and increase the risk of delayed or incorrect responses.

While subjective fatigue scales can capture perceived tiredness, they are often administered periodically and cannot reflect continuous fluctuations during operations. To complement self-reported measures, several studies employed physiological indicators such as blink rate, which has been shown to increase with cognitive fatigue [ 40 , 41 ] and reduced engagement [ 42 ] . A higher blink rate typically reflects increased cognitive fatigue, serving as a sensitive indicator of resource depletion over time [ 40 ] . The blink rate is non-intrusive, continuously measurable, and effective in detecting fatigue in real time without interfering with task performance [ 25 ] . This makes it particularly suitable for supporting task allocation based on real-time fluctuations in cognitive state.

2026-10-02.title: UniTrackPLA: Unified Panorama-Language-Action Model for Instruction-Guided Navigation and Dynamic Person Tracking
2026-10-02.authors: Pengfei Qi , Haoran Lin , Sizhuang Chen , Kai Luo , Sirui Zhang , Xinqi Liu , Fei Cheng , Wenrui Chen , Liming Yin , Kailun Yang
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)

2026-10-02.abstract: General-purpose embodied robots should support both navigation toward language-specified destinations and dynamic person tracking under arbitrary initial target azimuths. However, existing methods typically rely on forward-facing observations and address these tasks with separate policies, limiting omnidirectional perception and unified closed-loop control. We present UniTrackPLA , a unified panorama-language-action model for instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking. Its Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) preserves the temporal and azimuthal structure of perspective views projected from each panorama, enabling perspective-pretrained visual encoders to process omnidirectional observations. A shared vision-language backbone grounds instructions in the panoramic context and predicts continuous robot-centric waypoint chunks for both tasks. World-Action Consistency (WAC) further predicts action-conditioned future visual states and verifies waypoint prefixes online, allowing reliable actions to be reused while triggering replanning upon inconsistency. We also introduce OmniTrackNav-Bench , comprising 5,000 5,000 simulated tracking trajectories, 10,000 10,000 simulated VLN routes, and 96 96 verified real-world routes, providing 919,978 919,978 waypoint-supervision instances. UniTrackPLA improves overall tracking SR from 23.50 % 23.50\% to 35.00 % 35.00\% and Omni-VLN SR/SPL from 13.00 % 13.00\% / 12.77 % 12.77\% to 19.75 % 19.75\% / 19.29 % 19.29\% . Incorporating 76 76 real-world routes further improves held-out EP@0.2m from 42.92 % 42.92\% to 92.08 % 92.08\% . Closed-loop experiments on a Go2-W robot demonstrate unified panoramic tracking and navigation across indoor and outdoor environments. The project page is at https://tw5775.github.io/UniTrackPLA .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Embodied navigation enables robots to move through an environment according to visual observations and task instructions, constituting a fundamental capability for household assistance, human accompaniment, inspection, and mobile manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Existing studies, however, have largely evolved along two separate paradigms. Vision-language navigation mainly focuses on reaching static semantic goals specified by language instructions [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , whereas embodied visual tracking emphasizes continuously following dynamic targets whose positions evolve over time [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction, improving instruction following and generalization in unseen environments [ 2 , 5 , 9 , 14 ] .
Nevertheless, static-goal navigation and dynamic person tracking are still commonly treated separately, with task-specific observations, action spaces, and policies.

We argue that these two tasks should instead be viewed as complementary instances of a broader embodied navigation problem. Instruction-guided navigation is primarily driven by relatively static semantic goals, while person tracking requires continuous adaptation to dynamically evolving physical targets. Despite this difference, both require the robot to ground task-relevant entities, reason about their spatial relationships, and continuously translate visual-language observations into motion decisions.
A more general embodied navigation system should therefore be able to bridge these two regimes within a shared perception-language-action paradigm. This raises a fundamental question: can a single policy support both instruction-guided navigation toward static goals and continuous tracking of dynamic persons under a unified observation and action interface?

Bridging static navigation and dynamic tracking requires a shared omnidirectional perceptual representation.
Panoramic perception provides a natural means of removing this heading dependence by exposing the surrounding scene within a single omnidirectional observation space [ 2 , 5 , 15 ] .
Prior studies have explored panoramic RGB-D observations [ 16 , 17 ] , omnidirectional images [ 18 ] , multiple perspective views [ 7 ] , panoramic environment generation [ 19 , 20 ] , and latent panorama prediction [ 8 ] for static-goal search and vision-language navigation. Recent approaches further incorporate panoramic scene parsing [ 21 ] , dynamic memory [ 22 ] , and global-to-local reasoning [ 23 , 24 ] . Nevertheless, existing panoramic systems mainly focus on static object search, route following, and scene reasoning, while dynamic target localization across arbitrary orientations and panorama boundaries remains insufficiently explored. More importantly, panoramic observations introduce a representation gap: most pretrained visual encoders are optimized for perspective images, whereas panoramic perception requires explicit reasoning over circular spatial structure and temporal evolution. Therefore, the key challenge is not merely to enlarge the field of view, but to retain the transferable representations of pretrained perspective-image encoders while recovering the spatial and temporal structure required for unified panoramic embodied navigation.

A unified policy must also handle the different temporal dynamics of static navigation and dynamic tracking. Continuous waypoint heads improve efficiency by predicting short-horizon action chunks [ 5 , 9 ] , but fixed-horizon execution may become unreliable as the visual world evolves: trajectories that remain valid in relatively stable navigation can quickly become stale when a tracked person changes direction, local traversability changes, or execution errors accumulate. Executing the full chunk risks propagating invalid actions, while using only the first waypoint sacrifices most of the predicted trajectory. The key challenge is therefore how long a predicted trajectory should remain trusted . Since pixel-level world models are costly for real-time control [ 25 , 26 ] , we instead employ lightweight action-conditioned latent future prediction to adaptively regulate the execution horizon.

To bridge static instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking across both perception and execution, we propose UniTrackPLA , a unified Panorama-Language-Action framework. UniTrackPLA formulates both tasks under shared panoramic observations and a continuous waypoint action space. Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) captures visual content, view azimuth, and temporal position while preserving compatibility with pretrained perspective-image encoders, and a shared multimodal policy predicts waypoint chunks for both navigation and tracking. We introduce World-Action Consistency (WAC), which predicts action-conditioned future states in latent space and adaptively determines whether to continue the current chunk or replan, enabling efficient yet responsive closed-loop control.

To support unified training and evaluation, we construct OmniTrackNav-Bench , comprising Omni-Tracking with 5,000 5,000 dynamic-following trajectories and Omni-VLN with 10,000 10,000 language-annotated panoramic navigation routes. Both tasks share the same panoramic observation and continuous waypoint representation, enabling unified multi-task learning within a single policy. We introduce a real-world
panoramic navigation dataset comprising 96 96 routes.

Closed-loop experiments show that UniTrackPLA achieves a 35.00 % 35.00\% success rate on Omni-Tracking, compared with 23.50 % 23.50\% for our reproduced TrackVLA
baseline, and reaches 19.75 % 19.75\% SR and 19.29 % 19.29\% SPL on Omni-VLN, outperforming the baseline results of 13.00 % 13.00\% and 12.77 % 12.77\% . Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of PAE and WAC. With this dataset, EP@0.2m
on held-out real-world routes improves from 42.92 % 42.92\% to 92.08 % 92.08\% . Real-world deployment on a Go2-W robot with an Insta360 X4 further demonstrates both dynamic person tracking and instruction-guided navigation
using the same policy.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose UniTrackPLA , a panoramic VLA framework that bridges dynamic person following and vision-language navigation through shared panoramic perception, visual-language representations, and a continuous waypoint action space. Its PAE module jointly models panoramic azimuth and temporal context while reusing pretrained perspective-image encoders.

We introduce a lightweight World-Action Consistency module that unifies temporal action execution across static navigation and dynamic tracking. By predicting the latent future consequences of waypoint prefixes, WAC adaptively regulates the effective action horizon and dynamically determines whether to continue the current chunk or trigger replanning.

We construct the OmniTrackNav-Bench to support joint training and consistent evaluation across static navigation and dynamic tracking, comprising Omni-Tracking for arbitrary-orientation human following and Omni-VLN for dense panoramic language navigation. Extensive simulation experiments and real-robot deployments validate the effectiveness and generality of the overall framework.

2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Embodied Navigation

Existing embodied navigation methods can be broadly divided into static-goal navigation and dynamic-person following.
Static-goal navigation guides a robot toward a specified location according to language instructions, target categories, or reference routes.
Recent methods unify multiple navigation tasks and improve generalization across environments, embodiments, and long-horizon routes [ 2 , 5 , 14 ] , while observation-instruction augmentation further facilitates transfer to unseen environments [ 27 ] .

Dynamic person following instead requires continuous target identification and motion adaptation.
Hierarchical approaches bridge high-level user instructions and low-level tracking actions through intermediate spatial goals [ 28 ] .
Other modular approaches employ visual foundation models, offline reinforcement learning, and vision-language models to improve target representation, failure recovery, occlusion handling, and cross-embodiment adaptation [ 10 , 11 , 29 , 30 ] . End-to-end methods further incorporate referring comprehension, target memory, competitive interaction, and trajectory planning into vision-language-action policies [ 9 , 12 , 13 , 31 ] , while recent benchmarks evaluate long-term tracking, socially aware following, and unified target seeking and following [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] . However, most existing tracking methods rely on limited-FoV forward-facing cameras and assume that the target is initially visible in front of the robot, leaving side, rear, and panorama-boundary initialization underexplored.

## II-B Panoramic-Aware Embodied Navigation

Panoramic-aware navigation methods can be broadly divided into panoramic-perception-based navigation and panorama-assisted navigation.
The former directly uses panoramic RGB-D observations, omnidirectional images, or multiple perspective views for target-driven, open-vocabulary, and language-guided navigation [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
In particular, view-decomposed panoramic representations preserve local visual details while retaining compatibility with visual encoders pretrained on perspective images.
The latter leverages generated panoramic environments, complementary views, or predicted latent panoramic features to bridge the observation gap between monocular and panoramic navigation [ 7 , 8 , 19 , 20 ] .
Recent methods further combine panoramic scene parsing, dynamic memory, panorama-to-local reasoning, and 3D scene representations for mapless object navigation and zero-shot vision-language navigation [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] , while other studies investigate spherical directional reasoning and establish benchmarks for panoramic urban navigation and general embodied navigation [ 6 , 24 , 35 ] .
Beyond navigation, omnidirectional perception has also enabled beyond-FoV humanoid manipulation and panorama-aware mobile manipulation [ 4 , 36 ] .
Nevertheless, existing panoramic embodied systems primarily focus on static object search, route following, scene reasoning, or manipulation, leaving dynamic person following under arbitrary initial orientations, particularly cross-view localization and identity preservation, less explored.
Moreover, navigation and person following are commonly modeled using separate representations, action spaces, and policies.
A unified panoramic vision-language-action policy for both instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person following remains insufficiently studied.

2026-10-02.title: Kinematic MeanFlow: One-Step Action Generation Policy for Robotic Foundation Models
2026-10-02.authors: Jiawei Fan , Sifeng Wang , Yuqing Hou , Anbang Yao
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

2026-10-02.abstract:
In this paper, we study how to achieve one-step action generation in Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs), aiming to overcome the high inference latency of multi-step flow matching. MeanFlow provides a promising framework for this goal, yet its direct application leads to performance collapse.
We discover that this stems from two distinctive dynamics exhibited in the RFM velocity field: (1) the “local acceleration” exhibits stability early on, but surges sharply towards the end of the denoising process, and (2) the spread of its magnitudes across samples widens as denoising progresses.
To address these issues, we introduce Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF) , a novel one-step action policy tailored for RFMs.
Specifically, grounded in a kinematic identity, K-MF decouples the time derivative term in the MeanFlow formulation into two sub-interval terms separated by an intermediate point.
This decoupled formulation enables the two terms to capture early-stage and late-stage denoising dynamics, respectively,
while mitigating the error amplification across the process.
As a result, our K-MF empowers RFMs to achieve one-step action generation in both training from scratch and fine-tuning paradigms across diverse tasks, while outperforming multi-step flow matching in most settings.
In terms of inference efficiency, K-MF reduces action-head latency of GR00T-N1.6 by 67.5%–74.4% across L40 and Jetson Orin in eager and compiled modes, yielding end-to-end latency reductions of 30.3%–54.9%. Code will be available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/K-MF .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Background. Robotic foundation models (RFMs) aim to establish a generalist robot manipulation policy
capable of real-time execution across diverse robotic embodiments.
Driven by this vision, the architecture of RFMs has continuously evolved.
The first evolution concerns the multimodal backbone. Early RFMs ( Jang et al., 2021 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) employ FiLM-conditioned convolutional neural networks to fuse the language instructions and visual observations.
Spurred by the remarkable generalization capabilities of large/vision language models (LLMs/VLMs) ( Touvron et al., 2023a ; Touvron et al., 2023b ; Beyer et al., 2024 ) , some studies ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) leverage them as the core foundation for RFMs. Generally, such architectures integrate a pre-trained VLM 1 1 1 For brevity, we use “VLM” to represent architectures that either employ a pre-trained VLM or pair a pre-trained LLM with a vision encoder, as their training and inference pipelines in RFMs are conceptually identical. as the backbone to autoregressively generate discrete action tokens. However, this creates a severe inference burden for real-time control and thus drives the second major evolution in action generation policies.
Recent RFMs ( Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) adopt transformer-based flow matching policies. Specifically, flow matching establishes a velocity field mapping Gaussian noise to valid actions.
Using features obtained from a single VLM forward pass, the policy iteratively queries the transformer to predict instantaneous velocities across denoising timesteps, progressively transforming noise into multiple actions in parallel.
Even as recent architectures ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) explore replacing VLM backbones with diffusion transformers (DiTs),
flow matching remains the prevalent choice for action generation in RFMs.

Motivation. Although this policy enables parallel action generation, its iterative forward passes required for denoising incur non-negligible inference overhead. Taking GR00T-N1.6 as an example, action head latency occupies about 40% of the end-to-end (E2E) inference time on desktop GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA L40) and up to 50% on robotic edge platforms (e.g., NVIDIA Jetson Orin).
In other words, the computational burden of the action head critically reduces the overall decision frequency of RFMs.
Therefore, reducing the number of denoising steps becomes a critical issue.
From a broader perspective, MeanFlow has recently emerged in image generation as a remarkably simple alternative to complex distillation or consistency constraints for one-step generation. Unlike flow matching that predicts instantaneous velocity 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} at timestep t t , MeanFlow aims to learn the average velocity 𝐮 t , r \mathbf{u}_{t,r} 2 2 2 Here, t , r ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t,r\in[0,1] , with 0 0 denoting clean data
and 1 1 denoting pure noise. We use 𝐮 t , r \mathbf{u}_{t,r} as shorthand

Once trained, by directly predicting the average velocity across the endpoint timesteps, the model achieves one-step denoising in a single forward pass. In action generation, there have been a few efforts that built upon the MeanFlow formulation.
In imitation learning, MP1 ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) couples 3D inputs with a dispersive loss on latent features to prevent representation collapse. Other studies improve MeanFlow in reinforcement learning (RL).
MVP ( Zhan et al., 2026 ) introduces an instantaneous velocity constraint to stabilize RL training; MeanflowQL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) reformulates MeanFlow into a residual mapping to enable joint optimization with Q-learning; DMPO ( Zou et al., 2026 ) combines dispersive regularization with PPO fine-tuning for one-step policy learning. These efforts remain focused on specialist policies , where directly applying MeanFlow typically yields viable, albeit degraded, performance. In contrast, we empirically find that MeanFlow breaks down under the standard training recipe in generalist RFMs , motivating us to investigate the fundamental issues underlying this failure.

Observations and underlying issues. In principle, the ground-truth average velocity between t t and r r is defined as the time-averaged integral of instantaneous velocities.
To avoid the costly integration, MeanFlow reformulates the learning target to a form that evaluates locally at timestep t t : average velocity 𝐮 t , r \mathbf{u}_{t,r} equals the combination of instantaneous velocity 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} and the time derivative term d d ​ t ​ 𝐮 t , r \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} (see Eq. 3 ).
As 𝐯 t \mathbf{v}_{t} remains constant for a given sample during training, the time derivative term primarily drives the optimization.
To investigate the challenges of adapting MeanFlow to RFMs, we compare the dynamics of “local acceleration” ( Δ ​ 𝐮 / Δ ​ t \Delta\mathbf{u}/\Delta t ) between image generation and action generation in RFMs across denoising timesteps. As shown in Figure 1(a) , the local acceleration of image generation is stable throughout denoising with a narrow spread. In contrast, RFMs exhibit distinctive dynamics, characterized by two key observations with corresponding issues:

The local acceleration surges sharply in the late denoising stage (i.e., t < 0.3 t<0.3 ), ultimately reaching 76 × 76\times its initial value at t = 1 t=1 . Issue 1: The time derivative term tends to incur substantial estimation errors if the model fails to infer the global trend from local observations 3 3 3 Local acceleration reflects d d ​ t ​ 𝐮 t , r \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} ( t − r < ϵ t-r<\epsilon ), whose temporal stability decides local-global consistency. .

The spread of local acceleration magnitude widens as denoising proceeds (indicated by the expanding red shaded area). Our further analysis in Figure 5 reveals that the extent of this spread is strongly correlated with the task diversity of the RFM training data. Issue 2: Minor estimation errors in the early denoising stage tend to be amplified as this spread widens.

Design insights and contributions. Our method builds on a fundamental kinematic identity: for any intermediate point c ∈ ( r , t ) c\in(r,t) , the average velocity 𝐮 t , r \mathbf{u}_{t,r} is exactly equal to the convex combination of the average velocities over the two sub-intervals 𝐮 t , c \mathbf{u}_{t,c} and 𝐮 c , r \mathbf{u}_{c,r} .
Leveraging this identity, we decouple the derivative d d ​ t ​ 𝐮 t , r \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,r} into two sub-interval terms, d d ​ t ​ 𝐮 t , c \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} and d d ​ c ​ 𝐮 c , r \frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r} . This is primarily driven by two considerations: (1) for the first issue, the term d d ​ t ​ 𝐮 t , c \frac{d}{dt}\mathbf{u}_{t,c} guarantees robust estimation in the early denoising stage, while d d ​ c ​ 𝐮 c , r \frac{d}{dc}\mathbf{u}_{c,r} focuses exclusively on corrections in the late denoising stage; (2) for the second issue, a second estimation at timestep c c serves as an anchor to reduce the impact of the widening spread and thereby mitigate error amplification throughout the denoising process.
Given this decomposition, we further investigate how to determine the intermediate point c c . We empirically find that a fixed midpoint clearly outperforms uniform random sampling, despite the latter covering a broader range of interval partitions. This suggests that the placement of the estimation anchor, rather than partition diversity, is critical.
We then introduce a learnable strategy that adaptively determines c c conditioned on t t and r r , yielding the best performance among the considered strategies.

This is validated by our systematic experiments across: (1) two training paradigms, including training from scratch and fine-tuning of pre-trained flow-matching RFMs; (2) different RFMs, including GR00T-N1.6 and SimVLA; (3) four datasets with varying training data scales, ranging from 658 to 87K trajectories; and (4) both Sim2Sim and Real2Sim evaluation settings.

# 2 Related Works

Diffusion and flow models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ) are initially designed for image generation.
To improve inference efficiency, previous studies have extensively explored how to reduce the required sampling steps.
One line of work focuses on deriving a few-step model from a pre-trained many-step baseline through score or flow distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Yin et al., 2024 ) .
Another line of research relies on consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2024 ) , which employ consistency constraints to ensure outputs along the same path share identical endpoints. Recently, MeanFlow models ( Geng et al., 2025 ; Geng et al., 2026 ) have emerged as a compelling alternative, which enables one-step generation by predicting the average velocity between any two timesteps. Several studies introduce intermediate points into MeanFlow to enforce consistency across interval partitions ( Li et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) or facilitate curriculum learning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
These studies primarily aim to improve training efficiency or mitigate gradient discrepancies of MeanFlow in image and audio generation tasks. This has clear differences from our method in motivation, scope, and design .

For specialist policies in robotics, Diffusion Policy ( Chi et al., 2023 ) pioneered the integration of diffusion algorithms into action generation.
Inspired by few-step algorithms in image tasks, FlowPolicy ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and Maniflow ( Yan et al., 2025 ) set a consistency constraint for flow matching in imitation learning, while CP ( Ding and Jin, 2024 ) adapts this concept to behavioral cloning and actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms.
Similarly, several recent studies adapt MeanFlow in action generation for both imitation learning ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) and reinforcement learning ( Zhan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ) , as we have discussed before.

Prevalent generalist RFMs ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) widely adopt flow matching for action generation. However, in stark contrast to specialist policies, research on few/one-step action generation in RFMs remains underexplored. Prior works ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Luan et al., 2026 ) typically apply methods developed for image generation directly to RFMs or restrict their evaluation to a limited range of tasks and models. Differently, we reveal the unique dynamics of RFM velocity fields, design K-MF accordingly, and comprehensively validate it across models, tasks, and training paradigms.

2026-10-02.title: Are Frontier VLM Agents Ready to Be Robot Generalists? An Empirical Study with the Embodied Agent Arena
2026-10-02.authors: Haojian Huang , Pukun Zhao , Zexi Li , Yehang Zhang , Yangkai Wei , Wenqian Li , Han Yang , Kaiwen Zhou , Ying-Cong Chen , Yinchuan Li
2026-10-02.comment: including appendices. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) combine scene estimation, interaction grounding, and executable actions. Understanding how these abilities support complete robotic tasks is central to evaluating their readiness as robot generalists. We introduce Embodied Agent Arena to examine where local competence supports, or falls short of, complete task success across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation. The arena contains 1,000 cases drawn from 32 established sources and GeoProbe, our new benchmark for geometric estimation on Blender renders and real-scene images. A minimal harness preserves source observations and operations while separating metric precision, functional grounding, and native goal completion. We evaluate seven VLMs, analyze Astra’s task-specific advantages, and compare richer-observation execution protocols and multi-round review. Across the arena, Astra’s advantage is strongest in precise estimation and usable-contact localization; completing coordinated, goal-directed actions remains the key gap to robot generalism.
2026-10-02.introduction:
A robot generalist must turn scene understanding into actions that satisfy a complete goal. Estimating where an object lies, selecting a usable contact, and executing a grasp are useful abilities, yet none establishes that the object reaches its required destination. Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly address spatial relations ( Ma et al., 2024 , Yang et al., 2024 ) and action-relevant grounding ( Wang et al., 2025a , Song et al., 2024 ) . Learned visuomotor policies connect observations to robot actions ( Kim et al., 2024 , Black et al., 2024 ) , while language-model controllers select skills or generate executable programs ( Ahn et al., 2022 , Liang et al., 2022 ) . Frontier VLM agents now combine observation, programming, and feedback-driven decisions ( Fu et al., 2026 , Guo et al., 2026 ) , making the relationship between local competence and complete execution a practical evaluation question.

Capability breadth and reliable completion require different evidence. An average score can hide whether errors concern metric scale, an object’s reference frame, or the final condition of a placement. Conversely, a terminal failure can conceal useful progress. Evaluating these outcomes separately reveals what a model can do and which additional requirements remain unsatisfied. Generalist readiness therefore calls for both cross-capability comparisons and task-level diagnoses.

We ask: Are frontier VLM agents ready to be robot generalists? Embodied Agent Arena evaluates the same models across Geometry, Spatial Reasoning, Affordance, Task Planning, and Manipulation (Figure 1 ). Its 1,000 cases combine 32 established sources with GeoProbe, our geometric-estimation benchmark. GeoProbe varies camera motion, object motion, and scale references to test which quantities remain accurately estimated as visual conditions change. A minimal harness preserves source observations and operations. Continuous errors, task-specific evidence, and terminal success reveal complementary aspects of agent capability.

Our comparisons locate the remaining gap in task requirements: Astra produces the closest paths yet often misses their endpoints, and its local manipulation strengths coexist with low household-goal completion. Under matched budgets and execution limits, richer visual observations reverse Astra’s CALVIN lead while producing gains on other tasks. A separate multi-round review study measures which answers improve after reinspection or specialist measurements. Our contributions are:

An evaluation perspective centered on task requirements. We distinguish local estimates and interaction evidence from complete goal satisfaction across five robotic capability domains.

A unified arena with a new geometric benchmark, GeoProbe. We combine 32 established sources with 168 GeoProbe cases, using controlled Blender scenes and real images to diagnose camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation.

A capability baseline for frontier VLM agents. We characterize seven agents across five robotic application domains within specified inference-time and execution budgets, with task-level comparisons and a deep dive into Astra’s strengths and failure modes.

2. A unified arena with a new geometric benchmark, GeoProbe. We combine 32 established sources with 168 GeoProbe cases, using controlled Blender scenes and real images to diagnose camera, motion, depth, and scale estimation.
