# 2 Related Work

Embodied evaluation has developed along two complementary directions. Control suites measure execution and task generalization through robot interfaces ( James et al., 2019 , Mees et al., 2021 ) , whereas visual diagnostics isolate spatial inference ( Ma et al., 2024 , Yang et al., 2024 ) and interaction grounding ( Song et al., 2024 , Qian & Fouhey, 2023 ) . The former establishes whether a goal is achieved; the latter resolves particular perceptual or reasoning requirements. Concurrently, Hard Vision, Easy Vision ( Rasheed et al., 2026 ) maps frontier models against specialist and human references across general vision, including geometry, grounding, and online navigation. Its visual-capability perspective complements our focus on action-conditioned contacts, robot control, and complete task goals.

Broader evaluations connect perception with decision-making ( Li et al., 2024b , Qi et al., 2025 ) , including navigation and object interaction through executable interfaces ( Yang et al., 2025a , Cheng et al., 2025 ) . Embodied Arena combines fixed probes and interaction ( Ni et al., 2025 ) . Interfaces also change the model’s work: code supports reusable controllers ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , while persistent state introduces memory demands ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Embodied Agent Arena connects visual diagnostics with robot execution by separately scoring geometric estimates, contact grounding, and terminal outcomes (Table 1 ), then examining how execution settings change model rankings.

2026-10-02.title: Reactive Humanoid Multi-Contact Using Learned Stability Models
2026-10-02.authors: Stephen McCrory , Beomyeong Park , Nicholas Kitchel , Nehar Poddar , Robert Griffin
2026-10-02.abstract: We present a planning and control approach to reactively use hand contacts to stabilize a humanoid in low stability scenarios, where only using feet contacts may result in a fall. Candidate contacts are sampled within the robot’s reachable workspace, and a preview is computed by rolling out the centroidal dynamics through pre-impact, impact and post-impact phases. Sampled points are scored based on the Center of Pressure (CoP) control authority at the post-impact phase. Central to our approach is a learned model of the robot’s CoP region during post-impact, which enables rapid evaluation of candidate contact points compared to traditional optimization-based methods. The presented planner has two stages: the first selects an optimal bracing region and the second computes an optimal bracing point within the region. Our simulation results demonstrate an average increase in impulse resilience of 89% over recovery without hand contacts and 17% over a naive planning strategy (closest reachable region). We validate our framework on hardware, performing push tests while standing and walking. The standing trials show an average 43% reduction in stabilization time compared to naive hand placement and the walking trials demonstrate a 18% reduction compared to baseline recovery (without hand contacts).
2026-10-02.introduction:
As humanoid robots become capable of performing tasks in real-world scenarios, reliability becomes increasingly important. For this reason, push recovery has a rich history in legged robotics, with the broad goal of maximizing robustness [ 12 , 24 , 7 , 16 ] . However, in spite of numerous successful strategies for bipedal push recovery, existing approaches are largely restricted to quasi-flat terrain and feet contacts. Making full use of the humanoid form-factor means utilizing upper body contacts to augment lower-body recovery techniques. Additionally, it requires models that go beyond quasi-flat terrain and handle arbitrary contact surfaces.

In this work, we propose a sample-based hand contact planner that reactively braces in low stability scenarios where the use of only foot contacts may result in a fall, such as the scenario in Fig. 1 . Sampled contact points are previewed by rolling out the robot’s centroidal dynamics through pre-impact, impact and post-impact phases. The pre-impact and impact phases can be rolled out using conventional closed-form models such as the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM) [ 12 ] . In contrast, the post-impact contact state cannot be modeled as a basic LIPM, but instead using optimization-based models that are compatible with arbitrary contact sets [ 3 , 21 ] . Each roll-out is scored based on the Center of Pressure (CoP) control authority at the post-impact phase.

A central part of our approach is a set of neural networks that predict the feasible CoP placement at the post-impact rollout phase. We train these models using reference CoP data computed through conventional optimization-based techniques. These networks enable rapid evaluation of the robot’s post-impact state, with around 40 × \times speed-up compared to optimization-based techniques. We apply these networks in a contact planner which performs two passes for each hand. The first pass selects the optimal bracing surface by scoring the closest reachable point on each candidate surface. The second pass samples within the optimal surface (if one exists) to compute the optimal bracing point.

Reactive contact planning for legged robots has been widely studied, with many successful hardware demonstrations. Reduced-order models such as the Linear Inverted Pendulum Model [ 12 ] , the Angular Linear Inverted Pendulum [ 10 ] and Single Rigid Body Model [ 13 ] enable efficient previews of the robot’s centroidal dynamics. In turn, these models have been leveraged in heuristics for step placement, such as Raibert’s heuristic [ 25 ] and the Capture Point [ 24 , 8 ] . Since these heuristics have closed-form linear representations, they have been applied in mixed-integer frameworks that select optimal contact surfaces online [ 1 , 14 , 29 , 5 ] . Following this approach, Mason et al. [ 18 ] reactively plan hand contacts by first previewing a footstep sequence containing a slack variable for centroidal tracking. If this slack variable is sufficiently high, a solver activates which scores candidate hand contacts based on a recovery preview, given a heuristic maximum hand pushing force. Such applications of centroidal models have been successful, but have the caveat of requiring linear or quadratic functions to encode cost and constraints and often are applied only to quasi-flat terrains.

A related line of research addresses motion feasibility under arbitrary contact conditions given unilateral, friction and actuation constraints. Seminal work by Bretl et al. [ 3 ] posed this as a Linear Program, enabling efficient quasi-static stability assessment. This approach has been extended towards improving solve times [ 6 ] , addressing dynamic stability [ 2 ] and modeling actuation constraints [ 21 ] . Marucci et al. apply a similar model to multi-contact planning on a piecewise affine map [ 17 ] . Other centroidal-based reactive recovery strategies have explored adapting gait frequency and posture to achieve high stability [ 15 , 9 ] .

There have also been machine-learning based approaches that aim to model stability and assess contact sequences. One approach, and the one taken in this work, is training a network to mimic an expensive optimization-based stability model [ 22 ] . Alternatively, Lin et al. use simulation data to train a set of networks to predict zero- and one-step capturability, given a robot’s state and environment [ 16 ] . These networks are applied in a graph-search that optimizes for predicted success in the presence of disturbances, such that the robot walks nearby potential bracing surfaces. This approach of using procedurally generated simulation environments has seen many applications in legged motion planning [ 4 , 19 ] . Rouxel et al. use datasets from teleoperated hardware experiments to train a network to load/unload a humanoid’s hand based on predicted stability [ 26 ] .

This work builds on the core concepts of reduced-order models to achieve reflexive response times, while maintaining accurate stability modeling under arbitrary contact conditions by applying learned stability models. Our work particularly builds on the MPC-style bracing planner by Mason et al. [ 18 ] and the concept of optimal region selection by Corbères et al. [ 5 ] . In building on these approaches, this work contains the following novel contributions.

A reactive ( ≤ \leq 10 ms) contact planner that models recovery for arbitrary (e.g. tilted or vertical) surfaces.

A reactive ( ≤ \leq 10 ms) contact planner that models recovery for arbitrary (e.g. tilted or vertical) surfaces.

A set of neural network models that predict the robot’s feasible CoP placement given arbitrary combinations of hand and feet contacts.

Simulation demonstrations of the planner’s capability to out-perform a naive heuristic through a comparison of the minimum unrejectable impulse.

Hardware demonstrations of the planner and controller’s capacity to use hand contacts to recover from high impulses.

2. A set of neural network models that predict the robot’s feasible CoP placement given arbitrary combinations of hand and feet contacts.

2026-10-02.title: TRACE: Privacy-Preserving Next-Best-View Selection over Distributed 3D Gaussian-Splat Maps
2026-10-02.authors: Amirhossein Mollaei Khass , Athanasios Cosse , Qiyu Sun , Nader Motee
2026-10-02.abstract:
Share the light, not the map. We study next-best-view selection for a team of robots,
each of which builds its own 3D Gaussian Splatting map and keeps it private. A robot
picks the view with the largest expected information gain (EIG) about the splats along
its own path. This gain depends on the other maps. Their splats occlude its own and shine behind them,
so the gain has to be evaluated against the pooled map. No robot has this map. We show that the coupling passes through only two ray quantities, the transmittance
in front of a splat and the radiance behind it, and that both are sums over the hits of
the ray. Hence, they decompose across the robots and each robot sums them over depth bins in its own map, along the rays of a
candidate view, and sends the sums with their pose derivatives. The robot planning the
view turns them into its EIG and gradient on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) . Transmittance and Radiance
Aggregates, Communicated for the EIG, give the protocol its name: TRACE. No robot shares its splats, and the message
size does not grow with a map. We prove that the reconstruction is exact unless a depth
bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. Over 100
next-best-view decisions in Habitat-Sim, TRACE picks a heading within 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} of the
centralized one in 83.3 % 83.3\% of the cases, and its views reach 97.9 % 97.9\% of the
centralized EIG.
2026-10-02.introduction:
A team of robots enters a building after an earthquake. Each robot maps what it sees and
plans where to look next, in order to reconstruct the part of the scene it must traverse
well enough to move through safely. The difficulty is that no robot sees everything it
needs from where it stands. The far side of a corner ahead of it is already behind a
second robot, and the top of a shelf it passes under was seen by a third that flew over
it. Such viewpoints are out of reach, yet they hold the geometry that keeps the first
robot safe. The value of a view is therefore a team
quantity [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . A robot that scores its views on its
own map alone looks where the team has already looked, and still misses what it cannot
see. Coordinating these views is hard under limited bandwidth, energy and
computation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

We build these maps with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 7 ] . A 3DGS map is
a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, and a view is rendered by projecting them onto
the image plane and compositing them front to back along each
ray [ 8 , 9 ] . The render is differentiable in the parameters of the
map and in the pose of the camera. Next-best-view (NBV) methods exploit this property to
pick poses that reduce the uncertainty of the
map [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . The rendering Jacobian
gives the sensitivities that build a Fisher information objective, which is then optimized over the pose.

In a team of robots, this objective couples the maps at the level of the render. A
centralized method sends the observations or the local maps to a server, which builds
one 3DGS map and evaluates the team objective on
it [ 14 , 15 ] . A distributed
method keeps them on board, and then no robot holds the whole scene. Along a shared ray,
the contribution of a primitive depends on the light that reaches it through the hits in
front of it, and on the radiance behind it. Both are set by the joint depth order of all
primitives on the ray, which no robot knows from its own map. A robot that renders only
its own map therefore biases the objective and its gradient.

We propose TRACE, a distributed NBV method that rebuilds these two quantities without
sharing observations or Gaussian parameters. Along the rays of a candidate view, each
robot reports the t ransmittance and r adiance a ggregates c ommunicated for the E IG, which is where the name comes from. These
aggregates are sums over depth bins. Hence, they carry what the other maps place along a
ray without revealing which splats placed it. Each robot then evaluates the pooled-map
gradient on its own and turns its camera, with no consensus over viewpoints.

Main contributions. (i) We show that the EIG of a view, and its pose-gradient, depend on the maps of the
other robots only through two quantities on each ray, the transmittance in front of a
splat and the radiance behind it. (ii) We derive the pose-gradient of the masked EIG on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) in closed form from the outputs of a standard rasterizer. (iii) We propose
TRACE, a protocol in which the robots exchange these two quantities in depth bins, with
their pose derivatives, and never their splats; the message size does not depend on the
number of splats. (iv) We prove that the EIG and its gradient are exact when no depth
bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. (v) We
test TRACE in simulation against the centralized computation.

Related work. NBV methods select camera poses that maximize information gain or improve coverage.
FisherRF [ 10 ] scores a view by the trace of a diagonal Fisher information
matrix, and COVER [ 13 ] builds an efficient coverage surrogate from an
approximation of it. GAVIS [ 11 ] models view-dependent uncertainty with an
anisotropic visibility field, and RT-GuIDE [ 16 ] uses the updates of the
Gaussian parameters as a cheap information proxy. Others add risk-aware
masks [ 17 ] or couple information gathering with safety-critical
control [ 18 , 19 ] . Across a team, views are classically picked from
finite candidate sets by greedy submodular maximization on one shared
map [ 20 ] . All of these score a view on a map the planner can access.
Multi-agent neural mapping solves the other half of the problem, which is to build one
consistent model from distributed observations. Di-NeRF [ 1 ] trains a NeRF by
consensus and RAMEN [ 6 ] maps asynchronously. For 3DGS,
MAGiC-SLAM [ 5 ] merges local submaps by loop closures,
MAC-Ego3D [ 2 ] enforces geometric consistency by Gaussian consensus, and
CoMA-SLAM [ 14 ] works on Gaussian
surfels, while others cut communication with compact
submaps [ 4 , 15 ] . All of these build one map of the whole scene.
Closest to our goal is distributed risk-averse NBV over 3DGS
maps [ 3 ] , where each robot scores its views on its own map and
consensus reconciles the team. That work distributes the optimization, and the splats of the other robots never enter a local render. TRACE distributes the render instead. No global map is formed, and each robot evaluates the gain of the pooled map from what it receives along the rays of its own view.

2026-10-02.title: Getting Out and Getting Back: World and Behavior Grounding in Real2Sim2Real Co-Training
2026-10-02.authors: Samuel Liu , Youngsun Kim , Martin Matak , Gilwoo Lee
2026-10-02.abstract: Simulation can expand scarce real demonstrations for co-training, yet how world fidelity and similarity to human behavior affect policy performance remains unclear. We distinguish world grounding , which aligns simulation with the real system, and behavior grounding , which aligns simulated trajectories with human motion. We build a real2sim2real pipeline that varies these axes independently to generate data for co-training. On a dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort task, fully grounded co-training raises success from 52% to 86%; averaged across configurations, world grounding improves success by 18 percentage points and behavior grounding by 10. Deployed policies behave like a mixture of real-derived and simulation-derived policies , imitating real demonstrations in covered states and relying on simulated behavior elsewhere, which we examine through latent-space analysis. Together, these results suggest complementary roles: world grounding lets policies use simulated experience beyond real-data coverage, while behavior grounding matters mainly when world grounding is imperfect. Grounded simulation remains beneficial when co-training foundation models.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Human demonstrations, particularly teleoperation, are a primary source of data for robot learning [ 1 , 28 ] . This is especially valuable for dexterous manipulation, where rewards are hard to design and high-dimensional space makes exploration difficult for reinforcement learning [ 18 ] . However, collecting diverse and high-quality demonstrations is costly [ 21 , 16 , 5 , 15 , 12 ] , while variations across demonstrations can introduce inconsistency [ 16 , 28 ] .

Simulation offers a way to achieve both diversity and quality. From a small set of real demonstrations, simulation data can be generated at scale, with domain randomization adding diversity [ 23 , 15 ] while success filtering preserves quality [ 15 ] . Such data have been shown to be especially valuable when co-trained alongside real data, even when real data is scarce [ 25 , 14 ] .

However, simulated and real data inevitably differ. To better understand the downstream effect of the sim2real gap, we separate the grounding of the simulation data into two axes: World Grounding and Behavior Grounding . The world gap lies in how the simulator’s rendering, physics, and robot control differ from the real system, while the behavior gap lies in how simulated trajectories differ from human demonstrations. Existing real2sim2real pipelines ground simulation in real environments and demonstrations through environment reconstruction, motion refinement, and demonstration adaptation [ 24 , 8 , 15 ] . Although these approaches improve policy performance, the individual and combined contributions of world fidelity and human-like behavior remain unclear.

We hypothesize that world grounding is the primary factor in co-trained policy performance since it determines whether actions learned in simulation have the same effect on the real robot. However, because world grounding is never perfect in practice, behavior grounding plays an important role in keeping simulated behavior close to real demonstrations, which the policy can fall back on.

We investigate the impact of world grounding and behavior grounding on policy performance on a dynamic dexterous pick-and-sort task with objects on a moving conveyor belt. We build a real2sim2real pipeline in which each axis can be independently set to grounded or ungrounded, letting us conduct a 2×2 factorial experiment. Policies for all four configurations are co-trained on 100 real demonstrations and 1,500 simulated episodes and evaluated over 50 real-world rollouts that include both nominal and shifted conditions.

Our main contributions are the following:

Independent grounding control. We introduce a pipeline that separates world and behavior grounding, enabling a controlled study of their individual and combined effect on dynamic dexterous manipulation.

Transition between real-derived and simulation-derived behavior. We observe that co-trained policies switch between the two within a rollout, adopting simulated behavior in states covered only by simulation, even when it differs substantially from human behavior.

Relevance to foundation models. We show that grounded simulation still benefits post-trained foundation models, extending these findings beyond policies trained from scratch.

1. Independent grounding control. We introduce a pipeline that separates world and behavior grounding, enabling a controlled study of their individual and combined effect on dynamic dexterous manipulation.

2. Transition between real-derived and simulation-derived behavior. We observe that co-trained policies switch between the two within a rollout, adopting simulated behavior in states covered only by simulation, even when it differs substantially from human behavior.

3. Relevance to foundation models. We show that grounded simulation still benefits post-trained foundation models, extending these findings beyond policies trained from scratch.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Sim-and-Real Co-Training. Co-training combines scarce real demonstrations with larger simulated datasets, improving generalization to conditions absent from the real data [ 14 , 25 , 13 , 20 ] . The benefit depends on simulation mismatch: Wei et al. find a greater sensitivity to physics gaps than to visual gaps, with small visual differences sometimes improving performance [ 25 ] . These findings motivate our controlled comparison of world fidelity and trajectory behavior, varying each independently on the same task.

World Grounding. Prior work aligns simulation through camera calibration, scene reconstruction, and identification of robot dynamics and control [ 9 , 24 , 22 ] , while randomizing appearance to broaden coverage [ 23 ] . The importance of each component varies across settings: physical mismatch dominates some co-training results [ 25 ] , whereas rendering fidelity matters more than contact parameters in a study of zero-shot VLA transfer [ 11 ] . We examine how world grounding affects co-trained policies under a common task and its interaction with behavior grounding.

Behavior Grounding. Synthetic trajectories can be generated by adapting human demonstrations [ 15 , 10 ] , reinforcement learning [ 27 , 29 ] , or motion planning with grasp synthesis [ 3 , 4 ] . These approaches differ in how closely their motions follow human demonstrations. Although machine-generated data can support strong policy performance [ 27 , 29 ] , whether preserving human motion improves co-training independently of world fidelity remains unclear. We compare demonstration-derived and machine-generated trajectories in both grounded and ungrounded worlds.

2026-10-02.title: ECoMEM: Explicit Concept Memory for Memory-Dependent Robot Control
2026-10-02.authors: Yize Liu , Ke Wang , Mac Schwager , Yiqing Xu , Jiajun Wu
2026-10-02.comment: Project website: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
A robot may lose sight of an object it must later retrieve, need to recall
what a person demonstrated earlier, or track which steps of a task it has
already completed. Current vision–language–action (VLA) policies often
fail once the information needed for action disappears from the current
observation, making memory critical for long-horizon robot behavior.
Existing approaches typically provide longer histories or learn implicit
memory from observation–action trajectories. But action supervision tells
a policy how to act , not what to remember : it does not specify
which past facts should persist or how they should change as new evidence
arrives. We therefore separate maintaining an evidence-grounded account of
the past from learning how to act on it . This insight motivates Explicit Concept Memory (ECoMEM) , which represents task-relevant
history with a reusable library of grounded concepts. An evidence-based
Writer selects and updates these records, while a learned Reader turns
them into memory tokens that directly condition the VLA. Across 16 RoboMME tasks, ECoMEM leads the evaluated robot policies on
15 tasks. On two new real-robot tasks, the same memory library either
transfers directly or requires only one new concept, achieving 86.1 % 86.1\% success versus 8.6 % 8.6\% for a no-memory VLA. These results show that
explicit concepts provide a reusable and extensible memory interface for
robot control. Project website .
2026-10-02.introduction:
A robot that acts over extended periods cannot treat every observation
as a fresh start. It may need to remember where an object was last seen
after it becomes occluded, which object a person interacted with earlier,
what parts of a task have already been completed, or the order in which
previous events occurred. In each case, the information needed for the
next action is no longer available in the current observation. Yet the
relevant past is often much smaller than the full interaction history:
what matters is a compact set of task-relevant facts about entities,
states, events, and progress.

Vision–language–action (VLA) policies increasingly incorporate history
through extended context, recurrent representations, learned memory
banks, and test-time adaptation ( Torne et al., 2025 ; Koo et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) .
These mechanisms can preserve rich perceptual history, but they leave an
important question implicit: what from that history should become
memory? Action supervision specifies what the robot should do, but not
which past facts should be retained, when a belief should be revised, or
when two observations correspond to the same event. When memory is
learned only through the control objective, the policy may instead rely
on shortcuts in current observations, previous actions, or
trajectory-specific correlations ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Successful action prediction therefore does not by
itself establish that the task-relevant history has been represented
reliably.

Making memory explicit helps, but does not remove the problem of memory
construction. Keyframe memories preserve visual evidence ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ) , leaving the policy to recover the
relevant facts from stored images. VLM-based approaches summarize
histories ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ; Anwar et al., 2025 ) , but place entity tracking,
state estimation, and temporal interpretation inside long-video
reasoning, where spatial and temporal errors remain challenging ( Qi et al., 2025 ; Seth et al., 2025 ) . Textual world states ( Yoneda et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) and scene graphs ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Rana et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) provide more structured
representations, but a robotic memory must additionally decide how
observations become persistent facts: what should survive occlusion,
what should be revised, what constitutes a completed event, and how
repeated evidence should be reconciled.

Our key idea is to separate maintaining an evidence-grounded
account of the past from learning how to act on it . Rather than
asking the policy to infer memory implicitly from history, we represent
task-relevant history as explicit facts about entities, states,
completed events, progress, and temporal order. These facts are updated
only when supported by visual and robot-state evidence, while the policy
learns how they should influence action. This separation also keeps task
requirements distinct from observations: the instruction specifies what
should be achieved, while memory records what has actually happened.

We instantiate this principle in Explicit Concept Memory
(ECoMEM) , an explicit memory channel for VLA policies
(Figure 2 ). First, a shared concept library provides reusable
memory primitives spanning entity and spatial grounding, state and
relations, events and progress, and temporal and procedural structure.
Second, an evidence-based Writer selects the concepts required by
the instruction, grounds them to task entities, and maintains their
records over time, while a learned Reader maps the resulting
structured memory into latent tokens. Third, these memory tokens directly
condition the VLA alongside visual and language inputs. Recognition and
memory writing remain fixed during policy training, so evidence determines what is remembered , while action supervision learns how that
memory should be used .

Across the 16 memory-dependent tasks of RoboMME ( Dai et al., 2026 ) ,
ECoMEM achieves the highest average success among the evaluated robot
policies and leads on 15 of 16 tasks. Controlled experiments show that
spatial grounding, event and progress information, temporal structure,
task-conditioned selection, and language grounding each contribute to
effective memory construction. More importantly, the same abstraction
transfers to new physical-robot tasks: CupSwitch reuses the
existing library without adding a new recognizer, while ScoopPour requires only one new event concept composed with the
existing memory machinery. Across shared real-robot conditions, ECoMEM succeeds in 68 / 79 68/79 trials ( 86.1 % 86.1\% ), compared with 5 / 58 5/58 ( 8.6 % 8.6\% )
for the no-memory π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} baseline. These results suggest that
explicit, compositional concepts can serve not merely as task-specific
memory annotations, but as a reusable and extensible interface between
a robot’s accumulated experience and learned control.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Implicit memory in robot policies

History-aware robot policies typically learn a latent representation of
past observations and actions. Long-context policies directly attend to
extended trajectories ( Torne et al., 2025 ; Koo et al., 2026 ) ; recurrent architectures propagate
learned state across time ( Li et al., 2026 ) ; memory-bank methods compress and
retrieve past perceptual features ( Shi et al., 2026 ) ; and test-time adaptation
stores history in model weights ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Predictive world models similarly
maintain latent state for control ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Samsami et al., 2024 ) . These approaches can
capture rich temporal dependencies without prescribing what the representation
must contain. However, what is retained, forgotten, or updated is learned
largely through downstream objectives and remains difficult to inspect
independently of the policy. ECoMEM instead externalizes a sparse set of
task-relevant facts and fixes their evidence-based updates, while learning only
how the policy should use them. Explicit and latent memory are therefore
complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

## 2.2 Explicit memory in robot policies

A second line of work stores selected parts of experience explicitly.
Keyframe and retrieval methods retain event-triggered images or trajectory
segments ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Memmel et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2024 ) ; MemER retrieves
task-relevant visual experiences and uses a high-level VLM to condition a
low-level policy ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches summarize experience into language ( Anwar et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , maintain textual world states ( Yoneda et al., 2024 ) , or organize persistent information in scene graphs ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Rana et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . These representations improve
access to past information, but visual memories still require the controller
to recover facts from stored observations, while language and graph memories
are commonly consumed by high-level reasoning or planning modules. ECoMEM
instead maintains typed, evidence-linked records of states, events, progress,
and temporal structure, and feeds them directly to a low-level VLA through a
learned Reader.

## 2.3 Neuro-symbolic methods in robotics

Neuro-symbolic robotics combines learned perception and control with
explicit, compositional abstractions. Knowledge representations such as
KnowRob organize persistent robot knowledge ( Tenorth and Beetz, 2009 ) ;
neuro-symbolic concept learning and structured world models ground
symbolic concepts in perception and compose them for reasoning ( Mao et al., 2019 ; Mao et al., 2022 ) ; and learned or invented predicates provide compact
abstractions for task planning ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Athalye et al., 2026 ; Silver et al., 2023 ) . Related work also
uses symbolic concepts to structure learned generative models for
manipulation and geometric reasoning ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) .
Recent systems further use vision–language models to construct symbolic
planning abstractions from demonstrations ( Lorang et al., 2026 ) , while
knowledge graphs provide structured memory for language-model agents ( Anokhin et al., 2025 ) . ECoMEM follows the same principle of grounding reusable symbolic concepts
in learned representations, but uses them for a different role: as the
interface between perceptual history and a learned control policy.

2026-10-02.title: DITTO-X: Forward and Reverse Teleoperation for Dexterous Manipulation and Human Intervention
2026-10-02.authors: Zhanpeng He , Joaquin Palacios , Zhangyu Wang , Chenhao Li , Katelyn Lee , Matei Ciocarlie , C. Karen Liu , Jiajun Wu
2026-10-02.abstract:
Teleoperated demonstrations are a primary source of data for robot manipulation, and teleoperated interventions are a primary mechanism for correcting policies at deployment. Yet most teleoperation systems close the loop through vision alone and are built around parallel-jaw grippers, limiting both what the robot can execute and what the operator can express through it.
This is most damaging in shared autonomy, where the operator sees the scene only through occluded cameras and must take over a dexterous hand mid-task, often with an object already grasped.
We present DITTO-X, a hand-agnostic dexterous teleoperation interface that renders joint-level force and fingertip contact events from sensing already on the robot hand, and drives three commercial dexterous hands (Sharpa, Wuji, and Inspire) without per-hand redesign. Because the exoskeleton is actuated, DITTO-X also supports reverse teleoperation , in which the robot back-drives the operator’s fingers into its own configuration before control is transferred, so the human enters the loop already matched to the state they inherit. Our results show that DITTO-X improves demonstration quality and throughput over a commercial hand-tracking glove, both in regular data collection and in human intervention during policy deployment for contact-rich manipulation tasks.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Teleoperation plays a fundamental role in modern robotics, letting humans directly supervise, guide, and demonstrate complex manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 ] . In robot learning, teleoperated demonstrations remain a critical complement to scripted motion, human video, and handheld collection devices [ 3 , 4 ] , capturing the precise, contact-rich interactions that passive or ungrounded approaches struggle to reproduce. At deployment time, shared autonomy and human-in-the-loop frameworks rely on teleoperation to let operators intervene at uncertain or safety-critical moments [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , and the interventions they produce can be used to improve the policy.

Despite their widespread use, most teleoperation systems are poorly matched to dexterous manipulation. They are built around parallel-jaw grippers, which bound the natural movement an operator can demonstrate in the first place, and they close the loop through vision alone. Humans do not manipulate this way; we regulate contact forces, detect incipient slip, and reshape a grasp from cues we feel rather than see. Without those cues, the operator is blind to contact, and demonstrations are rendered slow and conservative. The limitation is therefore not only what the robot can execute, but also what the human can express through it.

This limitation becomes a failure mode in shared autonomy . When collecting demonstrations from scratch, the operator can both position themselves to see the scene and restart a failed attempt at little cost. Intervening on a running policy affords neither. Perception is restricted to onboard cameras, under which self-occlusion by the arm and hand is often unavoidable, especially at critical contact moments. The operator also inherits the robot’s state mid-task, so the kinematic mismatch between the human hand and the robot hand must be resolved at that exact moment. During tool use or in-hand manipulation, a non-smooth transition at takeover is enough to drop or break the object, resulting in unrecoverable failures.

We present DITTO-X, a dexterous interface for transparent teleoperation that works across different robotic hands for both regular data collection and human intervention. Improving the design of DITTO [ 8 ] , which requires strict 1-to-1 kinematics between leader and follower and instruments only two fingers, DITTO-X is a hand-agnostic framework and currently drives three commercial, five-finger dexterous hands (Sharpa Wave, Wuji 2, and Inspire RH56DFX) without per-hand redesign. It closes the feedback loop at two levels: sustained joint-level force via motors on the exoskeleton and discrete fingertip contact events via haptics from sensing already available on the robot hand. This allows the operator to feel both when contact is made and how hard the robotic hand is squeezing, restoring cues that vision-only interfaces lack.

Our actuated exoskeleton can also be used to improve human intervention through a novel operating mode we call “reverse teleoperation” : while an operator is supervising an autonomous policy deployment, the exoskeleton can actively drive the operator’s fingers to match the robot’s current configuration. This allows for a seamless transition of control once the operator takes over and gives them a kinesthetic sense of the policy actions.

Our user study and policy learning results show that DITTO-X improves both the throughput and the quality of data collected for contact-rich policy training. With reverse teleoperation, operators intervene on a running policy fluently, without dropping objects already in hand, yielding better data for subsequent policy improvement.
We summarize our contributions as follows:

We present a dexterous teleoperation framework, equipped with force and haptic feedback, with support for three commercial robotic hands, spanning 6 to 22 actuated DoF, without hand-specific redesign.

We introduce reverse teleoperation , in which the actuated exoskeleton back-drives the operator’s hand to match the robot’s configuration, so that intervention on a running policy begins from a matched state rather than a discontinuous handoff.

We open-source the full system, including hardware design, forward and reverse teleoperation, and policy training and fine-tuning details. We also release all 1.8k episodes of contact-rich manipulation data from three embodiments, spanning teleoperated demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous policy rollouts.

1. We present a dexterous teleoperation framework, equipped with force and haptic feedback, with support for three commercial robotic hands, spanning 6 to 22 actuated DoF, without hand-specific redesign.

2. We introduce reverse teleoperation , in which the actuated exoskeleton back-drives the operator’s hand to match the robot’s configuration, so that intervention on a running policy begins from a matched state rather than a discontinuous handoff.

3. We open-source the full system, including hardware design, forward and reverse teleoperation, and policy training and fine-tuning details. We also release all 1.8k episodes of contact-rich manipulation data from three embodiments, spanning teleoperated demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous policy rollouts.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

Teleoperation for dexterous hands. Dexterous teleoperation has largely been studied as a problem of closing the kinematic gap between the operator’s hand and the robot’s: vision-based hand tracking [ 9 ] , non-wearable leader-follower designs [ 10 ] , and learned retargeting priors [ 11 ] each attack it differently, but none renders contact back to the operator, who is left to infer it from vision alone.
Motorized exoskeletons do render force, yet packaging actuators alongside the fingers forces a choice about what to render. DOGlove [ 12 ] reduces feedback to a single axis per finger, while GEX [ 13 ] and N2D [ 14 ] map forces in task space; neither tells the operator which joint is loaded. DITTO [ 8 ] recovers joint-level feedback by enforcing a one-to-one correspondence between leader and follower joints, at the price of being tied to a single two-fingered manipulator. In this work, we remove that restriction and extend the design to five-fingered hands.

Shared autonomy, human intervention and DAgger. A large body of work improves manipulation policies with human feedback, including interventions [ 15 , 16 ] , preferences [ 17 ] , rankings [ 18 ] , and scalar rewards [ 19 ] . Interactive imitation learning, in which the agent queries an expert during execution and aggregates the resulting corrections [ 20 , 21 ] , underpins systems that collect data where the policy actually fails [ 22 , 23 ] . Because continuous supervision is costly, much of this literature concerns when to request help [ 24 , 6 , 7 , 25 , 26 ] , and a parallel line supplies it through language rather than teleoperation [ 27 , 28 ] . Most of these works study when a human should intervene. In this work, we look into the problem of how to intervene on a policy.

How authority passes between an autonomous controller and a human has also been studied. Blended and traded control arbitrate continuously, predicting the operator’s goal and blending toward it [ 29 , 30 ] or applying guidance forces that shift authority without a discrete switch [ 31 ] ; when a switch is unavoidable, the resulting transient is well documented in automated driving [ 32 ] . Our setting differs in what must be made continuous. A dexterous hand transferred mid-task is usually already holding an object, so a pose mismatch at the instant of transfer releases or displaces it rather than merely perturbing a trajectory. Reverse teleoperation removes this discontinuity in the operator’s state rather than the controller’s, conforming the human to the robot before authority passes.

2026-10-02.title: Measuring Asset and Scene Reconstruction Effects in Real-to-Sim Robot Evaluation
2026-10-02.authors: Sanya Verma , Luca Cilio , Velissarios Christodoulou
2026-10-02.abstract: Simulated evaluation is increasingly used alongside real-world evaluation of robot policies because it is cheaper and easier to repeat; however, its value depends on how closely its outcomes track the real robot’s. We test whether our reconstruction pipeline, combining metrically scaled object geometry, authored physical parameters and scene reconstruction, reduces disagreement between simulated and real robot scores relative to a default open-source recipe. We constructed two simulated versions of one bimanual robot cell: an authored reconstruction, using object geometry at estimated metric scale, projected textures, authored physics and our own scene splat; and a baseline, referred to as the default reconstruction, using the open-source recipe of a generative single-image mesh, engine-default physics and a Gaussian-splat scene. Both reconstructions use the same object photographs and scene video. Two policies ran five tasks each, giving ten task-policy pairs, which we call cells; each cell was run twenty times in each reconstruction with all other settings held fixed. Both reconstructions were scored against the same real trials, graded by a third-party evaluator. Pearson correlation between the ten simulated and real cell means is r = 0.90 for the authored reconstruction and 0.51 for the default. Mean score error is 6.97 percentage points for the authored reconstruction and 17.54 for the default, a reduction of 10.56 percentage points. These results show that improving the quality of the environment reconstruction through higher visual fidelity, authored physics and metric scale makes the simulation more faithful to the real world and narrows the sim-to-real gap. We release the harness, the per-trial scores, every reported run’s configuration, and the assets and scenes of both reconstructions.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Evaluating a robot policy on hardware is costly and labour-intensive, and because real rollouts can be stochastic and hard to control systematically, a result is difficult to repeat exactly [ 1 , 2 ] . One alternative to hardware is a digital twin: a simulated copy of the real robot cell in which the same policy runs the same tasks. SIMPLER [ 1 ] reported a strong correlation between simulated and real performance for the policies and tasks it studied. PolaRiS [ 2 ] and SimFoundry [ 3 ] build the twin from a short video scan of the robot cell and report Pearson correlations (r) of 0.90 and 0.91 respectively between simulated and real scores.

The remaining disagreement between real and simulated scores is attributed to two sources, both identified by SIMPLER [ 1 ] . The first is the visual gap: rendered images differ from real camera images. The second is the control gap: the simulated arm responds differently to the same command. Later work varies factors within these two categories. PolaRiS [ 2 ] compares four rendering conditions of the same scene, from Gaussian splatting to fully untextured, and measures the change in r and mean maximum rank violation (MMRV). Wang et al. [ 4 ] vary vision, language, layout and behaviour across nine tasks and five policies. How the manipulated objects themselves are reconstructed is not among the sources these studies vary.

In these pipelines, object physics is not investigated as a source of disagreement between real and simulated scores: it is left at engine defaults or estimated by a model without validation against measurement. PolaRiS builds object geometry with open-source TRELLIS [ 9 ] from several segmented views of each object, then sets “standard physics parameters for contact dynamics using default values from IsaacSim” and notes that “object mass parameters can be estimated by the users” [ 2 , Section 4 .1] ; object physics is left at engine defaults. SimFoundry [ 3 ] , like our pipeline, authors mass and friction per object, but reports only how well its complete output agrees with real, so the effect of that step is not measured.

Prior results suggest that the effect of authored physics is not negligible. Phys2Real [ 5 ] shows that better estimates of an object’s centre of mass raise real task success, although it measures success, not agreement between simulated and real evaluation. The nearest evidence on agreement between real and simulated evaluation is Wang et al. [ 4 ] , who find that agreement is governed by simulator fidelity instead of purely object-level mismatch; their test varies which object is present, not how well a fixed object is built. The only measurement of asset fidelity against agreement is on deformable objects: Zhang et al. [ 6 ] replace PhysTwin’s [ 8 ] optimised per-spring stiffness with a single global value and MMRV on a rope-routing task rises from 0.174 to 0.248. No study that we are aware of measures how the fidelity of a fixed set of rigid objects changes agreement between simulated and real evaluation (Section 2 ). We therefore build one cell twice: an authored reconstruction, with our pipeline, which reconstructs geometry from one photograph, estimates metric scale from a ChArUco calibration board and authors physics per object, and a default reconstruction, a PolaRiS-inspired recipe, TRELLIS at its single-image setting with engine-default physics (Section 3 ).

We test whether the authored reconstruction narrows the sim-to-real gap in robot performance relative to the default reconstruction. Both reconstructions are run with the same policies and tasks and scored against the same real trials (Figure 2 ). The reconstructions differ on three axes. Object geometry and texture: reconstructed and projected from a single photograph of the object, scaled from a printed ChArUco calibration board of known size (authored), against a generative single-image mesh scaled by eye (default). Object physics: mass, friction and restitution authored per object, against engine defaults. Scene: our reconstruction splat pipeline, against a PolaRiS-inspired Gaussian-splat recipe, both from the same handheld video. Every other part of the run (robot model, controller, camera, placement and step budget) is identical between the reconstructions (Section 3 ).

Our main finding is that a reconstruction with metrically scaled geometry, authored physics and our own scene reconstruction taken together narrows the sim-to-real gap relative to the default recipe used in the literature: score error is 10.56 percentage points lower and progress disagreement 8.32 percentage points lower across five tasks and two policies, both with 95% intervals that exclude zero. The other two agreement measures, correlation and failure-stage disagreement, do not separate the two reconstructions with ten cells. We release the harness, the four agreement measures and the real reference of 200 paired trials, five tasks by two policies, run and graded by a third-party evaluator [ 11 ] , and the assets and scenes of both reconstructions, so the comparison can be repeated on other cells and pipelines.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Prior work relevant to this study falls into three groups: real-to-sim evaluation systems, the pipelines those systems use to create assets, and methods that estimate physical properties.

For real-to-sim evaluation systems, SIMPLER [ 1 ] reported a strong correlation between simulated and real performance for the policies and tasks it studied, named the visual and control gaps, and introduced mean maximum rank violation (MMRV), which measures whether a simulator ranks policies in the same order as the real robot. PolaRiS [ 2 ] reconstructs the robot cell from a video scan and reports r of 0.9 on average and 0.81 at worst over six environments and four policies. Its ablation of the environment itself is visual: the same scene is rendered in four ways, as a Gaussian splat, as a ray-traced textured mesh, with the background untextured, and fully untextured, and both r and MMRV worsen as texture is removed. SimFoundry [ 3 ] reports r = 0.911 and MMRV 0.018 over seven tasks and five policies, and a higher correlation than a PolaRiS baseline on its own tasks; it varies nothing about the assets. Wang et al. [ 4 ] extend to nine tasks and five policies and argue that a reliable simulator must also reproduce failure modes. Their one test on objects replaces the manipulated object in a pick-and-place task (a banana replaced by five other produce items) and finds the policy ranking unchanged, from which they conclude that simulator fidelity, not the choice of object, drives the gap between real and simulated performance. Each of these studies builds one simulated copy of each real setup and reports how well that copy agrees with reality; none builds the same setup twice and measures how the agreement changes.

Among pipelines that create assets, PolaRiS [ 2 ] leaves mass unset unless the user enters it, so PhysX assigns a density of 1000 kg/m 3 over the collider volume, friction 0.5 and restitution 0.0. Its published object assets carry a single uniform root scale and convex-decomposition colliders. SimFoundry [ 3 ] is the pipeline closest to ours in what it automates: from an RGB video it segments objects, generates meshes with an image-to-3D model, aligns them to the scene’s RGB-D reconstruction, builds CoACD convex colliders, and assigns mass and friction per object from a scene-understanding vision-language model. It differs from our authored reconstruction in geometry (a different image-to-3D model), scale (from depth, not a ChArUco board), collision (convex decomposition throughout, against signed distance fields on seven of our sixteen object kinds) and physics (per object from a vision-language model in both; ours combines the model’s class, mass and restitution with a per-class friction table).

The third group estimates physical properties of objects. Phys2Real [ 5 ] combines vision-language priors over an object’s centre of mass with online identification from interaction, and finds that better estimates raise real task success. TwinAligner [ 7 ] optimises mass, friction and centre of mass against real trajectories. Both methods improve the estimate of an object’s physical properties, but neither measures how the quality of the estimate changes agreement between simulated and real evaluation. The nearest such measurement is on deformable objects: Zhang et al. [ 6 ] remove PhysTwin’s [ 8 ] per-spring stiffness optimisation, leaving a single global value, and MMRV on a rope-routing task rises from 0.174 to 0.248. No study we are aware of varies the geometry, scale or physics of a fixed set of rigid objects and measures the change in agreement.

2026-10-02.title: CF-JEPA: Improving Robustness of JEPA World Models via Controllability Factorization
2026-10-02.authors: Morgan Byrd , Robert Wright , Sehoon Ha
2026-10-02.comment: Website: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: Controlling an agent with vision requires being able to separate useful information from irrelevant background information. JEPA-style latent world models seem like a natural approach for this, as they do not perform pixel-level reconstruction; however, they are still sensitive to these distractor signals and experience latent collapse. In this work, we introduce Controllability Factorized JEPA (CF-JEPA), a JEPA-style world model which splits the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces. This factorization allows us to capture all the distractor information into the uncontrollable region, while we use the control-relevant latent information for our task. With this, we show comparable performance across 2D and 3D control tasks under nominal conditions and improved performance under distracted conditions, where CF-JEPA is the only model that does not experience latent collapse. We also validate our model under distracted conditions for a simulated robot task, highlighting the practical application of such a scheme.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humans are capable of performing tasks using visual control, regardless of what sort of background visual distractor information or noise might be present. Random objects moving into the visual field can be easily ignored and do not interfere with task progress or break our understanding of the world. Robots deployed in diverse environments should likewise accomplish their tasks despite such visual distractors. Thus, a reasonable expectation of a generative world model might be to have a similar invariant nature to these kinds of external visual stimuli.

However, typical world models [ 1 , 2 ] struggle under these conditions as they rely on pixel-level reconstruction to learn their representations, and reconstructing such random content is difficult and wasteful. There have been attempts to handle this [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , but they often still rely on reconstructing the scene along with additional techniques or rely on assumptions that may not hold in realistic robotic scenarios.

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) appear to be a natural way to handle this kind of distraction, as they remove the generative model built on pixel-level reconstruction and predict dynamics in latent space instead. However, we find that such JEPA world models [ 6 ] like LeWM are still very susceptible to task-irrelevant visual distractor signals, and the latent space collapses as a result. Incorporating an inverse dynamics loss as in Sensorimotor World Model (SMWM) [ 7 ] improves robustness, but it still uses the full latent rather than separating distractor elements from control.

Building on the JEPA framework, we propose CF-JEPA, a world model with additional latent structure for improved robustness under visual distractor signals. We incorporate controllability factorization, where we partition the latent space into a control-relevant, action-conditioned region and a control-irrelevant, action-free region. This explicit partition has a minimal to moderate impact on nominal performance and offers a strong benefit in the presence of visual distractors, where CF-JEPA is the only tested model that does not collapse.

We evaluate CF-JEPA against LeWM and SMWM on four visual control tasks and a simulated robot task. With two visual distractors, LeWM collapses on all tasks, and SMWM collapses on Reacher, where its success rate drops to 0.10 while CF-JEPA retains 0.48. As the number of distractors grows, SMWM degrades rapidly, and its success rate on PushT and TwoRoom falls from 0.86 and 0.98 respectively to 0.27 and 0.46 as it collapses, while CF-JEPA maintains 0.57 and 0.82 respectively. We further hypothesize that the benefit of controllability factorization is most evident when the action space requires perceiving the state of the agent, and we confirm this on the simulated robot task. Finally, a diagnostic decoder on Reacher shows that the controllable latent of CF-JEPA preserves the agent, whereas the baseline latents lose the agent.

Our key contributions are the following:

CF-JEPA, a simple world model architecture that improves robustness to irrelevant visual distractors via controllability factorization, where we separate the irrelevant, uncontrollable environment features from the relevant, controllable features in our latent space.

CF-JEPA, a simple world model architecture that improves robustness to irrelevant visual distractors via controllability factorization, where we separate the irrelevant, uncontrollable environment features from the relevant, controllable features in our latent space.

We thoroughly compare against benchmarks and show that we match under nominal conditions and outperform under visual perturbations, across a suite of 2D and 3D control tasks, along with a simulated robot task.

We analyze the latent space to examine the effect of the controllability factorization.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A World Models

World models [ 8 ] are a way of learning the dynamics of an environment via generative models directly from data. Learning the latent representation via reconstruction of the input pixels is a common method, seen in the Dreamer [ 1 , 9 , 10 ] series of models, along with many others including [ 2 , 5 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Other methods for learning models without reconstruction include contrastive learning [ 3 , 14 ] and prototypical representations [ 15 ] . More recently, joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) [ 16 ] have gained prominence by constructing the model via predicting feature-space targets rather than pixels. JEPA style models vary widely and include many methods for preventing collapse, including using a pretrained encoder as in Dino-WM [ 17 ] , via a VICReg loss [ 18 ] as in PLDM [ 19 ] , and via a SIGReg [ 20 ] loss as in LeWM [ 6 ] . We build off LeWM for our work, where we add an inverse dynamics loss and augment the latent space with additional structure in order to improve robustness.

## II-B Inverse Dynamics for World Models

Inverse dynamics is the process of computing the required forces or torques to produce a given reference trajectory. It is popularly used in robotics for control of manipulator arms [ 21 , 22 ] and walking robots [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] as well as used in guidance application [ 26 ] . In machine learning, it is leveraged for computing actions given a reference video [ 27 , 28 ] or motion capture sequence [ 29 ] and for representation learning [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] . For world modeling specifically, learning an inverse dynamics model is commonly used for acting in imagination, as in [ 1 , 33 ] , as well as representation learning, as in [ 7 , 34 , 35 ] . The most relevant case for our work is the concurrent work Sensorimotor World Models (SMWM) [ 7 ] , which builds off LeWM, removing the SIGReg loss and adding an inverse model as an anti-collapse mechanism. We also leverage an inverse dynamics loss, but we use it to structure the latent space into controllable and uncontrollable subspaces, giving improved results in terms of robustness over the standard inverse dynamics loss.

## II-C Distractor Robustness

Rejecting irrelevant distractor signals and focusing on only task relevant information is key for effective visual control. The reconstruction free world model methods above tackle this by not spending capacity modeling every pixel but capturing the underlying state [ 3 , 15 ] . In model-free RL, bisimulation [ 4 , 36 ] is one method for generating useful, robust representations from pixel based environments without reconstruction. Task Informed Abstractions [ 5 ] and Denoised MDPs [ 37 ] partition the latent space similarly to ours, but still require reconstruction and thus still expend some model capacity for representing the pixel level view of the environment, which can be especially difficult if there are distractor signals. We avoid pixel level reconstruction and gain robustness via separating the controllable latent subspace from the uncontrollable portion, and using only the controllable section for control.

2026-10-02.title: Toward Humanoid Robots in Construction: A Teleoperation Feasibility Study
2026-10-02.authors: Parastoo Ali Pour , David R. Martin , Chang Min Hur , Bo Zhang , Tommy Zhou , Brandon Thomas Lichter , Shane Stanfield , Pramod Khargonekar , Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque
2026-10-02.comment: Accepted at IROS 2026 Workshop on Future of Construction
2026-10-02.abstract: We present a teleoperation system that enables a single operator to perform construction tasks on a Unitree G1 humanoid, combining extended reality (XR) based upper body control with pedal-based locomotion to enable simultaneous manipulation and locomotion. Motivated by persistent labor shortages, hazardous working conditions, and challenges in humanoid autonomy, we investigate teleoperation as a practical near-term approach for reducing physical strain on workers while generating high quality demonstration data. We evaluate the system on two representative construction tasks drawn from O*NET occupational database, and report task success and completion time relative to a manual baseline. The system achieved 100% success on tool transport and 80% success on surface painting, with teleoperation requiring substantially more time compared to manual execution.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Humanoid teleoperation systems span a spectrum of control coupling. Decoupled systems control the upper and lower body through separate interfaces [ 14 , 15 ] , while recent whole-body systems track the operator’s full pose to drive the entire body [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . These systems have enabled humanoids to perform diverse real-world tasks, including locomotion [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , object manipulation and transport [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , and even dexterous medical procedures [ 17 , 18 ] . Many existing systems [ 11 , 12 ] also require the operator to physically reproduce the robot’s motions, including walking comparable distances and squatting to reach low objects retaining much of the physical burden and limiting the feasibility of sustained operation.

Construction robotics has pursued task-specific automation [ 5 ] [ 6 ] as well as autonomous humanoids such as HRP-5P, which demonstrated drywall installation but relies on extensive environmental modeling and remains slow outside scripted conditions [ 19 ] . More recently, teleoperation has been applied to construction arms for precise pick-and-place tasks while collecting imitation-learning data [ 20 ] , as well as semi-humanoid mobile manipulators for construction tasks [ 21 ] . However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has evaluated the feasibility of full body teleoperation of a humanoid robot for construction tasks.

2026-10-02.title: TacDyn-WAM: Learning Implicit Tactile Dynamics in a Heterogeneous Visuo-Tactile World Action Model
2026-10-02.authors: Enyi Wang , Mingxin Wang , Quan Shi , Hetian Guo , Hongyu Wang , Xi Wang , Bin Qian , Yupeng Zheng , Wenxuan Song , Houde Liu , Yong Xu , Cheng Chi , Wenchao Ding , Yilun Chen , Yan Wang
2026-10-02.abstract:
World action models improve robotic manipulation by conditioning actions on predicted futures, yet existing tactile variants largely inherit video-generation pipelines that reconstruct future tactile observations through iterative denoising.
Such prediction can become unreliable under deployment drift: small changes in contact position or force may substantially alter tactile pixels even when the underlying contact evolution remains predictable.
We introduce TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that predicts implicit tactile dynamics rather than reconstructing future tactile observations.
It learns TacRep, a dynamics-aware tactile target space trained through masked spatio-temporal prediction on tactile clips and regularized by relational structure distillation.
A visual expert and an Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert predict future visual and tactile representations in separate target spaces while interacting through joint attention; the tactile expert predicts future representations and their changes at multiple horizons in a single forward pass, and a read-only tactile memory supplies the current tactile state.
On UniVTAC, TacDyn-WAM achieves an average success rate of 81.5% using only the provided demonstrations, reaching state-of-the-art-level performance and remaining competitive with models pretrained on large-scale visuo-tactile trajectories.
Ablations confirm the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives.
On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM reaches 71.0% average success, and modest-scale pretraining raises it to 85.0%, further validating our method. Project page .
2026-10-02.introduction:
World models forecast how observations evolve, while world action models use this foresight for policy learning, allowing actions to depend on predicted futures rather than current observations alone ( Cai et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026c ; Ye et al., 2026a ) .
Yet in existing world action models, this foresight comes primarily from vision.
In contact-rich or precision manipulation tasks, such as insertion and alignment under occlusion, cameras cannot fully resolve contact states, local geometry, or interaction forces.
Early efforts incorporated tactile sensing into VLA models, giving rise to vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) models that encode tactile observations alongside vision and language ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Bi et al., 2026b ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
By understanding the current tactile state, they improve contact-rich manipulation over vision-only policies.
However, they do not predict how this state will evolve, leaving policies reactive to tactile feedback.
Recent tactile world action models close this gap by predicting future tactile observations as part of the world model ( NeoteAI Team et al., 2026a ; Lou et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026 ) .
These models have achieved promising results, with some further benefiting from large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining.
Despite this progress, a core design question remains: what should tactile world models predict?

Most existing methods simply reuse video-generation pipelines: the same VAE encodes camera and tactile frames, while video backbones iteratively denoise future tactile latents.
This slows inference and ties prediction to pixel reconstruction, which is poorly suited to tactile observations.
Expert demonstrations cover only tactile images near correct contacts, whereas closed-loop errors may cause policies to drift from them.
This drift may leave camera views nearly unchanged, yet even slight changes in contact position or force can substantially alter tactile images, pushing them farther from the demonstration distribution.
Despite these pixel-level changes, contact evolution—whether an imprint deepens, slides, or rotates—often remains predictable.
We therefore argue for implicit tactile dynamics modeling : predicting contact evolution in a dynamics-aware representation space rather than reconstructing future tactile observations.

Latent prediction is a step toward this goal, but not every latent space is equally suited to forecasting tactile evolution. N 0 N_{0} -VTLA ( NeoteAI Team et al., 2026b ) predicts the net tactile change at a single horizon in the feature space of a frozen DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) .
However, DINOv2 is trained on static natural images and is not explicitly optimized to capture frame-to-frame tactile evolution; recent tactile representation learning also shows the limitations of single-frame encoders in modeling such dynamics ( Feng et al., 2026 ) .
In contrast, V-JEPA 2.1 ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) learns representations by predicting masked spatio-temporal features in videos, encouraging its encoder to capture predictable motion rather than exact pixel details.
Building on this objective, we learn a target space from tactile video clips that captures temporal change, while preserving spatial structure to support robust prediction under tactile distribution shifts.
Moreover, because a single net change can hide intermediate contact events when a squeeze or slip returns to a similar final state, we predict both future representations and their changes from the present at multiple horizons.
This captures contact evolution rather than only its endpoint.

In this paper, we present TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model whose two world-model experts use separate parameters and target spaces.
The visual expert predicts future visual latents, while the Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert (ITDE) predicts tactile evolution in the TacRep space.
Joint attention couples their predictions at every layer and allows the Action Expert to use both.
The ITDE requires only a single forward pass without iterative denoising.
A separate Tactile Understanding Memory provides direct access to the current tactile state, while staged training progressively integrates the tactile modules with the pretrained experts.

On UniVTAC ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance using only the provided demonstrations.
It is competitive with the two strongest models on this benchmark, N 0 N_{0} -VTLA and N 0 N_{0} -TWAM, both of which rely on large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining.
Notably, N 0 N_{0} -TWAM follows the video-generation recipe and has roughly twice the parameters of TacDyn-WAM.
Ablations show the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep’s advantage over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives.
On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM trained on per-task demonstrations alone reaches 71.0% average success, 16 points above the tactile policy FTP-1, and modest-scale pretraining on about 6,000 real visuo-tactile trajectories raises it to 85.0%.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

We propose TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that jointly predicts future visual latents and tactile evolution in distinct target spaces, while a read-only Tactile Understanding Memory provides the current tactile state.

We introduce TacRep, a dynamics-aware representation space for implicit tactile dynamics prediction, enabling one-pass multi-horizon prediction without pixel reconstruction or iterative denoising.

TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on UniVTAC using only the provided demonstrations, and ablations validate the design.
On a real robot, it outperforms vision-only and tactile baselines and benefits further from modest-scale tactile pretraining.

1. We propose TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that jointly predicts future visual latents and tactile evolution in distinct target spaces, while a read-only Tactile Understanding Memory provides the current tactile state.

2. We introduce TacRep, a dynamics-aware representation space for implicit tactile dynamics prediction, enabling one-pass multi-horizon prediction without pixel reconstruction or iterative denoising.

3. TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on UniVTAC using only the provided demonstrations, and ablations validate the design.
On a real robot, it outperforms vision-only and tactile baselines and benefits further from modest-scale tactile pretraining.
