2026-10-02.title: The Effect of Gait Stability Based on Two Types of Impact Strategies for Two-Link Walking and Brachiating Robots
2026-10-02.authors: Alan Estrada Flores , Nelson Rosa Jr
2026-10-02.comment: submitted for review; code available at this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-02.introduction:
The two-link walking models of Garcia et al. (1998) and Goswami et al. (1998) and the
brachiating model of Gomes and Ruina (2005) have provided valuable insight into the
mechanics of limbed locomotion in the fields of biomechanics and robotics.
Figure 1 shows example motions of the model in Gomes and Ruina (2005) .
In addition to contributions to human and robot gait analysis, these works show
that the underlying impulsive dynamics exhibit rich nonlinear phenomena.

For bipedal walking, these results include the existence of passive dynamic
walking gaits (i.e., unactuated periodic walking motions of the impulsive
dynamics), period-doubling bifurcations, strange attractors, and chaotic motion Garcia et al. (1998) ; Goswami et al. (1998) . A large body of work has since explored
variations of these canonical walking models with the addition of, e.g., springs
and dampers, limbs, and forcing functions (see Safartoobi et al. (2022) and
references therein). Common results include the existence of period-doubling (PD)
bifurcations and their associated route to chaos. The results for brachiation
are much more sparse, but a core result is the existence of unstable passive
dynamic gaits with zero energy loss across impacts and
energetically-conservative swing dynamics Gomes and Ruina (2005) . These results have
been extended to show the existence of stable and unstable passive dynamic and
actuated gaits and observations of fold (FD) and Neimark-Sacker (NS) bifurcations Rosa et al. (2012) ; Rosa and Lynch (2013) .

Given past work, a gap that still persists is the lack of a unified bifurcation
analysis of two-link models and their set of walking and brachiating gaits Rosa and Lynch (2013) . Ultimately, both of these fields study the same equations of
motion, but results are only reported in isolation. Specifically, both fields
analyze the behavior of fixed points of a discrete step-to-step map. The map
represents the continuous swing motion of the robot as it pivots about its hand
or foot followed by an instantaneous plastic collision with an inclined surface.
Because of the bilateral symmetry of many two-link models, a periodic motion
(i.e., a gait) can be identified after just one step and a relabeling of
coordinates Garcia et al. (1998) ; Goswami et al. (1998) ; Safartoobi et al. (2022) ; Rosa et al. (2012) ; Rosa and Lynch (2013) .
The periodicity of a fixed point is thus defined with respect to the number of
steps the robot takes. In other words, a gait that takes n n steps is a
period- n n fixed point.

Another understudied facet in both fields is the switching function of the
impulsive dynamics. In our numerical study, we explore a step-to-step map under
state-based switching (SBS) and time-based switching (TBS) strategies. In SBS, a collision occurs whenever the distance between the surface and the
end effector of the robot (serving as a foot for walking or hand for
brachiating) is zero. In the literature, SBS is the de facto choice with the
slope of the surface treated as a free parameter of the system. For TBS,
collisions occur after a pre-determined duration of time has elapsed. In this
case, switching time is the free parameter. TBS is a viable control option for
robots in vertical environments (e.g., Rosa et al. (2012) ; Mbewe and Boje (2025) ) as contacts
can be made at any point in time on the surface.

As further motivation for this study, an interesting aspect of switching strategies is that both strategies produce the same set of period-one gaits. We omit a
formal proof as this is intuitively true. For every gait under SBS, we can
take a stopwatch to determine the switching time, and, for every gait under TBS,
we can record the slope at the switching time. Given this fact, we still
observe different long-term gait behaviors across impacts depending on the
switching strategy. This leads to our core contributions.

In this paper, we explore the impulsive dynamics common to single-joint,
two-link models of walking and brachiating gaits with respect to slope and
switching time. In particular, we expand on the observations made in Rosa and Lynch (2013) with respect to how the stability of a gait and bifurcations
encountered within a family of gaits change under TBS and SBS of the impulsive
dynamics. Our contributions are

A numerical study of gait stability under two switching
strategies . We study the stability of gait families with respect to
time-based and state-based switching functions of the impulsive dynamics. When
there is a loss of stability in a gait family, we observe PD, NS, and FD bifurcations.

An exploration of the role of symmetry with gait families .
Two-link models with bilateral symmetry have period-one gait families that are
mirror images of each other about the switching time axis. We investigate the
evolution of unstable gaits in these families for one such model. In
particular, we find that near FD bifurcations, unstable gaits that start in one
gait family converge to stable gaits in the mirrored family of gaits under TBS.

Figure 2 provides a visual summary of these
contributions.

2026-10-02.title: Closed-Loop Refinement and Execution for Learned Driving Planners
2026-10-02.authors: Huaijin Hu , Shanting Wang , Zhongyu Mo , Andreas A. Malikopoulos
2026-10-02.comment: . Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC 2027)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Learning-based driving planners are usually trained and evaluated in open loop
against logged trajectories. In closed loop, a trajectory with small
displacement error can still stall the vehicle, steer it into a conflict
with surrounding agents, or be executed with abrupt braking. We introduce Closed-Loop
Refinement and Execution (CLRE), a hierarchical receding-horizon control
framework designed to mitigate these failure modes while leaving the upstream
planner frozen and adding no new learned model. The upper layer treats the
nominal trajectory as a reference and solves a finite-horizon optimal control
problem that trades route progress against interaction with predicted agents.
Solving it from several initializations gives a candidate set, and a prediction-conditioned oriented-bounding-box (OBB) feasibility test retains
only candidates whose minimum predicted OBB clearance over the horizon meets a
threshold. The lower layer
executes the lowest-cost survivor, or a route-centerline backup when none
remains, through the tracking controller supplied with the planner, augmented
by a range-based speed bound and a saturated proportional braking law. In
closed-loop simulation on 126 Bench2Drive routes with VAD as the upstream
planner, CLRE raises the driving score from 43.41 to 56.42 and route completion
from 57.27 to 72.23, and reduces collision events from 70 to 53.
2026-10-02.introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving has emerged as an alternative to
conventional modular pipelines by learning driving decisions directly
from sensor observations and scene representations. Methods such as
UniAD [ 1 ] and VAD [ 2 ] predict a
short-horizon ego trajectory that is subsequently converted into
vehicle commands by a downstream tracking controller. These planners
are commonly trained and evaluated in open loop against logged expert
trajectories. However, accurate open-loop trajectory prediction does
not necessarily imply reliable closed-loop execution.

In closed loop each executed action changes the next observation, so
planning errors accumulate. Open-loop and closed-loop performance can be
substantially misaligned [ 3 ] , Li et
al. [ 4 ] showed that open-loop displacement metrics can
be largely explained by the ego status alone, and
NeuroNCAP [ 5 ] reported that planners with strong
open-loop performance still collide in interactive scenarios. Bench2Drive
makes the point sharper by testing end-to-end systems in closed-loop CARLA
scenarios, where collisions, stalling, and route incompletion all count
against the score [ 6 ] . In this work, we focus on three
practically important failure modes that arise when learned trajectories are
executed in closed loop: insufficient route progress or stalling, motion
toward predicted conflicts, and abrupt longitudinal intervention.

Several lines of work try to close this gap, and each handles part of it. One line adds learned machinery around the planner, by retraining it with a
kinematic refinement network [ 7 ] ,
a learned cost that picks among sampled candidate trajectories [ 8 ] , or online adaptation through test-time training [ 9 ] . These methods improve closed-loop behavior, but they need extra training or a learned model at deployment. A second line uses the learned trajectory as a reference for explicit optimization. Examples include coupling learned prediction with a differentiable planner [ 10 ] , tracking learned waypoints with model predictive control [ 11 ] , or handling uncertain predictions with chance constraints [ 12 ] . Here, the interaction with nearby agents enters the optimization as objective terms that are traded off against other costs, or as chance constraints on uncertain predictions, and the resulting trajectory is not checked separately. So a trajectory with low total cost can still leave too little clearance. A third line checks a planned trajectory at runtime and replaces it or falls back when it fails a safety check, either for a learned plan [ 13 ] or for an optimized one [ 14 , 15 ] . This screens the nominal plan but does not improve it. A stalled or overly cautious plan passes the check unchanged, and a rejected plan has no better plan to put in its place.

Supervising a nominal policy with a separate safety layer is well established
in control. Predictive safety filters, control barrier functions, and
reachability-based methods modify or override nominal inputs to maintain
prescribed safety
conditions [ 16 , 17 ] , and barrier
certificates [ 18 ] and safety-prioritized receding-horizon
control [ 19 ] have been applied to vehicle coordination.
These methods check safety against an explicit model of the environment. A learned driving
stack instead supplies its own predictions of surrounding agents, so any
runtime condition built on them inherits their limitations.

These gaps motivate our approach. We propose the Closed-Loop Refinement and
Execution (CLRE) framework, which keeps the upstream planner frozen and adds no
new learned model. Unlike waypoint-tracking MPC or runtime filters that operate
on a single nominal plan, CLRE first refines the plan to recover progress and
reduce predicted interactions, and then independently screens the resulting
candidates with a prediction-conditioned OBB feasibility test. The lower layer
executes the selected candidate with additional intervention when needed.

The main contributions of this paper are the following.

We propose CLRE, a training-free framework that improves the
closed-loop behavior of a frozen learned planner through trajectory
refinement, OBB feasibility testing, and execution-level intervention.

We develop a receding-horizon refinement method that balances
nominal-path tracking, route progress, and predicted-agent interaction,
followed by an OBB feasibility test that screens the resulting candidates
against predicted agent motion.

We introduce an execution layer with a forward-range speed bound,
backup policy, and saturated braking, and evaluate the complete framework
on Bench2Drive through ablation, sensitivity, and cross-planner studies.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section II formulates the receding-horizon refinement problem
and Section III constructs the objective, the OBB feasibility test,
and the execution layer. Section IV reports closed-loop
benchmark results. Finally, we draw concluding remarks in
Section V .

1. We propose CLRE, a training-free framework that improves the
closed-loop behavior of a frozen learned planner through trajectory
refinement, OBB feasibility testing, and execution-level intervention.

2. We develop a receding-horizon refinement method that balances
nominal-path tracking, route progress, and predicted-agent interaction,
followed by an OBB feasibility test that screens the resulting candidates
against predicted agent motion.

3. We introduce an execution layer with a forward-range speed bound,
backup policy, and saturated braking, and evaluate the complete framework
on Bench2Drive through ablation, sensitivity, and cross-planner studies.

2026-10-02.title: In CEM, a World Model Is Also a Proposal Mechanism
2026-10-02.authors: Oliver Obst , Frieder Stolzenburg
2026-10-02.comment: including appendix
2026-10-02.abstract:
The cross-entropy method (CEM) uses world-model scores to select action
sequences and fit the distribution sampled in its next iteration. A scoring
error can therefore change both the present decision and the candidates
considered later. We evaluate these two roles separately. Four types of
predictive model generate CEM traces, and every model rescores every saved
candidate pool. Executing the same candidates in the environment provides a reference
elite set and proposal update.
2026-10-02.introduction:
A world model used for planning determines which actions receive further
consideration. In model-predictive control (MPC), the planner predicts the
outcomes of candidate action sequences, selects a sequence, and executes its
first action before replanning. The cross-entropy method (CEM) performs this
search by repeatedly sampling candidates and fitting a new sampling
distribution to those with the lowest predicted
cost [ Bharadhwaj et al., 2020 ] . We call that distribution the proposal and the retained candidates the elite set .

As an illustrative example, consider two candidate pools for the same physical state and cost objective.
Pool A contains a sequence with realised cost 1, but the scorer selects one
with realised cost 5. This is a selection error: a lower-cost sequence was
available. Pool B contains only sequences with realised cost 8 or higher. Its scorer orders
every candidate correctly and selects the cost-8 sequence. Earlier CEM
updates could have left the planner searching this second region. Correct
ordering within that pool still produces a higher-cost choice than the
misranked choice from pool A.

A fixed-pool comparison with environment executions can measure ranking
errors, elite membership, proposal-refit disagreement, and selection regret
among the available candidates. In the example, it can expose the error in
pool A and confirm the ordering in pool B. It cannot show which lower-cost
sequences another proposal would have sampled. Correct within-pool ordering
does not ensure that the pool contains low-cost actions.

Evaluation also depends on where the candidates came from. Logged rollouts
use a data-collection policy; actor-centred ranking tests perturb a reference
action sequence. These tests can measure prediction or ordering on their
chosen action distributions. CEM changes its own distribution after each
elite decision. We call this planner-induced query shift : model
scores change the optimiser’s future queries. The physical system need not
change.

Rank agreement measured along a CEM trace already captures how ordering
changes during search [ Wang et al., 2026 ] . Our comparison adds
pools produced by other models’ update histories. Applying the same scorer
to those pools tests whether its disagreement depends on pool source;
applying different scorers to one pool compares their decisions on identical
actions. Realised candidate costs separately record which pools contain
lower-cost sequences.

Our comparison uses four predictors fitted over frozen Dreamer
contexts [ Hafner et al., 2020 ] . A context is the backbone’s internal
representation of the observation history. Each predictor replaces the full
Dreamer dynamics during planning, so we call it a surrogate . It
predicts future contexts under a candidate action sequence. A fixed readout
maps those contexts to the task variables used in the planning cost. The
four surrogates share data, transition form, cost, and CEM settings; their
feature maps differ.

Each surrogate first runs its own CEM search. We save the candidate pool at
every iteration, execute its candidates from the same restored simulator
state, and then score that pool with every surrogate. This separates two
roles: the generator produced the pool through its earlier updates;
the scorer ranks the saved pool now. We call this a crossed design because each of the four generators is paired with each of the four scorers,
giving all 16 combinations. A column follows one
scorer across pool sources. A row holds the pool fixed and compares scorers.
The matrix describes proposal disagreement associated with generators,
scorers, and their pairings. It does not assign causal effects to those
components.

The intervention tests a consequence that rescoring alone cannot establish.
At the first update, we fit one proposal from model-ranked elites and another
from environment-ranked elites in the same pool. Both branches then continue
with the original scorer and matched random samples. This one-update
splice changes how later candidates are generated through one earlier
decision. Its endpoint is the realised cost of the sequence selected after
the remaining CEM iterations. Figure 1 shows the audit
and intervention together.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Model evaluation has long depended on the decisions that use the model.
Value-aware model learning weights errors through downstream value
functions [ Farahmand et al., 2017 ] . DeepMDP connects reward and latent
transition prediction to the properties of the learned
representation [ Gelada et al., 2019 ] . Value equivalence compares models
through their effects on specified value functions and
policies [ Grimm et al., 2020 ] . Lambert et al. [2020] examine the mismatch between
one-step prediction likelihood and downstream control performance. These
works give distinct reasons to evaluate a model through its intended use.
We hold the predictors fixed and examine the finite candidate decisions
made by CEM.

Yu et al. [2026] make a broader case for evaluating world models by
interventional action fidelity, policy ranking, and optimisation utility.
Their proposed reset-matched action branches are directly relevant to our
environment reference: every candidate starts from the same physical state. Bhamidipaty et al. [2026] define model exploitation through a reversal
of policy preference between the model and the environment, and analyse when
such reversals can occur. Our elite and ranking measurements examine finite
candidate disagreements; they do not estimate the worst-case exploitability
of a model over a policy class.

The closest CEM diagnostic is the CEM-stage Spearman analysis of Wang et al. [2026] . It measures agreement between model and realised
cost rankings as search moves from initial candidates towards concentrated
and elite populations. This already evaluates the model on queries made
during search. Our crossed design compares a scorer’s own pools with pools
generated by other surrogates. Holding the scorer fixed tests how its
disagreement varies with pool source. Holding the pool fixed compares
scorers without changing candidates. We also compare the means and widths
fitted from the two elite sets, because these parameters determine the next
queries. A rank correlation alone does not specify that refit.

Li et al. [2026] execute all candidates in saved proposal pools to
distinguish failed selection from the absence of a feasible candidate.
Their adjacent-set method then reconstructs an action sequence from a
neighbourhood of low-cost candidates. We use the same basic control of
executing candidates from a common initial state. Our intervention changes
an earlier elite refit and follows its consequence through later pools. This
tests how the proposal history changes the candidates available at final
selection.

Several recent methods change components that our audit keeps fixed. Chahe et al. [2026] train a cost-ranking objective that penalises
increasing action perturbations. Huang et al. [2026] add a
trajectory-level cost to endpoint scoring, and Singh [2026] change the planning objective without retraining the predictor. Sommer and Schilling [2026] learn a plan-improvement operator through
imagined rollouts. These methods change candidate scores or proposal updates.
Applying the crossed comparison before and after such a change would test
which measured disagreements it reduces.

2026-10-02.title: Lang3DSeg: Annotation-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Segmentation with Point Transformers
2026-10-02.authors: Cigdem Kokenoz , Amir Salarpour , Alkim Domeke , Christopher Salas , Pedram MohajerAnsari , Long Cheng , Mert D. Pesé , Bing Li
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
2026-10-02.abstract: Accurate 3D semantic perception is critical for safe autonomous navigation. However, supervised LiDAR segmentation remains tied to closed taxonomies and to the cost of point-wise manual annotation. Open-vocabulary methods avoid that cost by projecting the output of 2D vision-language models onto LiDAR and distilling it into a 3D network. These methods rely almost exclusively on voxel-based sparse convolutions, and point transformers have so far been limited to indoor environments, where 3D data is dense and bounded.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Accurate 3D semantic perception underpins autonomous navigation safety in unstructured environments. Supervised point transformers reach high benchmark accuracy, but they depend on dense point-wise annotation and are bound to the closed taxonomy they were trained on. Both properties limit a robot that must operate around rare obstacles, unfamiliar vehicle types, or terrain the annotation schema never
anticipated to mark or label.

Open-vocabulary distillation offers a way out. A 2D vision-language model labels camera images, those labels are projected onto the LiDAR sweep, and a 3D network learns from the result without human annotation. What has not changed across this literature is the 3D backbone: most methods in the setting, from CLIP2Scene [ 1 ] through Better Call SAL [ 2 ] , OV3D [ 3 ] , and GGSD [ 4 ] , build on a voxel-based sparse convolutional network, which imposes a spatial quantization not present in the raw point measurements. Point transformers remove that constraint and have been adopted for open-vocabulary segmentation indoor environments [ 5 ] , where scenes are dense and bounded. Outdoor LiDAR is the opposite regime: sweeps are sparse, ring-structured, and span a hundred meters, and to our knowledge no point transformer has been trained for annotation-free open-vocabulary segmentation in it.

Lang3DSeg closes that gap with two components. We train a PointTransformerV3 [ 6 ] backbone from scratch on open-vocabulary supervision, with no geometric pre-training and no supervised initialization; and because a from-scratch backbone has no prior to fall back on and reproduces the errors present in the projected pseudo-labels, we pair it with an offline curation stage that corrects those errors at the projection step rather than compensating for them afterwards. Together they outperform every published annotation-free result on both driving benchmarks.

Prior work treats the 2D-3D projection noise statistically, by temporal voting [ 7 ] , adaptive label correction [ 8 ] , or keeping a vision-language model in the loop at inference [ 9 ] . Each method introduces computation or memory cost that may be unsuitable for resource-constrained deployment, and much of the error is not statistical in the first place: a point behind a car is mislabeled identically from every similar viewpoint, so voting reinforces it. We instead remove these labels at the projection stage itself. A per-pixel occlusion test does not suffice, since a point behind an object typically lands on its own unoccupied pixel inside that object’s mask; we therefore test each mask instance as a whole for points that lie beyond the surface it describes.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

We create a new annotation-free open-vocabulary 3D learning framework , and validate its effectiveness through 3D LiDAR outdoor semantic segmentation task by training a point transformer from scratch without projected pseudo-label errors.

We identify and quantify occlusion bleed as a dominant and
systematic error during 2D-to-3D label projection, concentrated in the
foreground categories that significantly matter for class-averaged accuracy.

We introduce a priority-ordered rasterization with an instance-wise depth approach to handle this error, requiring neither registration nor cross-frame voting.

We attain the SOTA annotation-free accuracy on
both benchmarks, 52.8% mIoU on nuScenes and 41.4% on SemanticKITTI, while
keeping the vision-language model out of the inference path.

2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Cross-Modal Distillation and Open-Vocabulary Frameworks

Early zero-shot methods keep the 2D model in the loop at test time.
PointCLIP [ 11 ] and OpenScene [ 9 ] project point clouds onto image planes and aggregate
CLIP [ 12 ] features during inference, and
OpenMask3D [ 13 ] refines projected masks with
SAM [ 14 ] before extracting free-form features. Accuracy is
competitive, but evaluating a vision-language model across several cameras for
every sweep is not viable on an embedded platform.

Offline distillation removes that cost. ULIP [ 15 ] aligns points to
text directly, while SLidR [ 16 ] , Seal [ 17 ] and
CLIP2Scene [ 1 ] learn correspondences across driving
sequences that can later be fine-tuned. Better Call SAL [ 2 ] ,
OV3D [ 3 ] , GGSD [ 4 ] and AFOV [ 18 ] generate pseudo-labels offline and distill them into 3D-native networks, which is
the setting we adopt. AFOV additionally pre-trains the backbone with a tri-modal
contrastive objective, and LOSC [ 7 ] initializes from
ScaLR [ 19 ] ; both therefore depend on a self-supervised stage that
we do not use.

## II-B Backbones for Open-Vocabulary LiDAR Segmentation

What has not varied across this literature is the 3D architecture.
CLIP2Scene [ 1 ] and AdaCo [ 8 ] use Sparse Point-Voxel Convolution (SPVCNN) [ 20 ] ;
CNS [ 21 ] , OpenScene [ 9 ] , Better Call
SAL [ 2 ] , 3D-AVS [ 22 ] , OV3D [ 3 ] ,
GGSD [ 4 ] and AFOV [ 18 ] use MinkowskiNet [ 23 ] or
SparseConvNet; LOSC [ 7 ] uses WaffleIron [ 24 ] . Every one either
voxelizes the sweep or projects it onto a dense grid.

Point transformers instead attend over serialized neighborhoods of the raw
points, and PointTransformerV3 [ 6 ] scales to the point counts a
LiDAR sweep produces. The architecture has reached open-vocabulary segmentation
indoor environments: SpaCeFormer [ 5 ] couples a space-curve transformer
with sliding-window attention for instance segmentation and reports
PointTransformerV3 as a strong baseline there. Its evaluation is on ScanNet200
and Replica indoor scenes, where scenes are dense, bounded and roughly uniformly sampled;
outdoor LiDAR is the opposite regime, with point density falling off
quadratically with range. To our knowledge, Lang3DSeg is the first to distill
open-vocabulary supervision into a point transformer for outdoor LiDAR
segmentation, and the first to do so from scratch.

## II-C Noise Mitigation and Geometric Consistency

The treatment of projection noise can substantially affect segmentation accuracy. Better
Call SAL [ 2 ] applies DBSCAN [ 25 ] within individual frames to
discard spatial outliers. LOSC [ 7 ] consolidates labels across a
voxelized sequence by temporal voting, which suppresses per-frame flicker
effectively and currently gives the strongest published results in this setting.
AdaCo [ 8 ] corrects supervision during training through an
adaptive label corrector, and AFOV [ 18 ] propagates labels through
an approximate-flat interaction module that fills unobserved regions.

These approaches primarily address projection noise as a stochastic quantity to be averaged or
down-weighted, and much of it is neither. The label assigned to a point behind a
car is wrong identically from every similar viewpoint, so temporal voting
reinforces it; and the quantity that would reject it, its range along the camera
ray, is available at projection time and discarded. Lang3DSeg filters at the
source instead, cutting each projected instance at the first gap in its depth
distribution and resolving the residual ground ambiguity with a per-sweep plane
model, as Sec. III details.

2026-10-02.title: Reward as Observation: Learning Reward-Based Policies for Rapid Adaptation
2026-10-02.authors: Morgan Byrd , Maks Sorokin , Robert Wright , Sehoon Ha
2026-10-02.comment: Website: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humans readily adapt when the appearance of a familiar task changes. A gamer who masters a racing game can play immediately after a graphics engine upgrade, because the underlying rules and controls remain the same. Similarly, a robot trained to navigate a corridor should not need to relearn from scratch when its camera is replaced with a higher-resolution, wider Field-of-View or upgraded from RGB to RGB-D. In both cases, the core task structure, including dynamics, controls, and reward, is preserved; only the observation representation changes. However, typical deep RL policies treat such observation shifts as entirely new problems, requiring full retraining and discarding all previously learned task knowledge, because standard policies are tightly coupled to the specific observation space used during training.

We consider the problem of transferring a policy between two Markov Decision Process (MDP) environments that share the same underlying task structure, including state space, action space, transition dynamics, and reward function, but differ entirely in their observation space. Most prior transfer work in robotics focuses on transition dynamics shift, as in sim-to-real transfer [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Instead, we address the complementary case: fixed dynamics, but a completely different observation space. We impose no constraint on the relationship between source and target observations; they may differ arbitrarily in modality, dimensionality, or structure. We intentionally fix the dynamics to isolate the observation shift problem, and we expect our approach to compose naturally with existing methods that handle transition shifts.

Our key insight is that the reward signal directly encodes the task structure and remains consistent across both MDPs, and therefore serves as a natural bridge to enable rapid transfer between environments with different observations. Let us consider a driving task: if the reward stays high, the agent should continue its current behavior; if the reward drops, a steering correction is needed. This intuition holds whether the agent observes a 2D top-down view, a 3D camera feed, or the onboard camera of a Stretch mobile robot in a scanned 3D environment. This suggests that a scalar reward signal alone may carry sufficient information to address the challenge of drastic observation shift, but only if it is sufficiently dense and informative. Under this condition, the reward signal has the potential to provide effective guidance in the target environment, regardless of how the observations change.

We propose a reward-based policy as a transferable teacher that bridges source and target environments under drastic observation shifts. Training such a policy is inherently challenging, as the reward signal is only a scalar projection of the underlying state space with limited information for control. To overcome this, we adopt an LSTM-based architecture that processes the temporal history of reward and action pairs, and incorporate a guidance loss from an observation-based expert policy to stabilize training. Once trained in the source environment, the reward-based policy is deployed in the target environment as a teacher, and we use DAgger to train an observation-based policy significantly faster than learning from scratch.

We demonstrate that a reward-based policy can serve as an effective transferable teacher across environments with arbitrary observation shifts. First, reward-based policies achieve 66 66 % to 95 95 % of state-based performance across three environments. Second, they transfer zero-shot under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D rendering changes and deployment on photorealistic Habitat-Sim [ 5 ] reconstructions of real building interiors with a Stretch mobile robot. Third, using the reward-based policy as a DAgger teacher enables substantially faster learning in the target environment. Finally, reward estimation proves far more tractable than state estimation under limited data.

The technical contributions of this paper are:

We define the reward-based MDP and discuss its theoretical properties, including feasibility conditions and an optimality gap bound (Appendix).

We propose a practical implementation for training reward-based policies, and a DAgger-based algorithm that uses the reward-based policy as a zero-shot teacher to train an observation-based policy in the target environment.

We demonstrate reward-based policy training across diverse environments and validate rapid transfer under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D transfer and zero-shot deployment on a Stretch mobile robot in photorealistic Habitat-Sim reconstructions of real building interiors.

1. We define the reward-based MDP and discuss its theoretical properties, including feasibility conditions and an optimality gap bound (Appendix).

2. We propose a practical implementation for training reward-based policies, and a DAgger-based algorithm that uses the reward-based policy as a zero-shot teacher to train an observation-based policy in the target environment.

3. We demonstrate reward-based policy training across diverse environments and validate rapid transfer under drastic observation shifts, including 2D-to-3D transfer and zero-shot deployment on a Stretch mobile robot in photorealistic Habitat-Sim reconstructions of real building interiors.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

Transfer via Expert Demonstrations. Transfer learning in RL leverages existing information for rapid adaptation in a new scenario, which has been approached by a wide range of algorithms. One possible approach is learning from demonstration [ 6 ] , where expert demonstrations are available to guide the learning process. Offline methods can use these demonstrations for offline RL [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] and for pretraining to learn value functions or policies [ 10 , 11 ] . Online methods use expert demonstrations to improve policy exploration during learning, and include policy iterations [ 12 , 13 ] , policy gradients [ 14 , 15 ] , and Q-learning approaches [ 16 , 17 ] . Our reward-based policy serves a similar role, as it automatically provides guidance in the target environment through the shared reward signal.

Transfer via Representation Learning. Another way to transfer knowledge is representation learning, which establishes reusable representations in the action or state spaces that can be shared between source and target environments. Progressive networks [ 18 ] and PathNet [ 19 ] directly train common reusable representations and leverage them during policy training. There exists a line of works that split networks into general and reusable modules [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] and learn an invariant feature space in order to better transfer between tasks. [ 23 , 24 ] learn inter-task mappings to deal with state differences between tasks.
Successor representations [ 25 ] seek to separate the environment dynamics from the reward function. These have seen widespread use [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] for transferring knowledge for different tasks with the same state and action spaces. [ 29 ] does a similar approach of separating dynamics and reward for learning a better policy for transfer. In contrast, our method avoids the observation alignment problem by using the shared reward signal as a bridge.

Transfer via Policy Distillation. The most relevant method of transfer for our work is to transfer at the policy level. A popular method to transfer involves distilling information from an expert policy. This method uses supervised learning to match action distributions between the student and teacher policies, and is widely used for robotic applications operating under observation shift between student and teacher [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Policies can also be directly reused for updating policies in a transfer setting, as in [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] . Our method is most closely related to this line of work, but uses a reward-based policy trained in the source environment as the teacher, requiring no observation alignment.

Reward-Conditioned Policies. Another very similar sounding work to ours is the reward-conditioned policy [ 33 ] . However, this work trains standard observation-based policies with an additional reward conditioning that allows for using suboptimal trajectories as optimal supervision. In contrast, our method uses the reward signal to train a transferable teacher in the source environment, which accelerates learning in the target environment.

2026-10-02.title: Learning Transferable Skills using Goal-Conditioned Bisimulation
2026-10-02.authors: Mohammad Amin Abbasfar , Farbod Azimmohseni , Mohammad Hossein Rohban
2026-10-02.abstract: Unsupervised skill discovery has emerged as a promising approach for leveraging reward-free datasets to pretrain general-purpose policies. However, current skill discovery methods either require access to expert data or exhibit limited generalization, failing to transfer effectively to previously unseen layouts. A key challenge is to learn representations that capture the temporal structure of the environment while remaining robust to variations across layouts. To address this issue, we present an objective for learning action-aware temporal representations that satisfy the functional equivariance property while preserving the local temporal structure of the environment. Building upon this embedding, we further propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation , which learns transferable skills by conditioning the behavior of skills exclusively on the subset of state features that directly affect their execution. This enforces invariant behavior across different layouts, enabling skills to transfer effectively to other configurations. Finally, through comprehensive empirical evaluations, we show that skills learned in a given environment can be effectively applied to solve downstream tasks in various environment layouts, demonstrating strong out-of-distribution generalization. 1 1 1 The code and videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/usb-atr/ .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Leveraging large unlabeled datasets has substantially contributed to the advancement of deep learning in recent years. Unsupervised and self-supervised techniques such as masked language modeling in natural language processing ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) and contrastive losses in computer vision ( Chen et al., 2020 ) have enabled deep neural networks to benefit from vast and low-cost unlabeled data. Numerous attempts have been made to apply the same strategy in the context of reinforcement learning (RL), where the goal is to pretrain the agent’s policy using only pre-collected offline datasets ( Chebotar et al., 2021 ; Reed et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2023a ; Park et al., 2024a ; O. X.-E. Collaboration et al., 2024 ) .

Unsupervised skill discovery has been recognized as a promising approach for pretraining such policies. These methods aim to learn a versatile set of latent - conditioned policies, each demonstrating a distinct behavior, such that together they cover the state space. Prior work has proposed various objectives to train such skill policies, either via behavioral cloning ( Pertsch et al., 2021 ; Ajay et al., 2021 ) or by diversifying their state visitation distribution ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Park et al., 2023b ; Park et al., 2024a ) . These skills can then be used to perform downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner, or harnessed as low-level policies within a hierarchical approach ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ) .

Many applications of reinforcement learning in locomotion and robotic manipulation involve frequently occurring temporally-extended actions that appear during the accomplishment of a wide range of tasks ( Hauskrecht et al., 1998 ; Sutton et al., 1999 ; Pateria et al., 2021 ) .
For instance, in the AntMaze environment ( Fu et al., 2020 ; Park et al., 2025 ) , where a quadruped agent must navigate to different goals within a maze, the ability to move in the four cardinal directions constitutes a sufficient set of skills for performing any task, regardless of maze layout. Similarly, in the Kitchen environment ( Gupta et al., 2019 ) , which consists of several long-horizon manipulation tasks, a temporally-extended action such as placing the kettle from the cupboard onto the oven top should be performed independently of other environmental features, such as whether the microwave door is open or closed. In such structured environments, learning reusable skills is essential for generalizing to previously unseen configurations.

Despite the importance of such reusable behaviors in structured domains, existing skill discovery methods are not explicitly designed to account for this structure. For instance, the Hilbert foundation policy (HILP) ( Park et al., 2024a ) , which is a state-of-the-art distance-maximizing skill discovery method, learns skills that span the state space reasonably well. However, it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution layouts ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) . To illustrate, suppose HILP learns to move a kettle only when the microwave door is closed. In a scenario where the microwave door is open, despite being irrelevant to the task, the behavior of the kettle-moving skill may change drastically, making it incapable of completing the task. In contrast to distance-maximizing skill discovery methods, behavioral cloning-based methods offer better out-of-distribution generalization ( Pertsch et al., 2021 ) . Nevertheless, they fall short when using suboptimal datasets, as they tend to replicate the exact action sequences that exist in the dataset.

Motivated by this, we aim to extract skills that are transferable to out-of-distribution layouts, even when only a single training layout and low-quality datasets are available during training. Our method consists of two components. First, we introduce an objective for training an action-aware temporal representation (ATR) that aims to learn a structured state embedding with functional equivariance ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2022 ) property, while preserving local temporal distances. This allows us to enforce each skill to show monotonic behavior while retaining the benefits of temporal representations when learning from suboptimal data. To train such representations, we employ bisimulation metrics ( Ferns and Precup, 2014 ) , which have demonstrated well-established capabilities for improving generalization ( Zhang et al., 2021 ; Agarwal et al., 2021 ) . In particular, we use goal-conditioned bisimulation ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2022 ) to enforce this property for state-goal pairs that share similar underlying action sequences.

Second, we build upon this representation to propose unsupervised skill discovery using bisimulation (USB), a modification of HILP in which the behavior of skills is conditioned only on the state features that are relevant to their execution, rather than on the full state. To achieve this, we again employ bisimulation metrics to learn a state representation in which states with similar transition dynamics are embedded close to one another. Conditioning each skill on this representation encourages the learned skills to exhibit consistent behavior across dynamically similar states, even when the corresponding action sequences are not present in the dataset for all such states. In this way, we encourage skills to disregard layout-specific features of the environment and to acquire generic behaviors that improve their transferability. These generic skills can then be equipped with a planning approach or composed by a high-level controller to accomplish downstream tasks across diverse layouts.

Finally, to evaluate the out-of-distribution generalization capability of our method, we assess the learned skills in both a test-time planning setup and a hierarchical approach. By conducting experiments across environments with different layout maps, we demonstrate that our method offers strong generalization and outperforms existing state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods.

In summary, our main contributions in this work are as follows:
1) We propose ATR, a novel structured temporal representation for the states with the functional equivariance property.
2) Building on this representation, we propose USB, an unsupervised skill discovery method for pretraining latent-conditioned policies that learn generic and transferable skills.
3) We extend the popular OGBench ( Park et al., 2025 ) , a standard offline goal-conditioned RL benchmark, by adding a feature for generating random maze layouts and datasets, enabling a more thorough evaluation of the generalization ability of different methods.
4) Through experiments in several maze environments, we empirically demonstrate that USB+ATR learns effective and transferable skills across different layouts and offers strong out-of-distribution generalization.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Offline goal-conditioned RL. Goal-conditioned objectives have been widely used in unsupervised RL to learn latent representations for states that preserve temporal distances (i.e., the minimum number of steps required to reach a goal from a given state under an optimal policy).
Under certain assumptions, the optimal goal - conditioned value function is equivalent to the discounted temporal distance between pairs of states ( Kaelbling, 1993 ) .
Inspired by this, prior work has explored learning universal value functions as a proxy for learning temporal representations ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2023a ) .
Another line of work has sought to learn such representations by incorporating contrastive losses ( Eysenbach et al., 2022 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Myers et al., 2024 ) .
Since optimal goal-conditioned value functions satisfy the triangle inequality ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Pitis et al., 2020 ) ,
several model architectures ( Wang and Isola, 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) and objective functions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Myers et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to leverage this inductive bias in order to learn temporal embeddings more efficiently.

Unsupervised skill discovery. Skill discovery is a powerful approach in unsupervised RL aiming to pretrain a latent-conditioned policy that encodes a diverse set of behaviors. These skills are often trained by behavioral cloning ( Pertsch et al., 2021 ; Ajay et al., 2021 ) , maximizing mutual information between skills and their future state distributions ( Gregor et al., 2017 ; Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ) , or maximizing the distance between these distributions ( Park et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2023b ; Park et al., 2024b ; Park et al., 2024a ) .
The closest to our work is HILP ( Park et al., 2024a ) , which incorporates a temporal representation to train each skill by encouraging movement along a random unit vector in that representation. This is achieved by defining directional rewards for each skill, computed as the inner product between the temporal displacement caused by executing this skill and its corresponding target vector.

Bisimulation. Many approaches have been proposed for clustering states in general Markov decision processes (MDPs) to make a form of state abstraction. Bisimulation ( Larsen and Skou, 1991 ) is the strictest approach, which groups only states that are indistinguishable and behaviorally equivalent under the optimal value function.
Bisimulation metrics ( Ferns et al., 2011 ; Ferns and Precup, 2014 ) relax this assumption by defining a notion of behavioral similarity between states. Castro (2020) introduces on-policy bisimulation, which is a scalable and computationally efficient approach for approximating bisimulation metrics by using the similarity between on-policy behaviors of states, for deterministic MDPs. Zhang et al. (2021) propose a gradient-based method for learning a latent representation for high-dimensional state spaces in general MDPs with stochastic transitions.
Finally, our action-aware temporal representation is based on the goal-conditioned extension of bisimulation metrics ( Hansen-Estruch et al., 2022 ) , where an embedding of state-goal pairs is learned to cluster such pairs with similar underlying reward or action sequences.

2026-10-02.title: Spatial Strategies, Not Actions: Vector-Quantized Geodesics as Tools for LLM-Driven Agents
2026-10-02.authors: Gabriel Turinici
2026-10-02.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Large language model (LLM)
based agents are often criticized for lacking spatial understanding and mainly exploiting statistical text patterns. We investigate their spatial comprehension through an architecture combining geometrical tools with a LLM serving as a high-level orchestrator in grid-world environments. The agent first collects geodesic trajectories, which are then vector-quantized to extract a representative subset.
Offline, the LLM associates a natural language description of the underlying behavioral patterns to each selected trajectory, making it a tool.
Online, the LLM chooses the appropriate tool conditioned on the current state and goal. Low-level control is handled by primitive actions that execute the trajectory associated with the tool. From an agentic AI perspective, this approach separates learning into two levels: tool discovery is handled through unsupervised quantization of trajectories, while reasoning and decision-making are handled by the LLM. We test the approach in a partially observable dynamic 2D grid environment with an open vision-language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B). Pairing the geometry-derived tool library with an agent-centered zoom tool and a collision detection tool lets a fast, non-reasoning configuration match the goal-reaching rate of a much more costly chain-of-thought version, while cutting the cost of a decision from minutes to seconds.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have become the de-facto controller in many recent agentic systems, chaining natural-language reasoning steps with external tool calls to solve tasks that go beyond pure text generation ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Wei et al., 2022 ) . Spatial reasoning, however, remains a recognized weak spot: LLMs are trained on token sequences and have no built-in notion of metric space, obstacles or continuous motion so they tend to fall back on superficial statistical regularities of text rather than genuine geometric reasoning about the environment they are asked to act in. This is problematic for any application that requires an agent to move through, or reason about, physical or simulated space - navigation, warehouse robotics, game-playing agents, and embodied assistants among them. Difficulties accumulate when the simulators used (for instance in a reinforcement learning framework) face uncertainties or use approximations about spatial movements or future scenarios.

Interestingly, humans do not solve navigation problems by directly reasoning over raw coordinates either. When giving directions inside a building, we do not say “move 1.5 meters north, then 3.2 meters east”; we say “go straight ahead, take the elevator, go around the corner office, then turn left.” The instruction is a short composition of a handful of reusable, generic strategies - go straight, take the elevator, turn, avoid an obstacle - each of which packages several nontrivial low-level motions into a single high-level decision. A closely related approach appears in recreational mathematics: solving a Rubik’s cube does not require deriving new moves from scratch for every configuration. Instead, a small fixed library of move sequences, called algorithms in the cubing community (e.g., R U R’ U R U2 R’ or F R U R’ U’ F’ , see https://alg.cubing.net ), is reused across arbitrary starting positions; the solver’s actual skill lies in recognizing which algorithm applies to the current configuration, not in re-deriving the moves themselves for each starting configuration. We take this as our guiding analogy: if LLMs are weak at direct, low-level geometric planning, perhaps they should not be asked to do it. Instead, they can be asked to do what they are comparatively good at: recognizing patterns and selecting among a small set of well described, precomputed options.

This paper explores exactly this division of labor for spatial tasks. We equip an LLM-driven agent with a library of tools , each one a short, reusable motion pattern extracted directly from the geometry of the environment rather than hand-designed or learned through reinforcement learning; we view these geometry-grounded modules as structured inductive biases. Concretely, we (i) sample many geodesic trajectories - shortest, obstacle-aware paths - inside a partially observable 2D grid world, capturing the environment’s topology and spatial structure, (ii) compress this large trajectory set into a small number of representative prototypes using a vector quantization (VQ) procedure, each prototype becoming a reusable strategy, (iii) in an LLM interpretation step, use an LLM offline to translate each prototype into a natural-language description of its geometric behavior, its strengths, and its risks, turning it into a callable tool , and (iv) use the same (or another) LLM online , at decision time, for LLM orchestration : picking the tool best suited to the current partial observation and goal. Low-level actuation is then simply “play out the chosen tool’s fixed action sequence,” mirroring the way a Rubik’s cube solver executes a memorized algorithm once it has recognized the pattern.

From an agentic AI perspective, this design yields an agentic separation of two steps that are often entangled: skill discovery , handled by unsupervised geometric quantization and requiring no labels or reward signal, and skill selection / reasoning , handled by the LLM using its native strengths in language-conditioned decision-making. Our key insight is that LLMs appear to be more effective as orchestrators of geometry-derived skills than as direct spatial planners.

We present the synthetic 2D grid world with moving obstacles and partial observability in Section 3 and the methodology in Section 4 ; results
in Section 5 show that routing decisions through the geometry-grounded tool library improves significantly the target-reaching success rate
over querying the LLM directly.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Our approach sits at the intersection of three lines of work that are, to our knowledge, rarely combined in this particular way.

LLM agents and tool use. LLM-driven agents increasingly interleave natural-language reasoning with calls to external tools or actions, as in ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) and Toolformer ( Schick et al., 2023 ) , and benefit from decomposing a task into intermediate reasoning steps, as in Chain-of-Thought paradigm of ( Wei et al., 2022 ) . These works treat tools mostly as external APIs (calculators, search engines, code interpreters); we instead derive the tool set itself from the geometry of the environment, so that the LLM orchestrates a set of skills that is neither given a priori not invented by the LLM alone.

Quantization and skill discovery. Vector quantization has a long history as a way to compress a large or continuous dataset into a small number of representative prototypes, from classical VQ codebooks to VQ-VAE-style discrete representation learning ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ) and to measure-theoretic versions ( Turinici, 2024b ) which can handle signed measures - a property that could be exploited to let new skills emerge from novel trajectory patterns rather than fixing the tool set in advance.

Spatial reasoning and geodesics. Geodesics - minimal paths that reflect the intrinsic (possibly curved, possibly obstacle-constrained) geometry of a space, as opposed to paths that are straight only in some extrinsic embedding - are a classical tool in geometry and robotics for capturing the true topology of an environment. A growing body of work documents that LLMs and vision-language models struggle with exactly this kind of geometric reasoning when it is left implicit in raw or visual input: Patel and Pavlick (2022) find that only the largest LMs learn to ground directional/spatial concepts in a grid world, and only from explicit examples; Aghzal et al. (2023) show with their PPNL benchmark that GPT-4 plans spatially only when prompted to interleave reasoning and acting, and still fails at longer-horizon temporal reasoning; Martorell (2025) show that grid-navigation success depends heavily on how coordinates are textually encoded, scaling with model size; Sandfuchs et al. (2026) find that under strict partial observability only reasoning-tuned LLMs reliably reach the goal in text gridworlds, and still less efficiently than an oracle path; Gao et al. (2025) use a Rubik’s-cube benchmark to isolate long-horizon spatial state tracking under partial observation, reporting a uniform 0 % 0\% pass rate for current LLM agents once external solver tools are removed; and Rodríguez Salgado Gonzalo (2026) show that vision-enabled models solving maze images are largely performing brute-force path enumeration in token space rather than genuine visual planning. Complementary work instead sidesteps this weakness by keeping the LLM out of low-level geometric computation: Zhu et al. (2023) plan long-horizon Minecraft tasks over structured text actions and memory rather than raw pixels; Song et al. (2024) and Rahimi et al. (2025) each pair the LLM with a dedicated non-LLM module - a text-based topological map, or a vision-based localizer - that handles metric geometry so the LLM only reasons over a simplified representation; Dang et al. (2025) equip an LLM wayfinding agent with externally maintained spatial-memory representations instead of inferred geometry; and Zhao et al. (2025) tackle city-scale embodied question answering via a hierarchical planner/manager/actor agent built around an explicit object-centric cognitive map rather than a single LLM call over raw city-scale geometry. Rather than asking an LLM to reason directly about such geometric objects, which is precisely the kind of task token-based models handle poorly, we use geodesics purely as an offline data-generation and skill-discovery mechanism, and reserve the LLM’s role for the language-native tasks of describing and selecting among the resulting skills.

2026-10-02.title: MIKASA-Robo-VLA: Benchmarking Memory in VLA Models for Long-Horizon Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Egor Cherepanov , Nikita Kachaev , Aleksandr I. Panov , Alexey K. Kovalev
2026-10-02.abstract:
Vision-language-action policies often see only one or a few recent frames,
which makes it difficult to evaluate how they use information that disappears
during a task. We introduce MIKASA-Robo-VLA, a benchmark of 90
language-conditioned manipulation tasks.
All but 10 hide the cue an action depends on. Those
10 are reactive controls.
MIKASA-Robo, the suite it rebuilds, has 32 tasks and uses language only in a
representative VLA subset. Here every task provides an instruction, while
memory-dependent tasks hide a task-relevant cue and reactive controls keep it
available. For 70 tasks, environment phase timings specify an
information gap, and for 28 of them the gap
exceeds the 16-frame window of the widest
fixed-context VLA we survey. The gap counts only the interval the cue is
provably absent, not the full duration a policy must retain it, so every
memory-dependent task still requires memory by construction, including the
ones whose measured gap is short. We release 22,500
oracle trajectories across 10 memory types in RLDS and
LeRobotDataset v3.
A reference π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} baseline with current images and proprioception,
but no observation history or explicit memory module, is fine-tuned on
14 tasks and achieves 0.211 ± 0.044 0.211{}\pm 0.044{} mean task success. Its lower success on the evaluated Long-split tasks is
confounded by open-loop chunking and the memory types represented in that
subset.
Project page: mikasarobo.github.io .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly use pretrained visual and
linguistic representations to control robots from demonstrations. Models such
as OpenVLA and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} execute diverse manipulation skills and generalize
across tasks and environments ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .
Sustained interaction makes memory a central requirement: a robot must act on
information that may no longer be visible.
It may need to recall an object’s identity after an occlusion, reproduce a
previously observed sequence, or track which steps of a task have already
been completed. The instruction specifies the goal, but the observation
history determines how to achieve it.

Explicit-memory methods address this challenge in different ways. MemER
retrieves relevant visual experiences for hierarchical
control ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) , while MEM combines visual and textual
memory at different temporal scales ( Torne et al., 2026 ) . Their physical
setups make systematic memory sweeps costly to reproduce. Simulation offers
a more scalable alternative, yet
widely used suites such as CALVIN and LIBERO emphasize skill composition
and knowledge transfer ( Mees et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) rather than
explicit control of what must be remembered and for how long. In complex multi-stage
tasks, aggregate success also mixes memory demands with perception, planning,
and motor execution. Memory-focused suites, including MemoryBench,
LIBERO-Mem, RoboMME, and RoboMemArena, make these demands more explicit, but
cover a narrower range of tasks and memory types ( Fang et al., 2025 ; Chung et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Lei et al., 2026 ) .

We introduce MIKASA-Robo-VLA , an extension of
MIKASA-Robo ( Cherepanov et al., 2026a ) , originally developed to evaluate
memory in reinforcement-learning (RL) agents, to language-conditioned VLA
training and evaluation. The suite expands from 32 tasks and
4 memory types to 90 tasks spanning
10 types, with natural-language instructions and a shared
observation and action interface. It asks two questions: what must a
policy remember, and for how long? Task families vary the
content and structure of memory, including object attributes, sequences,
counts, and pending actions. Difficulty variants adjust factors such as the
number of items, sequence length, and delay before recall. Configured episode
horizons range from 25 to 2,160 steps, organized into
Short, Medium, and Long splits, and retention intervals are characterized
separately from episode length.

Dense rewards support online RL fine-tuning, and demonstrations for every
task support imitation learning. A common evaluation protocol fixes the
policy interface, episode seeds, and success metric.

Our main contributions are as follows:

A broad, parameterized benchmark for memory in VLA policies. We provide 90 language-conditioned manipulation tasks across
10 memory types, with difficulty variants spanning memory
content and temporal demands, and three horizon splits covering
25–2,160 steps (Section 3 ).

Demonstrations and rewards for policy training. We release 22,500 oracle demonstration episodes, comprising
6,306,953 timesteps, collected using PPO policies and motion planning.
Every task is available in both RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3 formats, with
dense environment rewards supporting subsequent RL fine-tuning
(Section 4 ).

Standardized evaluation and a reference analysis. We provide a common evaluation protocol in the released code, a per-task characterization
of retention intervals, and a reference π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} baseline on
14 tasks (Section 5 ).

2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

RL memory evaluation includes both diagnostic tasks and diverse partially
observable environments. T-Maze and bsuite probe retention across delays ( Bakker, 2001 ; Osband et al., 2020 ) , while POPGym and Memory Gym
broaden the range of observations, task structures, and temporal demands ( Morad et al., 2023 ; Pleines et al., 2025 ) . Other work separates memory from
credit assignment ( Ni et al., 2023 ) or develops taxonomies of memory
capabilities ( Cherepanov et al., 2025 ) . MIKASA-Robo applies this
diagnostic framing to robotic manipulation ( Cherepanov et al., 2026a ) .
We extend its RL setting to language-conditioned policies, with an expanded
taxonomy, a common VLA interface, demonstrations, and dense rewards.

Generalist policies typically condition actions on limited visual history:
OpenVLA uses a single image ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , while RT-1, Octo, and
RoboVLMs use windows of six, two, and 16 frames,
respectively, in their reported main configurations ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Explicit memory extends this design space through perceptual and cognitive
storage in MemoryVLA ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , recurrent state in μ \mu VLA ( Cherepanov et al., 2026b ) , experience retrieval in
MemER ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) , and visual–textual memory at multiple scales
in MEM ( Torne et al., 2026 ) . MIKASA-Robo-VLA provides tasks for comparing such
designs across memory contents and retention intervals. Its information-gap
analysis relates task structure to observation windows without treating window
size as a limit on recurrent or external memory.

CALVIN evaluates language-conditioned skill composition ( Mees et al., 2022 ) , LIBERO studies lifelong knowledge transfer ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , SIMPLER targets correspondence between simulated
and real-world policy performance ( Li et al., 2024 ) , and RoboCasa
broadens evaluation to everyday kitchen activities ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) . Their standard evaluations do not systematically
vary memory content and retention delay. A long sequence can remain locally
observable, while a short task can depend on a cue that has disappeared.
MIKASA-Robo-VLA makes this distinction explicit.

MemoryBench introduces spatial-memory and action-recall tasks ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . LIBERO-Mem formalizes four object-centric non-Markov
factors ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , and RMBench distinguishes one-shot from
repeated-exploration memory ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . RoboMME covers temporal,
spatial, object, and procedural memory across sixteen tasks ( Dai et al., 2026 ) , while RoboMemArena composes longer tasks and annotates
memory-relevant keyframes ( Lei et al., 2026 ) . RoboTwin-MeM isolates
transient intermediate visual evidence and explicitly scales the number of
required keyframes ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and MEMOBench instead diagnoses
storage, update, and compression through executable checkpoints ( Sun et al., 2026 ) .
MIKASA-Robo-VLA adds 90 parameterized tasks over 10
memory types (Table 1 ), dense rewards, a common evaluation
protocol, and 22,500 demonstrations in RLDS and LeRobotDataset v3 –
the only suite among these to combine controlled retention and load
variation, horizon stratification, dense rewards, and GPU-parallel execution
(Table 35 , Appendix I ).
