2026-10-05.title: Detect and Suppress: A Mechanistic Defense against Adversarial Patches in VLA Models
2026-10-05.authors: Yukiya Horiba , Koshiro Aoki , Shunsuke Yasuki , Bum Jun Kim , Taiki Miyanishi
2026-10-05.abstract:
Adversarial patches can disrupt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by manipulating visual observations, leading to failures in robot control.
However, it remains poorly understood which internal mechanisms underlie these failures and how targeted interventions can mitigate them.
In this work, we mechanistically analyze VLA representations using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) and identify a feature whose activation strongly correlates with the presence of an adversarial patch.
Based on this analysis, we suppress the identified feature at inference time only when a linear probe detects an attack.
This intervention improves robustness without the cost of fine-tuning the VLA.
We evaluate our method against VLA adversarial patch attacks on LIBERO-10.
Conditional intervention improves success rate under intermittent attacks, whereas continuously applying the same intervention substantially degrades policy performance.
These results show that attack-related internal representations can provide useful targets for VLA adversarial defense and that controlling when to intervene is important for limiting disruption to nominal policy behavior.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Adversarial patches can disrupt vision-language-action (VLA) policies by altering the visual observations used for robot control [ 23 , 27 ] .
Existing VLA defenses modify either the inputs, through image preprocessing [ 24 ] , or the model parameters, through adversarial fine-tuning [ 27 ] .
Adversarial fine-tuning, however, incurs the computational cost of additional policy training.
We ask whether VLA robustness can instead be improved by directly targeting attack-related internal features at inference time, without fine-tuning the policy.

Mechanistic interpretability provides a basis for investigating this question.
Recent studies have identified internal directions and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features whose manipulation influences VLA behavior [ 7 , 21 , 10 , 4 ] .
These studies primarily examine nominal behavior, leaving the use of such features for adversarial defense underexplored.
However, indiscriminately suppressing attack-related features may also disrupt nominal policy behavior.
An effective defense therefore requires examining both which feature to target and when to suppress it.

We investigate these questions through SAE-based analysis and conditional intervention in VLA representations.
We identify an SAE feature associated with patch presence and train a linear probe to detect attacks from the VLA’s internal state.
At inference time, we suppress the feature’s contribution only when the probe detects an attack, while keeping the VLA parameters fixed.
On LIBERO-10 [ 15 ] under Untargeted Action Discrepancy Attack (UADA) [ 23 ] , this conditional intervention improves task success under intermittent attacks, whereas continuous suppression of the same feature substantially degrades performance.
Our results suggest that internal features associated with adversarial patches can serve as targets for VLA defense, and that intervening only during detected attacks limits disruption of nominal behavior.

2026-10-05.title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Chenzhi Liu , Yue Zhang , Jiehong Lin , Jianan Wang , Bo Wang , Zhongrui Wang , Xiaojuan Qi
2026-10-05.comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent , a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable atomic skills . It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference.
Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations.
Evaluations on RoboCasa, BEHAVIOR-1K, and real-world tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MobiAgent. It outperforms π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -TA by 22.5 percentage points on BEHAVIOR-1K and enables robust recovery from execution failures. Through autonomous data recycling, success improves from 7.50% to 27.50% on RoboCasa and from 32.5% to 57.5% on Astribot S1.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires executing complex, multi-stage tasks to achieve global goals, necessitating the seamless interleaving of distinct behavioral modes including global navigation and precise prehension. This domain poses significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and the capacity interference inherent in jointly modeling disparate sensorimotor mappings for locomotion and arm control.

Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, notably OpenVLA [ 14 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} [ 37 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 36 ] , have demonstrated exceptional proficiency in tabletop environments by directly mapping multimodal observations to continuous actions. Building on this foundation, systems like Mobi- π \pi [ 45 ] and N2M [ 2 ] extend VLAs to mobile platforms, primarily optimizing the navigation-manipulation hand-off. Nevertheless, these monolithic architectures function predominantly as reactive policies tailored for short-horizon objectives. In long-horizon scenarios, they lack the hierarchical reasoning necessary for semantic task decomposition and struggle to maintain the long-term context required for closed-loop replanning, fundamentally limiting their autonomy and reliability.

To transcend short-horizon reactive policies, recent research explores hierarchical agentic frameworks that layer Large Language Models (LLMs) or Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over low-level controllers [ 47 , 24 , 12 , 22 , 10 , 39 , 50 , 21 ] , typically adopting a plan-execute-verify paradigm. Beyond their confinement to stationary manipulation, these architectures exhibit three critical bottlenecks: 1) Constrained Planning via Sub-task Mapping: They typically assign an individual, isolated policy to each decomposed sub-task. High-level planning is then reduced to discrete selection from a predefined list rather than open-ended generation, inherently limiting scalability and increasing system overhead as the required sub-task repertoire expands. 2) Inflexible Verification and Replanning: Stemming directly from this rigid policy mapping, dynamically replanning after a verification failure becomes highly cumbersome. This inflexibility is particularly fatal in mobile manipulation, where reflection and error recovery demand complex, continuous spatial reasoning (e.g., dynamic navigation, distance and viewpoint adjustments) prior to interaction. 3) Absence of Data Curation and Policy Self-Improvement: The vast majority of these frameworks operate open-loop regarding lifelong learning. While rare exceptions like RoboClaw [ 21 ] introduce automated data collection, the field still lacks a comprehensive pipeline for unconstrained data curation and recursive self-improvement.

To bridge the gap between robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement, we propose MobiAgent , a dual-loop agentic system tailored for long-horizon mobile manipulation, as shown in Fig. 1 . MobiAgent decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control based on atomic skills, partitioning the system into a deployment-time Inner Loop and an offline-training Outer Loop.

To overcome the bottlenecks of constrained planning and inflexible replanning, the Inner Loop shifts the execution paradigm from rigid sub-task policies to highly composable atomic skills within a receding-horizon control flow. First, a Task Planner dynamically composes these skills on the fly. By replanning after completing each plan, it swiftly adapts to environmental changes and enables open-ended plan generation, bypassing the scalability limits of predefined sub-task lists. Next, by breaking down traditional sub-tasks into finer-grained actions, the Skill Executor employs skill-specific flow-matching experts built upon a shared VLM backbone. This semantic partitioning allows diverse sub-tasks sharing the same underlying action to reuse a single action expert, maximizing reusability while avoiding capacity interference. Finally, a Reflection Critic provides continuous visual verification to trigger flexible replanning. Operating at this granular level allows the Critic to explicitly manage the complex spatial reasoning essential for robust error recovery.

The Outer Loop drives the automated data curation and evolution of the skill library, eliminating the need for manual data curation. First, a VLM-powered Data Curator processes startup demonstrations and deployment rollouts to autonomously segment and verify trajectory clips with instruction captions. Next, an Skill Generator clusters these instructions to establish a discrete vocabulary of atomic skills, seamlessly standardizing new rollout data into this inventory. Finally, a Skill Trainer uses this curated data to instantiate and continuously fine-tune the skill policies.

To evaluate MobiAgent on long-horizon mobile manipulation, we conduct experiments across the simulated RoboCasa [ 31 , 32 ] and BEHAVIOR-1K [ 19 ] benchmarks, as well as four real-world tasks on Astribot S1. On BEHAVIOR-1K, MobiAgent achieves a 65.0% mean success rate, outperforming the task-specific π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -TA baseline [ 16 ] by 22.5 percentage points, while component ablations demonstrate the importance of dynamic planning, skill-specific experts, and visual verification. Its critic-driven global replanning further enables recovery from failures such as object drops and pose misalignments. Finally, deployment-to-training updates improve success from 7.50% to 27.50% on RoboCasa and from 32.5% to 57.5% on Astribot S1, validating the Outer Loop’s ability to drive continuous, annotation-free policy improvement through autonomous data recycling.

# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies for short-horizon manipulation. Recent foundation models have popularized VLA policies that directly map language and visual observations to short-horizon robot actions [ 1 , 14 , 33 , 37 , 36 , 20 , 38 , 13 , 23 , 49 ] . To model these short-horizon action distributions, architectures typically adopt one of two paradigms: models like RT-2 [ 1 ] and OpenVLA [ 14 ] co-train web-scale VLMs to output discretized action tokens, whereas recent state-of-the-art approaches like π 0 \pi_{0} [ 37 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 36 ] leverage flow matching to directly generate continuous action trajectories.

Hierarchical agentic frameworks for long-horizon tasks. Hierarchical frameworks typically layer LLMs or VLMs over low-level controllers using a plan-execute-verify paradigm [ 47 , 24 , 12 , 22 , 10 , 39 , 50 , 35 , 9 , 29 , 3 , 30 ] . While effective, they often rely on fixed skill repertoires. For instance, CaP-X [ 4 ] composes predefined primitives but cannot learn underlying continuous sensorimotor behaviors. MobiAgent instead employs a unified, skill-conditioned VLA for native vision-based control. Additionally, existing error recovery mechanisms are often rigid; RoboClaw [ 21 ] , for example, requires explicitly paired forward and reset policies. Adaptive World Action Models use future–reality verification [ 42 ] , whereas MobiAgent performs skill-level verification and task-level replanning.
Finally, unlike most open-loop systems that leave failed behaviors unchanged, MobiAgent introduces a deployment-to-training pipeline to continuously refine its skills from curated rollouts.

Mobile manipulation systems. Current mobile manipulation systems [ 44 , 17 , 6 , 5 , 28 , 41 , 48 ] , including recent VLA extensions like Mobi- π \pi [ 45 ] and N2M [ 2 ] , excel at reactive control and navigation-manipulation hand-offs. However, they lack the closed-loop replanning, online verification, and deployment-driven refinement required for long-horizon execution. Furthermore, state-of-the-art approaches like π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -TA [ 16 ] (the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner) rely on isolated, task-specific models. Their use of time-indexed stages forces distinct behaviors to share a single prediction head, causing capacity interference.

2026-10-05.title: I2CD: Direct Image-to-Convex Decomposition for Simulation-Ready Collision Geometry
2026-10-05.authors: Qian Wang , Liam Merz Hoffmeister , Brian Scassellati , Daniel Rakita
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.abstract: Physics simulators and motion planners require convex collision geometry, yet image-to-3D generative models output dense, frequently non-manifold visual meshes. Bridging the two today takes a slow, brittle reconstruct-then-decompose pipeline of repair, decimation, and approximate convex decomposition. We present I2CD, which predicts a convex decomposition directly from a single RGB image. Rather than train a new image-to-3D model, I2CD freezes the pretrained Hunyuan3D-2 image-conditioned diffusion transformer and shape decoder and trains only a lightweight cross-attention head (38 M parameters, under ten GPU-hours) whose learned “convex-slot” tokens emit the halfplane parameters of K K convex polytopes. The output is compact, convex by construction, and loads into physics engines without any post-processing, in ∼ 0.5 {\sim}0.5 s per image. On 227 227 held-out OmniObject3D and Google Scanned Objects instances, I2CD attains the highest volumetric IoU among eight reconstruct-then-decompose pipelines while running 6 6 – 37 × 37\times faster end-to-end. In a cross-simulator study in MuJoCo, PyBullet, Genesis, and Isaac Sim, every engine uses I2CD geometry as delivered, whereas raw generated meshes “load” everywhere but are silently replaced by a different collision shape in most cases or need seconds to minutes of per-object preprocessing. On a physical xArm7, I2CD produces planner-ready geometry for a 20 20 -object cluttered scene in 11 11 s versus 328 328 s for the strongest baseline, at comparable pick-and-place execution success ( 85 85 vs. 90 90 of 100 100 trials).
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

Image-to-3D generation. Single-image reconstruction has progressed from template deformation [ 23 ] and implicit fields [ 24 , 25 ] to large feed-forward generators [ 26 , 27 ] built on diffusion [ 28 ] and flow matching [ 29 ] . The state of the art samples a compact shape latent [ 30 , 31 ] with an image-conditioned DiT and decodes it to a dense mesh [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Robotics has begun to use these models to build scene geometry from images [ 14 , 16 , 15 ] , but always through their mesh output followed by post-processing. We exploit an asymmetry in these systems: their meshes are unsuited to collision geometry, yet their pretrained shape decoders encode a rich, general-purpose geometric prior that a small head can read out into a different output modality.

Approximate convex decomposition (ACD). The dominant recipe for collision geometry is to clean a mesh and partition it with V-HACD [ 9 ] or CoACD [ 10 ] ; recent variants improve the speed–quality trade-off [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] . ACD works well on watertight, well-conditioned meshes. It degrades sharply on the noisy, non-manifold meshes emitted by image-to-3D models, and it takes seconds to tens of seconds per object even on clean inputs (Table I ).

Learned convex decomposition. CvxNet [ 19 ] represents each part as an intersection of H H halfplanes and trains an encoder–decoder on occupancy. BSP-Net [ 20 ] learns binary space partitions, and Neural Parts [ 36 ] generalizes to non-convex primitives. Vavilala et al. [ 37 , 38 ] fit convexes to RGB-D scenes with test-time optimization. Yang et al. [ 39 ] supervise a per-point feature field with a contrastive loss derived from straight-line containment in convexes. CvxNet and BSP-Net also offer single-view RGB modes, but these are trained end-to-end per category (ShapeNet) and have no open-world weights, so they cannot handle arbitrary household objects without retraining a full image-to-3D model.

Positioning. Closest in goal is SPARCS [ 15 ] , which estimates simulation-ready cluttered scenes by jointly optimizing the shapes and poses of a few objects (up to 5 5 , represented by up to 22 22 convex hulls in total) under a shape-differentiable contact model. SPARCS is a scene-level, optimization-based refinement that starts from learned per-object initializations and inherits their convex hulls. I2CD is an object-level, feed-forward source of exactly such convex geometry (in 0.5 0.5 s, for 20 20 -object scenes). The two are complementary: our output could initialize their optimization, while their physics-aware refinement could correct the pose-registration errors that dominate our robot failures (§ IV-C ). I2CD is, to our knowledge, the first method to adapt a pretrained image-conditioned 3D foundation model to directly output simulation-ready convex geometry. We keep the CvxNet halfplane representation and Yang et al.’s containment principle, but apply the contrastive loss directly to the per-convex soft responsibilities of our head, without an auxiliary feature field.

2026-10-05.title: KungfuAthleteBot: learning high-dynamic humanoid motion from video with unified robust recovery
2026-10-05.authors: Zhongxiang Lei , Lulu Cao , Xuyang Wang , Tianyi Qian , Jinyan Liu , Xuesong Li
2026-10-05.abstract: Video is an abundant, inexpensive source of human motion data that is rich in extreme athletic behaviours. Making it usable for humanoid robots, however, is not a matter of simply retargeting a reconstructed trajectory: video-derived motion is physically inconsistent , devoid of actuation information , and says nothing about failure or recovery . We present KungfuAthleteBot (KAB), a framework that treats “learning high-dynamic motion from video” as the central problem and resolves each of these three failure modes in turn. (C1) We build the KungfuAthlete dataset from videos of national-level martial artists and introduce a physics-guided parabolic trajectory correction that removes height floating, ground penetration, and high-frequency jitter from reconstructed aerial and landing phases. (C2) Because video carries no force information, strict tracking of a reconstructed trajectory is dynamically infeasible, and error-driven initialisation keeps re-launching the policy from infeasible aerial poses. We introduce physics-driven pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling , our central mechanism for making such references learnable: it biases initialisation towards dynamically feasible states, letting the policy discover feasible actuation patterns instead of imitating infeasible ones. (C3) Finally, we introduce a direct training paradigm in which disturbance rejection and fall recovery are learned inside the same policy that tracks the video motion, requiring no recovery reference data and no manual mode switching. On a real humanoid robot, KAB learns highly dynamic skills from video and recovers from arbitrary falls in ≈ 0.7 \approx 0.7 s, to our knowledge the fastest reported recovery for a unified policy. Ablations on the unified policy confirm the necessity of its components, supporting the view that repairing and compensating video data – rather than only collecting more of it – is what unlocks high-dynamic humanoid skills. Code and data: https://kungfuathletebot.github.io/ .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Humanoid robots that can execute highly dynamic, athletic skills – aerial spins, flips, and explosive strikes – are a long-standing goal of the field (Fig. 1 ). The dominant bottleneck is no longer the control algorithm but the data that drives it Liao et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Sun et al. (2025) . Motion-capture pipelines require instrumented studios, wearable hardware, and bespoke collection procedures: they are expensive, slow to scale, and restricted to controlled environments. This paper starts from a different premise: compared with motion capture and wearable systems, video is abundant, inexpensive, and able to capture elite athleticism outside the laboratory.

Learning high-dynamic motion from video, however, is harder than learning from curated motion-capture data, and this is the problem we address. Retargeting a reconstructed human trajectory to a humanoid and running reinforcement learning on it does not work out of the box, for reasons that are specific and diagnosable:

(C1) Video reconstructions are physically inconsistent. Monocular reconstruction methods such as GVHMR Shen et al. (2024) and generative models such as GENMO Li et al. (2025a) produce motion that is globally smooth but locally unphysical: during flight the root height “floats” instead of following a ballistic arc, the feet penetrate the ground on landing, and frame-wise noise appears as joint jitter. This is not a cosmetic issue – a floating root makes the aerial phase dynamically impossible for any robot.

(C1) Video reconstructions are physically inconsistent. Monocular reconstruction methods such as GVHMR Shen et al. (2024) and generative models such as GENMO Li et al. (2025a) produce motion that is globally smooth but locally unphysical: during flight the root height “floats” instead of following a ballistic arc, the feet penetrate the ground on landing, and frame-wise noise appears as joint jitter. This is not a cosmetic issue – a floating root makes the aerial phase dynamically impossible for any robot.

(C2) Video contains no actuation information. A trajectory reconstructed from pixels describes where the body goes , not how the joints are driven to get there. In explosive motions such as a backflip, the human and the robot realise the same joint trajectory with radically different torque profiles (e.g. at the knee); demanding strict tracking therefore asks the robot to reproduce a physically infeasible joint trajectory, and learning stalls.

(C3) Video says nothing about failure. A video ends when the motion ends; it provides no model of disturbance, loss of balance, or recovery. A policy that faithfully tracks video motion is therefore also a policy that has no idea what to do once the real world pushes it off the reference trajectory.

Our central claim is that these three failure modes are not incidental implementation details but the actual obstacles to learning high-dynamic motion from video, and that they can only be overcome jointly. Accordingly, the paper is organised as a single pipeline, where each technical contribution is precisely the remedy for one failure mode, and where an ablation shows that removing any one of them breaks the pipeline.

The video-to-robot pathway. Videos are segmented into clips, reconstructed to a kinematic sequence 𝐪 hum 1 : T \mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{hum}}_{1:T} , retargeted Araujo et al. (2025) to the robot to give a reference 𝐪 ref 1 : T \mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{1:T} , and tracked by a policy π \pi . The last three steps are where the pathway breaks, and they require two sub-systems: a repair stage that restores physical validity, and a compensation stage that supplies, through learning, the dynamics and the failure model that video never contained. These are not independently swappable: without the compensation, strict single-stage tracking of an infeasible reference collapses (Fig. 4 a), and without the unified recovery the robot cannot return to the motion once disturbed (Sec. 6.5 ).

Contributions.

A video-derived professional high-dynamic dataset (addresses C1). In collaboration with national-level martial artists, we construct KungfuAthlete from 197 training videos, segmented into 1,726 sub-clips, reconstructed and retargeted to a Unitree G1. It covers both sustained ground skills and highly non-stationary aerial skills, with higher body linear and angular velocities than the corpora compared in Table 1 . Dataset, licence and released artefacts are detailed in Sec. 3.1 .

A physics-aware repair of video artifacts (addresses C1). We replace the floating root trajectory with a physically consistent one: ground alignment from the lowest body point, event-aware propagation with contact detection, ballistic (constant-acceleration) interpolation of flight phases, penetration removal, and Savitzky–Golay smoothing. Unlike prior work that simply discards jump segments as unusable, our correction recovers them, preventing a large-scale waste of the most valuable video data.

Physics-driven sampling for missing actuation (addresses C2). We introduce pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling , our central mechanism for making unreliable video references learnable: rather than initialising wherever the current tracking error is largest, it derives the initial-state distribution from a kinetic-energy proxy of the reference and therefore never concentrates capacity on dynamically infeasible aerial poses. A standard progressive-tolerance curriculum complements it (Sec. 4.3 ); Sec. 4.4 contrasts our setting – unreliable video-derived references – with prior high-dynamic tracking work that assumes faithful references.

A unified robust policy over video data (addresses C3). We propose a direct formulation in which one policy tracks the video motion, rejects disturbances, and recovers from arbitrary gravity-induced falls, with no recovery-specific reference data and no manual switching. It attains ≈ 0.7 \approx 0.7 s recovery – to our knowledge the fastest reported for a unified policy – validated on real hardware.

Sec. 2 positions this work against prior art. The remainder of the paper is organised around the three failure modes: Sec. 3 presents the dataset and the repair of reconstructed motion (C1); Sec. 4 addresses missing actuation (C2); Sec. 5 presents the unified policy (C3); Sec. 6 evaluates tracking, recovery and ablations, with additional material in the appendix.

# 2 Related Work

Humanoid motion tracking has largely been driven by motion-capture corpora such as AMASS Mahmood et al. (2019) and LAFAN1 Harvey et al. (2020) , which are natural and continuous but confined to low-to-medium dynamics, and by hardware-based collection such as exoskeletons (HOMIE, HumanoidExo) Ben et al. (2025) ; Zhong et al. (2025) or VR teleoperation (TWIST2, SONIC) Ze et al. (2025b) ; Luo et al. (2025) , which are physically consistent but require specialist hardware and scale poorly. Video is therefore attractive: monocular reconstruction such as GVHMR Shen et al. (2024) and PromptHMR Wang et al. (2025) recovers complex motion from arbitrary footage, at the cost of global drift, temporal jitter and error accumulation that make the result unusable for control without repair.

FARM Jing et al. (2025) , HDMI Weng et al. (2025) and SONIC Luo et al. (2025) retarget GVHMR or GENMO Li et al. (2025a) output to a humanoid; ZEST Sleiman et al. (2026) combines MegaSaM Li et al. (2025c) and TRAM Wang et al. (2024) . None of them treats reconstruction artifacts systematically. Exbody2 Ji et al. (2024) filters out hard motions with a tuned threshold, while ASAP He et al. (2025a) and KungfuBot Xie et al. (2025) mask or offset physically invalid frames; all of them discard what cannot be made compliant, which is precisely the high-dynamic data we want. Our correction instead repairs the aerial phase.

ASAP adds a delta-action model and fine-tuning; KungfuBot filters via centre of mass and adapts the tracking tolerance to the current error; HuB Zhang et al. (2025) and Agility Meets Stability Pan et al. (2025) regularise foot and centre-of-mass behaviour. BeyondMimic Liao et al. (2025) uses diffusion models and dynamic sampling, and Robot Dancing Sun et al. (2025) uses residual actions and domain randomisation, but neither sustains long high-dynamic sequences nor handles a fall. OmniXtreme Wang et al. (2026) scales policy capacity and refines for actuation, assuming high-fidelity references.

HumanUP He et al. (2025b) and HoST Huang et al. (2025) learn standing-up policies without data, and Unified Humanoid Get-Up Spraggett (2025) generalises across morphologies, but all treat recovery as an isolated task. SafeFall Meng et al. (2025) switches to a protective policy, and FIRM Xu et al. (2025) unifies prevention, mitigation and get-up from limited demonstrations; BFM-Zero Li et al. (2025b) unifies tracking and recovery but needs auxiliary data. StableMimic Wu et al. (2026) also unifies tracking and recovery in one policy, and reports smoother, more human-like post-fall motion; it obtains that style by shaping recovery toward a library of retargeted human get-up references . Our recovery is shaped by no human reference at all: it is learned from the same tracking objective as the motion itself (Sec. 5 ), which is what makes it applicable when no paired get-up demonstration exists. None of the works above learns recovery jointly with tracking from video , and none does so without human reference data.

2026-10-05.title: Equivariant Visual-Tactile Diffusion Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Lik Hang Kenny Wong , Yiyao Ma , Xiu-Shen Wei , Zelong Tan , Zhuheng Song , Dongsheng Xie , Kai Chen , Qi Dou
2026-10-05.comment: . Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
2026-10-05.abstract: Imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation requires high-quality expert data that is expensive to obtain. This makes learning a sample-efficient policy a key issue. To address this, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy for data-efficient contact-rich imitation learning. VISTA projects visual and tactile observations into spherical tokens, injects tactile contact cues into visual spherical directions through permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, and rotates the fused harmonic representation using the end-effector orientation. The resulting representation conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict spatially consistent actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings show that VISTA substantially improves data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation learning baselines. Project website: https://vista-paper.github.io/
2026-10-05.introduction:
Many daily contact-rich tasks, such as inserting a USB drive or wiping a table, require tactile sensing in addition to vision. For robots, however, using both modalities effectively remains challenging. Recent robotics research has increasingly adopted imitation learning with visual and tactile feedback for contact-rich manipulation [ 41 , 8 , 37 ] , but expert demonstrations are expensive to collect and often cover only a limited range of object poses, gripper poses, and contact configurations [ 29 ] . Moreover, for tasks such as insertion, success depends heavily on the policy’s robustness to small deviations in observed object and robot poses [ 16 ] . Therefore, how can we learn robust visuotactile policies with fewer demonstrations?

Equivariance provides a principled way to reduce the spatial coverage required from data for a policy to achieve spatial robustness [ 36 , 4 , 26 , 6 , 15 ] . In an equivariant policy, if the observation is transformed by a spatial transformation from a symmetry group, the predicted action should transform in the corresponding way.
By building this symmetry into the architecture, the model can improve spatial generalizability across object poses, gripper poses, and scene configurations with fewer demonstrations than non-equivariant policies [ 35 , 33 ] . This is especially appealing for contact-rich manipulation, where demonstrations are costly, and task success is sensitive to small spatial deviations. However, existing equivariant manipulation policies are still largely vision-centric. They are typically designed around RGB images, point clouds, or other global geometric observations [ 20 ] , limiting their ability to handle contact-rich settings where local tactile feedback is critical.

In this paper, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy. Our method is inspired by the observation that both egocentric camera and tactile sensors are often mounted on the end effector of a robot for manipulation tasks; therefore, global workspace rotations change the sensor-to-world transform while preserving the local contact measurement. Concretely, our method first maps egocentric vision and tactile observations into local spherical representations. It then performs permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, allowing tactile contact cues to modulate visual directions while preserving the spherical structure of the representation. The fused spherical representation is then transformed by the end-effector pose rotation and processed with an equivariant diffusion policy to achieve workspace-level equivariance. As a result, VISTA improves data efficiency and generalization under limited demonstrations. We evaluate VISTA on both contact-rich simulation tasks and real-robot experiments and show that the proposed framework enables more data-efficient contact-rich manipulation learning.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce VISTA, extending the workspace-level equivariant backbone from Image-to-Sphere Policy (ISP) [ 12 ] to the visuotactile setting for contact-rich tasks, enabling more data-efficient learning by incorporating local tactile feedback into an equivariant policy.

We design a spherical cross-modal fusion module that integrates tactile cues into the structured visual representation, allowing the downstream equivariant diffusion policy to leverage the fused representation effectively. Across eight simulated tasks, this design improves mean success by 6.8 percentage points over direct visual-tactile feature concatenation on the sphere.

We demonstrate data-efficient contact-rich manipulation across eight simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks: VISTA achieves 80.9% mean success, outperforming EquiDiff+Tac by 15.9 percentage points, and 73.3% average success on real robots.

1. We introduce VISTA, extending the workspace-level equivariant backbone from Image-to-Sphere Policy (ISP) [ 12 ] to the visuotactile setting for contact-rich tasks, enabling more data-efficient learning by incorporating local tactile feedback into an equivariant policy.

2. We design a spherical cross-modal fusion module that integrates tactile cues into the structured visual representation, allowing the downstream equivariant diffusion policy to leverage the fused representation effectively. Across eight simulated tasks, this design improves mean success by 6.8 percentage points over direct visual-tactile feature concatenation on the sphere.

3. We demonstrate data-efficient contact-rich manipulation across eight simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks: VISTA achieves 80.9% mean success, outperforming EquiDiff+Tac by 15.9 percentage points, and 73.3% average success on real robots.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Equivariance in robot manipulation

Equivariance embeds workspace symmetry into the policy class by requiring that transformed scenes, objects, and robot states yield actions transformed in the same physical manner [ 23 , 5 , 30 , 3 , 4 ] . Existing equivariant manipulation methods primarily enforce this constraint in two observation domains. The first operates on 3D geometry such as point clouds [ 24 , 7 , 26 , 6 , 20 , 40 , 28 , 42 ] , where scalar, vector, or higher-order features are attached to 3D points and propagated according to their transformation rules [ 40 , 28 , 42 ] ; translation is typically handled by centering, relative coordinates, centroid recovery, or canonicalization, while rotation can be modeled with vector neurons [ 6 ] . Although this provides a natural interface for workspace-level equivariance, it often relies on reliable depth sensing, calibration, point cloud extraction, and alignment. The second route starts from RGB observations, motivated by large-scale robot datasets and practical systems based on monocular or wrist-mounted cameras; recent work has explored planar transport, bi-equivariant pick-and-place, equivariant diffusion for 6-DoF actions, and image-to-sphere projection for egocentric RGB inputs [ 14 , 32 , 18 ] . However, both routes remain largely vision-centric: their symmetries are defined over visual observations, proprioception, and actions.

## 2.2 Contact-rich visuotactile manipulation

Tactile sensing provides contact-local cues—geometry, deformation, shear, slip, and force—that vision often cannot resolve, making it crucial for contact-rich manipulation. Existing work studies visuotactile representation learning through contrastive or simulation-based pretraining, while also integrating touch into policies for precise or reactive control [ 8 , 38 , 1 , 19 , 13 , 37 , 39 , 27 , 11 , 16 ] . Although these methods show the value of tactile feedback when vision is insufficient, they focus mainly on representation, benchmark design, or reactive feedback rather than explicitly modeling workspace-level symmetry. Thus, tactile observations are usually encoded by CNNs, pretrained encoders, deformation features, or temporal modules and then fused with visual and proprioceptive inputs, allowing policies to use touch effectively but without explicitly enforcing consistent transformations among vision, touch, robot state, and 6-DoF actions under changes in object pose, gripper pose, or task frame. VISTA addresses this geometric gap by organizing visual and tactile RGB observations within a shared steerable latent interface before equivariant action generation.

## 2.3 Tactile equivariance and geometric contact policies

The most closely related works also study symmetry in tactile or contact-driven manipulation, but they realize equivariance in different settings and through different mechanisms. EquiTac defines tactile equivariance for in-hand object rotation by reconstructing tactile normal maps whose in-plane components transform as S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) SO(2) vectors while out-of-plane components remain invariant, and then uses an equivariant network to predict an angular residual for correcting a base policy [ 45 ] ; however, this symmetry is local to the fingertip/object-in-hand frame and serves as a residual orientation correction, rather than a global workspace-level policy that jointly transforms RGB observations, tactile feedback, proprioception, and 6-DoF action chunks. In contrast, geometric contact policies achieve workspace-level symmetry from a control-theoretic perspective: contact-rich S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) -equivariant manipulation relies on body-frame error and wrench representations with impedance control [ 22 ] , while hierarchical variants further combine global reference-frame estimation with localized compliant policies [ 21 ] . Thus, although these methods provide important forms of tactile or contact equivariance, VISTA complements them by building workspace-level equivariance directly into an end-to-end diffusion policy over visuotactile and proprioceptive observations.

2026-10-05.title: HexVIO: Towards All-Day Stereo-Inertial Tracking Through Commodity DSPs
2026-10-05.authors: Patrick Wolf , Mateo de Mayo , Daniel Cremers
2026-10-05.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-05.abstract:
The ability of a device to localize itself within its surroundings is a fundamental prerequisite for spatial computing. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) has proven to be a cost-effective and accurate solution for this task.
Robots, wearables, XR devices, and drones can benefit significantly from efficient implementations of VIO since they allow for cooler, lighter, and cheaper devices with longer battery life and a better user experience. In this work, we propose to enhance the efficiency of a VIO system by leveraging the Hexagon DSP, a commodity co-processor present in many modern smartphones and XR devices. Our approach offloads the visual frontend of a stereo-inertial odometry system to the DSP while keeping the backend on the main CPU. By optimizing the implementation for the DSP architecture, we achieve significant reductions in power consumption and latency compared to CPU-only execution. Our system, HexVIO, demonstrates a 67% reduction in power consumption or an 86% increase in throughput on a commodity smartphone, with the ability to sustain long-term real-time 30 fps tracking for 0.83 W, corresponding to ∼ \sim 18 hours of tracking on the testing device. These results highlight the potential of commodity DSPs for enabling all-day visual-inertial tracking in robotics and mobile devices.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Recent advancements in robotics [ 1 , 2 ] , computer vision [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , and foundation models capable of complex reasoning [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] have started to show the possibilities of perception engineering [ 10 ] as a new discipline and of spatial computing [ 11 ] as the ever more common class of problems that require a computing device to understand its surroundings. Different instances of this problem arise in important applications like autonomous vehicles, drones, humanoid robotics, wearables like smartglasses, and VR headsets. A fundamental capability that allows much of this reasoning comes from the ability of the device to localize itself and its movements in space. Utilizing cameras and inertial measurement units (IMU) for visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and visual-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (VI-SLAM) has shown to be a particularly good combination thanks to the low cost of these sensors, their reduced power consumption, and proven accuracy [ 12 , 13 ] .

The field of VIO and VI-SLAM has made rapid progress in the previous decade enabling this technology to be deployed in commercial devices like VR headsets and smartphones. However, existing limitations in terms of accuracy per watt remain in the literature [ 14 ] , driving research into highly specialized hardware accelerators [ 15 , 16 ] . These accelerators reach their efficiency through custom silicon, so they only ship in devices designed around them. We instead use a co-processor that existing devices already carry. It is nowadays common to find systems, even low-end ones, that have a GPU alongside the CPU. DSPs have developed from fixed-function audio and modem processors into increasingly general-purpose compute units that run at a fraction of the energy cost of a CPU [ 17 ] . The Hexagon DSP is now present in a multitude of devices spanning smartphones, VR, AR, and robotics (e.g., Snapdragon 8, XR2, AR1, and RB5 respectively). The DSP provides very long instruction words with wide vector lanes coupled with fast local memory. When properly utilized, this results in significantly reduced power usage for certain tasks compared to using the CPU or GPU. This kind of co-processor allows robots, XR devices, and smartphones to do long-haul vision tasks thanks to the low power required to perform them on these accelerators. The low power not only extends operation, but can also directly improve the target application: smaller batteries for lighter and cheaper drones, lighter headworn devices for reduced neck strain, and cooler smartglasses for improved comfort. The goal we work towards is tracking that runs for a full day on a device’s own battery. Even with all these benefits, very few works in the literature exploit it for the fundamental task of visual-inertial tracking and, to the best of our knowledge, none of them for the stereo-inertial sensor modality.

In this work, we offload the frontend of a visual-inertial odometry system based on Basalt [ 18 ] to the Hexagon DSP of a Samsung Galaxy S23 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, Hexagon V73). A direct port does not beat the CPU. Sparse tracking branches per feature and reads scattered pixels, the vector unit runs all lanes together and its gather reads only on-chip memory, and each DSP call costs hundreds of microseconds, so calling the DSP once per stage spends much of the gain on round trips. Most of the work is restructuring the frontend around these three constraints. The contributions of this work are:

The first stereo-inertial odometry system in the literature leveraging the Hexagon DSP co-processor.

The first stereo-inertial odometry system in the literature leveraging the Hexagon DSP co-processor.

An optimized open-source 1 1 1 The source code will be released implementation of the VIO frontend providing insight into the DSP for vision tasks.

A thorough power, latency, and performance analysis that shows HexVIO achieving an 86% increase of throughput or a 67% reduction of power (Fig. 1 ).

An energy-focused configuration that sustains real-time 30 fps tracking for 0.83 W, corresponding to ∼ \sim 18 hours of tracking on the testing device.

2026-10-05.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Contemporary VIO and VI-SLAM pipelines generally decompose into a visual frontend, responsible for keypoint detection and feature tracking, an inertial integration stage, and a backend optimizer or filter tasked with fusing these modalities. A diverse set of representative systems has emerged in the literature, including optimization-based frameworks such as ORB-SLAM3 [ 13 ] , which augments feature-based pipelines with inertial measurements and map atlases, and VINS-Mono/VINS-Fusion [ 19 ] or OKVIS [ 20 ] , which rely on sliding-window nonlinear optimization. Filter-based approaches, notably ROVIO [ 21 ] and MSCKF [ 22 ] , also remain widely adopted. In this work, we build upon Basalt [ 18 ] , incorporating modifications from [ 23 ] . Basalt utilizes a fixed-lag smoother that couples patch-based Lucas-Kanade tracking [ 24 , 25 ] , implemented in its inverse-compositional form [ 26 ] to keep reference-side linear algebra out of the iteration loop, with FAST corner detection [ 27 ] , preintegrated IMU factors, and first-estimate-Jacobian marginalization. The open implementation of Basalt, along with its balance between performance and accuracy [ 23 ] , makes it a particularly strong target for frontend acceleration on embedded platforms.

Mobile VIO systems must additionally sustain the camera frame rate within a strict thermal and power envelope, a dual constraint formalized in embedded VIO benchmarking practices that report tracking accuracy alongside per-frame computational cost on target hardware [ 28 ] . One established strategy to meet these constraints involves redesigning the estimator itself. For instance, LEVIO [ 16 ] achieves 20 fps six-DoF tracking below 100 mW on an ultra-low-power RISC-V SoC by employing a streamlined ORB-based frontend alongside a comprehensive hardware-software co-design. In contrast, this work preserves Basalt’s complete pipeline and instead focuses on accelerating its execution. This is a reasonable approach given these SoCs are already widely adopted by different industries trying to leverage spatial computing.

The visual frontend is a natural hardware acceleration target, as its per-feature computations are easy to parallelize and its backend interface reduces to sparse correspondences. Prior work has largely targeted GPUs: vilib [ 29 ] and Jetson-SLAM [ 14 ] accelerate FAST-based frontends in CUDA (KLT as in ours, and ORB, respectively), while FastTrack [ 30 ] offloads portions of ORB-SLAM3 to the GPU. GLidE-SLAM [ 31 ] employs OpenGL compute shaders to circumvent CUDA lock-in and augments indirect features with direct GPU tracking. In contrast, our DSP-based approach frees the GPU for concurrent workloads and sidesteps the thermal constraints and higher power draw typical of GPU acceleration, while still delivering low-power, high-frame-rate tracking.

At the other extreme, custom silicon achieves the lowest reported energy per frame. Navion [ 15 ] integrates a complete VIO pipeline into a 2 mW ASIC via algorithm-hardware co-design [ 32 ] , albeit at the cost of fixing the algorithm. FPGA-based solutions offer a more flexible alternative: eSLAM [ 33 ] accelerates only ORB extraction and matching, while ac2SLAM [ 34 ] accelerates both the ORB-SLAM2 frontend and backend, though neither incorporates inertial fusion. PX4Flow [ 35 ] instead computes block-matching optical flow on a microcontroller inside the sensor. Compared to the Hexagon DSP, however, these custom accelerators lack broad availability on commodity platforms, and ASICs offer no post-deployment reprogrammability.

Hexagon DSPs occupy a middle ground: they are programmable, widely deployed, and optimized for energy-efficient single-instruction multiple-data (SIMD) vector processing. The Hexagon architecture [ 17 ] combines a VLIW scalar core with the HVX wide-vector coprocessor and a software-managed scratchpad. Originally designed for audio and modem tasks, it now supports general-purpose workloads, including LLM inference [ 36 ] , while vendor CV/ML stacks (FastCV, SNPE, QNN [ 37 ] ) and the Halide compiler [ 38 ] already target it for dense image processing. Despite this ecosystem, academic use of Hexagon for visual-inertial tracking remains limited. The closest prior work is Muffang’s thesis [ 39 ] , which offloaded OpenVINS [ 40 ] frontend routines to a Snapdragon 845 via FastCV; it reduced CPU load but the offloaded kernels ran slower than their CPU equivalents, and no source code was released. An open Hexagon port of the ORB-SLAM3 feature extractor and matcher exists for the Lynx R1 headset [ 41 ] , but it lacks inertial fusion and requires a rooted device. Crucially, none of the prior efforts support stereo-inertial tracking, a ubiquitous modality in consumer XR and robotics.

Relative to this body of work, our system is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to accelerate a multicamera VIO pipeline on the Hexagon DSP of a stock consumer smartphone. While LEVIO shares our energy efficiency goals, it fundamentally redesigns the estimator for minimal compute budgets sacrificing accuracy; approaches like vilib, FastTrack, Jetson-SLAM, and GLidE-SLAM target frontend acceleration but rely on higher-power GPUs; ASIC-, FPGA- and MCU-based solutions like Navion, eSLAM, ac2SLAM, and PX4Flow achieve high efficiency but require hardware that is unavailable on common platforms. Prior Hexagon-based tracking efforts either lack stereo-inertial support, remain closed-source, and/or require rooted devices. In contrast, our implementation is open-source, runs on unmodified consumer hardware, and demonstrates that the Hexagon DSP can effectively accelerate stereo-inertial VIO frontends at significantly lower power.

2026-10-05.title: DexJoCo-X: Benchmarking Action Representations for Multi-Hand Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Xiangwei Jiang , Yao Mu , Lixin Duan , Wen Li
2026-10-05.comment: . Project website: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: As dexterous hands proliferate, collecting data and training policies separately for every morphology becomes increasingly impractical. Scalable cross-embodiment learning therefore requires a unified representation that captures shared manipulation structure while preserving morphology-specific control. Differences in hands, tasks, datasets, and control interfaces prevent existing studies from isolating the effects of representation, pretraining, and architecture. We introduce DexJoCo-X, a benchmark and toolkit for controlled comparison across seven representative dexterous hands, six single-arm and bimanual tasks, and 2,100 balanced demonstrations. DexJoCo-X provides a matched multi-hand, multi-task protocol with common scenes, success criteria, and execution interfaces, redesigned glove-to-hand mappings, and an automated pipeline that expands reviewed demonstrations across randomized scenes. Using π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , Ego-Pi, and Being-H0.5, we examine whether a shared action interface is sufficient for multi-hand learning. Expanding π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} to an 80-dimensional bimanual output yields near-zero success. Ego-Pi preserves the pretrained action head through interleaved prediction and supports per-hand multi-task learning, but remains ineffective for seven-hand joint training. By contrast, Being-H0.5 combines cross-embodiment pretraining, a unified action space, and embodiment-aware experts, enabling one policy to control all seven hands. Within this architecture, function-aligned action slots achieve 47.7% mean success, compared with 47.0% for native coordinates and 33.1% for DexLatent. These results show that cross-embodiment representation depends on the entire learning system: action coordinates, pretraining, and architecture must jointly separate shared manipulation structure from embodiment-specific control.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Learning manipulation skills that can be shared across dexterous hands is essential for deploying general-purpose robots on diverse hardware. Diverse hand kinematics and actuation fragment demonstrations and policies, making separate training costly and limiting experience reuse. Multi-embodiment datasets and generalist policies, including Open X-Embodiment/RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, HPT, and the π \pi series [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] , establish a foundation for sharing robot experience. RT-2 [ 7 ] transfers vision–language knowledge to control. RDT-1B [ 8 ] uses unified action coordinates, and X-VLA [ 9 ] addresses embodiment heterogeneity through soft prompts, while Being-H0.5 [ 10 ] and Ego-Pi [ 11 ] connect human demonstrations with robot learning. Complementary approaches include diffusion policies with shared action latents [ 12 , 13 ] and cross-hand reinforcement learning [ 14 ] . These efforts motivate action representations that link shared skills to embodiment-specific execution. Recent dexterous foundation-model frameworks, including UniDex [ 15 ] and XL-VLA [ 16 ] , report promising multi-hand learning capabilities through different representations. Yet results obtained with different hands, datasets, and task protocols do not establish which approach best supports cross-hand manipulation under a common evaluation standard.

Existing benchmarks provide complementary capabilities: DexArt [ 17 ] studies articulated objects, Bi-DexHands [ 18 ] emphasizes bimanual control, DexJoCo [ 19 ] supplies functional tasks and demonstration tools, and DexVerse [ 20 ] broadens task and embodiment coverage. These benchmarks expand task coverage, but leave open which action representations best support cross-hand learning under matched conditions. A fair comparison requires the same hands, tasks, demonstrations, policy backbone, and success criteria. A shared control interface is also needed to evaluate new representations without rebuilding the hand-control pipeline. These needs motivate a dedicated benchmark for fair and accessible cross-hand evaluation.

To address these needs, we introduce DexJoCo-X , a unified benchmark and toolkit designed for fair comparison and straightforward integration of cross-hand policies (Fig. ). Built on DexJoCo, it combines seven hand interfaces, six tasks, and 2,100 demonstrations with a reusable collection pipeline. We fine-tune π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 6 ] with the Ego-Pi protocol [ 11 ] as a per-hand multi-task reference, training one Native-action policy for each hand. Our central cross-hand comparison instead trains one Being-H0.5 policy [ 10 ] jointly on all seven hands under Native, FAAS, or DexLatent, and evaluates every hand on independent scenes. Our contributions are:

A unified cross-hand benchmark. Seven hands and six tasks share evaluation scenes, success criteria, and control interfaces for fair comparison of action representations under matched training conditions.

A reusable demonstration collection toolkit. Redesigned glove-to-hand mappings for all seven hands support human teleoperation, while automated scene expansion and trajectory verification scale demonstration collection.

A balanced multi-hand demonstration dataset. We collect 2,100 demonstrations spanning six single-arm and bimanual tasks, with 50 trajectories for each of the 42 hand–task pairs.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Manipulation Benchmarks and Dexterous Tasks

RLBench [ 21 ] , CALVIN [ 22 ] , and LIBERO [ 23 ] benchmark arm–gripper manipulation; Robosuite [ 24 ] and ManiSkill2 [ 25 ] provide broader simulation infrastructure. Arm–gripper tasks do not test independent finger coordination.

Multi-finger hand benchmarks address bimanual coordination [ 18 ] , articulated objects [ 17 ] , deformable objects [ 26 ] , and trajectory tracking across hands [ 27 ] . Grasp-focused resources evaluate pose generation [ 28 , 29 ] and functional or language-guided grasping [ 30 , 31 ] . DexJoCo [ 19 ] evaluates complete functional tasks, while DexVerse [ 20 ] expands task and embodiment coverage. Building on DexJoCo, we enable fair comparison of cross-hand action representations through balanced seven-hand, six-task demonstrations, shared evaluation scenes and success criteria, and reusable control interfaces.

## II-B Human Demonstrations and Automated Expansion

Human-to-robot hand mapping spans joint, Cartesian, task-oriented, and reduced-dimensional formulations [ 32 ] . DexPilot [ 33 ] , Robotic Telekinesis [ 34 ] , AnyTeleop [ 35 ] , and DIME [ 36 ] use human motion to teach dexterous control. ALOHA [ 37 ] and UMI [ 38 ] broaden accessible demonstration capture, while LEAP Hand [ 39 ] provides an affordable dexterous embodiment.

DexMV [ 40 ] and ViViDex [ 41 ] learn from human video demonstrations. CyberDemo [ 42 ] augments simulated human demonstrations for real-world manipulation. MimicGen [ 43 ] expands demonstrations across contexts, and DexMimicGen [ 44 ] extends this approach to bimanual dexterity. Our toolkit supplies native demonstrations through seven glove mappings and verified scene expansion.

## II-C Cross-Hand Learning and Action Representations

Recent advances span action-chunking and diffusion policies [ 37 , 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 ] , vision–language–action models [ 7 , 3 , 5 , 6 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , and world-model-based control [ 49 , 50 , 51 ] . Cross-hand grasping shares contact points or maps [ 52 , 53 , 54 ] , interaction geometry [ 55 , 56 ] , and morphology-conditioned eigengrasps [ 57 ] . For closed-loop cross-hand control, shared keypoint commands [ 58 ] , retargeted human-hand actions [ 14 ] , morphology-aligned graphs [ 59 ] , and canonical hand descriptions [ 60 ] connect common skills to different kinematics. Particle-based world models [ 51 ] additionally share interaction dynamics.

Shared action spaces also enable learning from heterogeneous demonstrations. LAD [ 12 ] and OPFA [ 13 ] learn aligned action latents; AdvDex [ 61 ] aligns human and robot joints. UniDex [ 15 ] uses functional slots, while XL-VLA [ 16 ] learns cross-hand codecs. DexJoCo-X compares these representation principles under matched data, backbones, scenes, and control interfaces across seven hands.

2026-10-05.title: Beyond Reward Hacking: Proxy Divergence Across Four Layers of a Staged Humanoid Learning Pipeline
2026-10-05.authors: Arunabh Bora
2026-10-05.abstract:
A reinforcement-learning (RL) pipeline for a legged robot is assembled from proxies. A
reward stands in for intended behaviour, a curriculum gate stands in for competence, an
evaluation statistic stands in for robustness, and a reference motion stands in for an
achievable skill. The traditional view treats only the first of these as optimised
against, and so locates specification failure (reward hacking) in the reward alone. I
argue that all four are proxies in the same formal sense, that each has a characteristic
divergence mechanism, and that each admits a reformulation that closes it. For every
layer I state the traditional formulation, derive the condition under which it diverges
from its target, and give the alternative: first-order (L1) costs where quadratic
kernels are flat, peak and outcome statistics where curriculum gates average, gate
reachability and information checks, deterministic and phase-desynchronised evaluation,
curriculum state treated as part of the model, feasibility-first reference design with
residual feed-forward, and function-preserving input widening that lets one policy grow
instead of being retrained. The arguments are illustrated by measurements from one
continuous lineage of a PPO policy for a simulated 1.91 m humanoid, grown over four
stages and 13,500 iterations on a single laptop GPU. Among them, a curriculum gate built
on averaged error advanced at its rate limit on every check while the skill it gated was
absent, and a batched push test whose synchronised resets aliased the gait phase ranked a
0.5 m/s push as more dangerous than a 2.0 m/s one.
2026-10-05.introduction:
GPU-parallel simulation has made it routine to train a locomotion policy
in hours on one machine [ 1 , 2 ] . The resulting pipeline has a
standard shape: a weighted sum of shaped reward terms, a performance-gated curriculum over
terrain and commands, batched evaluation in the simulator, and, for skills beyond
locomotion, a tracking reward towards a reference motion [ 3 ] . Each of these
components replaces something physical with something computable.

The literature on specification gaming [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] studies
the gap between a proxy and its target, but in robot learning it is applied almost
exclusively to the reward. The other components are treated as plumbing: a curriculum
threshold is a tuning constant, an evaluation script is assumed to measure what it
reports, and a reference motion is assumed to be achievable. My thesis is that this
traditional view is incomplete. A curriculum gate is optimised against just as a reward
is, because the policy that passes it is the one the gate selects. An evaluation
statistic is a proxy whose bias can be created by the harness itself, with no
optimisation at all. A reference motion is a proxy for a skill, and it can be wrong in a
way that no reward design can repair.

A four-layer formulation of proxy divergence (reward, curriculum,
measurement, reference), with, for each layer, the traditional formulation, the
condition under which it diverges, and a reformulation (Sections IV – VII , summarised in Table III ).

A four-layer formulation of proxy divergence (reward, curriculum,
measurement, reference), with, for each layer, the traditional formulation, the
condition under which it diverges, and a reformulation (Sections IV – VII , summarised in Table III ).

Curriculum gates as estimators : a dilution bound showing that gates on
error averaged over joints and time cannot reject large localised failures, a
reachability condition, an information argument for counting gate refusals, and the
observation that curriculum state belongs to the model, not the environment
(Section V ).

Two systematic evaluation biases that do not shrink with sample size:
outcomes manufactured by exploration noise, and phase aliasing from synchronised
resets, with corrected estimators (Section VI ).

Feasibility-first reference design : why tracking an infeasible reference
converges to a qualitatively different behaviour regardless of reward shaping, and
a static test, a correction and a residual action that avoid it
(Section VII ).

Function-preserving policy growth through input widening and split
authority, as an alternative to retraining from scratch whenever the observation
changes (Section VIII ).
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

RL for legged and humanoid robots. Deep RL now produces deployed locomotion and
whole-body controllers [ 8 ] , including zero-shot humanoid walking [ 9 ] , agile whole-body skills with sim-to-real alignment [ 10 ] ,
and general motion tracking [ 11 ] . Most of these pipelines share the structure
analysed here, built on GPU-parallel simulators such as Isaac Lab [ 2 ] .

Reward design and specification gaming. Practical locomotion rewards are weighted
sums of heuristic terms [ 1 ] , and recent work automates their design with
language models [ 12 ] . Skalse et al. [ 4 ] showed that
unhackable proxy rewards are very restricted; Pan et al. [ 5 ] found that
more capable agents exploit misspecified rewards more, sometimes through abrupt phase
transitions; Gao et al. [ 6 ] measured scaling laws for over-optimising a
proxy; and Laidlaw et al. [ 7 ] defined reward hacking through the
correlation between proxy and true reward under a base policy. All of this work treats the
reward as the proxy. I extend the same lens to curriculum gates, evaluation statistics and
reference motions.

Curricula. In locomotion, terrain and command levels are raised when agents
perform well [ 1 ] , and adaptive command curricula are central to fast legged
locomotion [ 13 ] . The gate that decides promotion is treated as a tuning
constant; I analyse it as an estimator.

Evaluation methodology. Agarwal et al. [ 14 ] and Patterson et al. [ 15 ] showed that deep-RL conclusions are fragile to seeds,
aggregate statistics and experimental design. Those are largely variance effects; the
biases studied here are systematic and do not shrink with sample size.

Imitation and residual control. Tracking rewards towards reference motions [ 3 ] and adversarial motion priors [ 16 ] remain the basis of humanoid
skill learning [ 10 , 11 ] . References retargeted from human motion capture
approximately inherit the human’s dynamic feasibility; hand-authored references do not.
Residual formulations learn a correction on top of a fixed controller [ 17 ] , and ASAP applies a learned delta-action model on top of a pretrained
policy [ 10 ] .

Growing and continually training networks. Net2Net [ 18 ] introduced
function-preserving expansion. Plasticity injection [ 19 ] adds a new
network whose initial output is exactly zero, so predictions are unchanged at the moment
of injection; Neuroplastic Expansion [ 20 ] grows the network during training.
Loss of plasticity under continual training is now well documented [ 21 ] ,
including for on-policy methods such as PPO [ 22 ] , which is the regime of a
policy fine-tuned across many stages.

2026-10-05.title: Safe Streaming Flow Planning by Aligning Sampling Dynamics with Execution Dynamics
2026-10-05.authors: Seunghwan Jang , Jeongyong Yang , Siddharth Ancha , SooJean Han
2026-10-05.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). Project page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Generative planners based on diffusion / / flow matching can learn to synthesize long-horizon trajectories from demonstrations. However, real-world deployment requires (i) enforcing safety constraints during execution and (ii) tight online replanning at fast execution rates.
Prior safe diffusion / / flow planners generate the agent’s full trajectory at once , while repeatedly perturbing intermediate states to satisfy safety constraints. This approach is not only computationally intensive, but also introduces distribution shift since the learned sampling dynamics is distinct from the system’s execution dynamics.
We propose SafeStreamingFlow , a goal-conditioned planner that aligns flow sampling dynamics with execution dynamics by sequentially integrating a learned state vector field with hierarchical state prediction.
Importantly, we need to enforce safety constraints only for the executed step via high order control barrier functions.
Across navigation, racing, and locomotion benchmarks, SafeStreamingFlow reduces planning latency and improves safety compared to existing methods, while maintaining competitive goal-reaching success.
Code is available on our project page: https://jang-seunghwan.github.io/SafeStreamingFlowPlanning/ .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Generative models [ 11 , 20 ] that have driven rapid progress in image and language generation are increasingly being adapted to robotic tasks, particularly diffusion [ 14 , 8 , 15 ] and flow matching [ 30 ] .
Deploying such models for robot planning, however, requires more than producing a plausible trajectory.
Most diffusion/flow planners typically generate an entire horizon as a single object in trajectory space and refine it through K K denoising/sampling steps, where each step updates all H H states in the trajectory [ 14 ] .
In a closed-loop setting, this full-horizon procedure must be repeated at every control cycle to incorporate state feedback and new observations, generating H × K H\times K intermediate states per cycle [ 16 , 13 ] .

Another key challenge is enforcing safety constraints imposed at inference time, possibly never seen during training, in a manner that is both reliable and compatible with closed-loop execution. Many generative methods promote safety through guidance [ 7 , 12 ] , injecting heuristic costs, penalties, or constraint-related scores into the generation process to steer samples away from unsafe regions; such guidance either requires the constraint to be learned in advance or imposes it only softly, without formal guarantees [ 17 , 21 ] .
An especially promising approach to certified safety is to incorporate control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 2 , 1 ] into the sampling procedure by solving quadratic programs (QPs) at inference time; the constraints then hold whenever each QP is feasible.
However, because intermediate sampling states are not physically executed, enforcing safety during sampling can disrupt dynamical consistency of the generated trajectories and induce local-traps , discontinuous trajectories that remain safe but infeasible to execute [ 30 , 28 ] .

In addition, safety enforcement further increases the computational burden because CBF-based corrections are applied across both the horizon length H H and sampling iterations K K , resulting in ( H × K ) (H\times K) QP solves to generate a single trajectory. Streaming-based formulations [ 13 , 16 ] have been introduced for real-time execution by aligning sampling time with execution time.
However, existing streaming approaches are developed primarily as policies for action imitation, leaving both the system’s execution dynamics and start–goal-conditioned planning unaddressed.

We propose SafeStreamingFlow , a safe streaming planner that aligns the generative process with execution (Figure 1 ).
Instead of sampling at the full trajectory level, SafeStreamingFlow integrates a learned state vector field in physical time and produces a one-step-ahead reference.
In this one-step prediction, however, the learned field tends to become a local inertial extrapolator rather than a goal-conditioned planner; we suppress this with a hierarchical state predictor that sequentially updates position then velocity.
The one-step-ahead reference is then tracked by a PD controller, and the resulting nominal control input is filtered through high order control barrier functions that minimally modify the executed input to satisfy safety constraints that were never seen during training.

Table 1 positions SafeStreamingFlow along four properties that classical and generative planners typically trade off: a cost-function-free formulation, multimodal trajectory generation, execution-time safety, and real-time streaming.
Classical planners (RRT*, A*) satisfy safety constraints by construction but require engineered costs and produce a single non-streaming plan; generative planners (Diffuser, SafeDiffuser) gain cost-function-free multimodality but offer only partial, non-streaming safety. SafeStreamingFlow is the only paradigm attaining all four.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generative models such as diffusion [ 11 ] and flow matching [ 20 ] have recently been adopted for robot policy learning and planning by modeling multi-modal state/action distributions from expert demonstrations [ 14 , 6 , 5 ] .
Diffusion-based planners synthesize long-horizon plans through iterative denoising in trajectory space, while flow matching reduces the number of sampling steps via ODE-based generation [ 31 ] .
More recently, streaming formulations have been proposed to better align generation with closed-loop control by producing incremental updates [ 26 , 16 , 13 ] ; however, these methods are primarily formulated as action policies and do not directly address the system’s execution dynamics or finite-horizon, start–goal-conditioned planning.

Safety in generative planning is commonly incorporated either through guidance [ 17 , 21 , 4 ] , such as classifier/classifier-free guidance [ 7 , 12 ] and CBF-shaped objectives [ 23 ] , or through CBF-based safety filters embedded in the sampling pipeline [ 30 , 28 ] .
While guidance-based methods generally lack formal guarantees, safety filters provide them under their modeling assumptions: Hamilton–Jacobi reachability [ 3 ] scales exponentially with the state dimension and model predictive safety filters [ 27 ] solve a horizon-length problem at every step, whereas CBF filters [ 2 , 1 ] need a single optimization per control cycle.
However, trajectory-level CBF correction can introduce computational overhead, local traps, and dynamical inconsistency.
In contrast, SafeStreamingFlow extends streaming flow to start–goal-conditioned state space planning and enforces safety constraints only at the executed step, aligning generation, execution, and safety filtering in physical time.

2026-10-05.title: Subject-Specific Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulations of Lower-Limb Exoskeleton Assistance: Metabolic and Biomechanical Effects of Joint Assistance Strategies
2026-10-05.authors: Neethan Ratnakumar , Mariya Tohfafarosha , Xianlian Zhou
2026-10-05.abstract: Lower-limb exoskeletons have made considerable progress in reducing energy expenditure during walking. However, designing optimal assistance strategies remains challenging, particularly given inter-individual variability in anthropometry and biomechanics. This study explores energy-optimal lower-limb joint-assistance strategies using predictive simulations with musculoskeletal models. Subject-specific models of six able-bodied subjects, with BMI-based muscle strength scaling, were used in predictive simulations to generate gait at self-selected walking speeds. Ideal actuators were incorporated to simulate various combinations of joint assistance at peak levels of 25 ​ Nm 25~\mathrm{Nm\par} and 50 ​ Nm 50~\mathrm{Nm\par} to examine the effects of assistance on gait and metabolic savings. The effects of each assistance configuration were assessed through cost of transport ( \acs COT), joint kinematics, muscle activations, assistive torques, and joint-level power metrics to characterize the biomechanical and energetic impacts of different assistance strategies. At 50 ​ Nm 50~\mathrm{Nm\par} , combined H+K+A (hip–knee–ankle) assistance resulted in the greatest mean COT reduction of 48.50 ± \pm 4.55%
